title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
鄉試中式程文
第一場
四書義
唐虞之際於斯為盛一名林時望
同考試官進士方批〔本房全場作者多為此題所窘獨此篇文理通暢發明有周人才惟〕
〔唐虞為盛以見才之難得深合本旨必有學之士也〕
考試官教諭邵批〔此題言周室人材之多惟唐虞之際乃盛於周獨此篇体認明白文有發揮〕
〔聖人歎才難之意粲然可見宜表而出之〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此題場中作者多不繹上文之義故不得其本旨此卷深得吾夫子論唐虞〕
〔有周人才之本意發明親切辭融理會可謂卓然不群者矣〕
===
觀聖世君臣交會之時則知人材盛於有周之世蓋人才莫盛於有周尤莫盛於〔水最切齒〕
唐虞自非唐虞之盛則周之人才孰有加於此乎請申言之帝舜紹堯致治
當是時也貞元會合光嶽氣完人才之盛藹乎都俞吁咈之間觀其平水
土者禹也明五刑者皐陶也播百穀以厚民生者非后稷乎敷五教而掌
山澤者非契與伯益乎然此五臣特舉其尤者耳他如典禮典樂則有
夷夔焉納言共工又有垂龍焉則唐虞交會之際人才之盛曠世
而莫能及也迨夫有周之時太公望著鷹揚之勇周公旦盡篤棐之
忠宣德化者召公奭也迪天威者太顛閎夭也他如率下親上則有畢
punctuated:
鄉試中式程文

第一場

四書義

「唐虞之際，於斯為盛。」一名林時望。

同考試官進士方批：〔本房全場作者，多為此題所窘，獨此篇文理通暢，發明有周人才惟〕〔唐虞為盛，以見才之難得，深合本旨，必有學之士也。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔此題言周室人材之多，惟唐虞之際乃盛於周。獨此篇体認明白，文有發揮，〕〔聖人歎才難之意，粲然可見，宜表而出之。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔此題場中作者，多不繹上文之義，故不得其本旨。此卷深得吾夫子論唐虞、〕〔有周人才之本意，發明親切，辭融理會，可謂卓然不群者矣。〕

觀聖世君臣交會之時，則知人材盛於有周之世。蓋人才莫盛於有周，尤莫盛於〔水最切齒〕唐虞；自非唐虞之盛，則周之人才，孰有加於此乎？請申言之。帝舜紹堯致治，當是時也，貞元會合，光嶽氣完，人才之盛，藹乎都俞吁咈之間。觀其平水土者，禹也；明五刑者，皐陶也；播百穀以厚民生者，非后稷乎？敷五教而掌山澤者，非契與伯益乎？然此五臣，特舉其尤者耳。他如典禮、典樂，則有夷、夔焉；納言、共工，又有垂、龍焉。則唐虞交會之際，人才之盛，曠世而莫能及也。迨夫有周之時，太公望著鷹揚之勇，周公旦盡篤棐之忠；宣德化者，召公奭也；迪天威者，太顛、閎夭也。他如率下親上，則有畢
translation_en:
Model Answers of Successful Candidates in the Provincial Examination

First Session

Expositions on the Four Books

"At the juncture of Tang and Yu, talent was more flourishing than in this dynasty." First-ranked candidate, Lin Shiwang 林時望.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [Throughout the entire examination hall, most writers in this ward were stymied by this topic. This essay alone is coherent and fluent in reasoning and style, elucidating how the talents of the Zhou dynasty were surpassed in flourishing only by those of Tang and Yu, thereby showing how difficult it is to obtain talent. It deeply accords with the original purport of the passage; he must be a scholar of true learning.]
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao 邵: [This topic speaks of the abundance of men of talent in the house of Zhou, and how only the juncture of Tang and Yu was even more flourishing than Zhou. This essay alone grasps the meaning clearly and develops the argument well. The Sage's intent in sighing over the difficulty of finding talent can be seen vividly; it deserves to be singled out for distinction.]
Comment by Examiner, Former Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Yu 余: [Most writers in the examination hall on this topic failed to trace out the meaning of the preceding text and thus missed its fundamental purport. This paper deeply grasps our Master's original intent in discussing the talents of Tang, Yu, and Zhou. Its elucidation is incisive and apt, its diction harmonious and its comprehension thorough; it may truly be called outstanding above the crowd.]

When one observes the time when sovereign and ministers met in harmony in a sagely age, one knows how men of talent flourished in the age of the Zhou dynasty. For indeed, men of talent were never more flourishing than under the Zhou, except that they were even more flourishing under [marginal note, garbled: 水最切齒, perhaps "the opening is most apt" (?)] Tang and Yu. Apart from the flourishing of Tang and Yu, what could surpass the talents of Zhou? Allow me to explain this further. When Emperor Shun 舜 succeeded Yao 堯 and brought about great order, at that time thecosmic cycles of firmness and origination converged, the vital energies of the luminaries and sacred peaks were whole and complete, and the abundance of talented men shone harmoniously amid their courtly exchanges of praise and admonition ("Alas!" "Indeed!" "Oh!" "Nay!"). Observe how he who regulated the waters and land was Yu 禹, and he who clarified the five punishments was Gao Yao 皐陶. Was it not Hou Ji 后稷 who sowed the hundred grains to enrich the people's livelihood? And were they not Xie 契 and Bo Yi 伯益 who propagated the five teachings and took charge of the mountains and marshes? Yet these five ministers are merely cited as the most outstanding among them. As for others, to preside over rituals and music there were伯夷 Bo Yi (Yi 夷) and Kui 夔; to serve as Mouthpiece (nayan) and Forester/Director of Works (gonggong) there were also Chui 垂 and Long 龍. Thus, at the juncture of Tang and Yu, the flourishing of talent was such as no other age could match. Coming down to the time of the Zhou dynasty, Taigong Wang 太公望 displayed his hawk-like martial valor, and Zhougong Dan 周公旦 (the Duke of Zhou) exhausted his staunch and supportive loyalty; he who propagated moral transformation was Shaogong Shi 召公奭 (the Duke of Shao), and those who guided forth Heaven's majesty were Taidian 太顛 and Hong Yao 閎夭. As for others, in leading those below to cleave to those above, there were Bi…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
公榮公之徒疏附先後則有散宜生南宮适之輩無非一時輔治之臣
也然不特治外者有其人至於治内又有邑姜焉夫周之人才若此盛矣
然非唐虞之際孰有盛於此乎故曰唐虞之際於斯為盛以見周室
人才雖未及乎唐虞亦非夏商所能比倫也聖人言此其所以嘆美
唐虞有周人才之盛又所以深見夫人才之難得也噫以夏商人
才言之則周室為盛〔發明至此殆無餘蘊〕以周室人才言之則唐虞為尤盛非吾夫子之
聖又孰知虞周人才之所以為盛乎抑又考之上文言舜有臣五人
而天下治武王曰予有亂臣十人孔子曰才難不其然乎至此復以是為
言以見有周人才之盛惟唐虞之際乃盛於此宜乎雍熙泰和之治
===
後世並稱也歟
辟如天地之無不持載無不覆幬辟如四時之錯行如
日月之代明萬物並育而不相害道並行而不相悖
小德川流大德敦化此天地之所以為大也
七名劉武
同考試官進士方批〔此題子思子始以天地喻夫子終謂夫子即天地場中作者上下文意多不相属唯此〕
〔篇理明詞順体貼一章之旨發越詳盡故表而出之〕
考試官教諭邵批〔中庸題子思以天地造化喻夫子之德此篇深合題意而又有發越置之前列允恊輿論〕
考試官前侍講余批〔辭旨詳切結語尤妙〕
punctuated:
公、榮公之徒；疏附先後，則有散宜生、南宮适之輩，無非一時輔治之臣也。然不特治外者有其人，至於治内，又有邑姜焉。夫周之人才若此盛矣，然非唐虞之際，孰有盛於此乎？故曰：「唐虞之際，於斯為盛。」以見周室人才，雖未及乎唐虞，亦非夏、商所能比倫也。聖人言此，其所以嘆美唐虞、有周人才之盛，又所以深見夫人才之難得也。噫！以夏、商人才言之，則周室為盛；〔發明至此，殆無餘蘊。〕以周室人才言之，則唐虞為尤盛。非吾夫子之聖，又孰知虞、周人才之所以為盛乎？抑又考之上文，言「舜有臣五人而天下治」，武王曰「予有亂臣十人」，孔子曰：「才難，不其然乎？」至此復以是為言，以見有周人才之盛，惟唐虞之際乃盛於此。宜乎雍熙泰和之治，後世並稱也歟！

「辟如天地之無不持載，無不覆幬；辟如四時之錯行，如日月之代明。萬物並育而不相害，道並行而不相悖。小德川流，大德敦化，此天地之所以為大也。」
七名劉武。
同考試官進士方批：〔此題子思子始以天地喻夫子，終謂夫子即天地。場中作者上下文意多不相属，唯此篇理明詞順，体貼一章之旨，發越詳盡，故表而出之。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔《中庸》題子思以天地造化喻夫子之德，此篇深合題意，而又有發越，置之前列，允恊輿論。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔辭旨詳切，結語尤妙。〕
translation_en:
… such followers as the Duke of Bi (Bi Gong 畢公) and the Duke of Rong (Rong Gong 榮公); and as for those who drew the distant near and attended before and behind, there were the likes of San Yisheng 散宜生 and Nangong Kuo 南宮适—every one of them a minister who assisted in governing in that era. Yet not only were there the right men for governing external affairs; when it came to governing the inner palace, there was also Yi Jiang 邑姜. Now, the men of talent of the Zhou were as flourishing as this; yet apart from the transition between Yao (Tang 唐) and Shun (Yu 虞), what era was more flourishing than this? Therefore it is said: "From the transition between Yao and Shun, it is in this that talent is most flourishing"—to show that although the men of talent of the House of Zhou did not reach those of Yao and Shun, neither could the Xia and Shang dynasties compare with them. By saying this, the Sage sighed in admiration at the flourishing of talent under Yao, Shun, and the Zhou, and also deeply revealed how difficult it is to obtain men of talent. Alas! Speaking in terms of the talent of the Xia and Shang, the House of Zhou was flourishing; 〔The exposition reaches this point, leaving almost nothing unexpressed.〕 speaking in terms of the talent of the House of Zhou, the age of Yao and Shun was even more flourishing. Were it not for the sageliness of our Master, who would know why the men of talent of Shun and of Zhou were so flourishing? Moreover, if we examine the preceding text, it says, "Shun had five ministers and the Empire was well governed," King Wu (Wu Wang 武王) said, "I have ten ministers of governance," and Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) said, "'Talent is difficult to find'—is it not so?" Coming to this point, he again spoke in these terms to show that as for the flourishing of talent in the Zhou, only at the transition between Yao and Shun was it more flourishing than this. Is it not fitting that their reigns of harmonious peace and supreme concord are praised together by later generations!

"He may be compared to heaven and earth in their supporting and containing, their overshadowing and covering all things; he may be compared to the four seasons in their alternating progress, and to the sun and moon in their successive shining. All things are nourished together without their injuring one another; courses are pursued together without their colliding with one another. Smaller energies flow like river currents; greater energies transform abundantly. It is this that makes heaven and earth so great."
Seventh-ranked: Liu Wu 劉武.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: 〔In this topic, Master Zisi 子思子 begins by using heaven and earth as a metaphor for the Master, and ends by saying that the Master is himself heaven and earth. Among the writers in the examination hall, the meaning of the preceding and following parts mostly failed to connect; only this essay is clear in principle and smooth in diction, closely grasping the purport of the entire chapter and developing it thoroughly and in full detail. Therefore I have singled it out for distinction.〕
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao 邵: 〔In this Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸) topic, Zisi uses the creative transformations of heaven and earth as a metaphor for the Master's virtue. This essay deeply conforms to the meaning of the topic and also shows spirited development; placing it in the front ranks truly accords with public opinion.〕
Comment by Examiner, former Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Yu 余: 〔Its diction and purport are detailed and incisive, and the concluding words are especially fine.〕

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
大賢言聖德之盛同乎造化之妙復即天地之道以明聖德之大夫聖人
之德未易言也苟不即天地造化之道以明之又何以見聖德之所以為大
乎今夫夫子之德廣博深厚而天下之道無一之不該非如地之博厚載華
岳而不重振河海而不洩者乎夫子之德高大光明而天下之理無一之或
遺豈不猶天之高明日月星辰繫焉萬物覆焉者乎持載如地聖人博厚
之至也覆幬如天聖人高明之至也至於仕止久速之各當其可則與春夏秋
冬之迭運者無或殊仁義禮智之時出者則與日月代明乎晝夜者無以異
錯行如四時代明如日月此聖人悠久之至也然以造化喻聖人固足以見聖
德之大不即天地之大又何以見聖德之所以為大乎是故天覆地載飛潜
===
蠢動各正性命此萬物之並育未嘗或相害也四時日月錯行代明循
環無巳此道之並行未嘗或相悖也所以不害不悖者小德之川流所
以並育並行者大德之敦化小德者全體之分大德者萬殊之本川
流者如川之流脉絡分明而往不息萬物各具一太極也敦化者敦
厚其化根本盛大而出無窮萬物統體一太極也此天地之所以為
大也知天地之大則聖人之為大可知觀其渾然一理四端五典無不統於
其間則與並育並行者同一機泛應曲當萬物萬事莫不由是而行
則與不害不悖者無二致泛應曲當亦小德之川流一理渾然亦大德之
敦化也吁大哉天地之道乎至哉聖人之德乎非天地之道固不足以明聖
punctuated: 大賢言聖德之盛同乎造化之妙，復即天地之道以明聖德之大。夫聖人之德，未易言也；苟不即天地造化之道以明之，又何以見聖德之所以為大乎？今夫夫子之德，廣博深厚，而天下之道無一之不該，非如地之博厚，載華岳而不重，振河海而不洩者乎？夫子之德，高大光明，而天下之理無一之或遺，豈不猶天之高明，日月星辰繫焉，萬物覆焉者乎？持載如地，聖人博厚之至也；覆幬如天，聖人高明之至也。至於仕止久速之各當其可，則與春夏秋冬之迭運者無或殊；仁義禮智之時出者，則與日月代明乎晝夜者無以異。錯行如四時，代明如日月，此聖人悠久之至也。然以造化喻聖人，固足以見聖德之大；不即天地之大，又何以見聖德之所以為大乎？是故天覆地載，飛潜蠢動各正性命，此萬物之並育，未嘗或相害也；四時日月，錯行代明，循環無巳，此道之並行，未嘗或相悖也。所以不害不悖者，小德之川流；所以並育並行者，大德之敦化。小德者，全體之分；大德者，萬殊之本。川流者，如川之流，脉絡分明而往不息，萬物各具一太極也；敦化者，敦厚其化，根本盛大而出無窮，萬物統體一太極也。此天地之所以為大也。知天地之大，則聖人之為大可知。觀其渾然一理，四端五典無不統於其間，則與並育並行者同一機；泛應曲當，萬物萬事莫不由是而行，則與不害不悖者無二致。泛應曲當，亦小德之川流；一理渾然，亦大德之敦化也。吁！大哉天地之道乎！至哉聖人之德乎！非天地之道，固不足以明聖
translation_en: The great worthy [Zisi 子思] speaks of the flourishing of the sage's virtue as being identical to the subtlety of the creative transformations of nature, and then draws directly upon the Way of heaven and earth to illuminate the greatness of the sage's virtue. Now, the virtue of the sage is not easy to speak of; if one does not draw directly upon the Way of the creative transformations of heaven and earth to illuminate it, how else could one see why the sage's virtue is great? Now, the virtue of the Master [Confucius] is vast, broad, deep, and thick, such that not a single Way in the world is unincompassed by it—is this not like the breadth and thickness of the earth, which supports Mount Hua and the other sacred peaks without feeling their weight, and contains the rivers and seas without letting them leak away? The virtue of the Master is lofty, great, bright, and radiant, such that not a single principle in the world is left out by it—is this not like the loftiness and brightness of heaven, from which the sun, moon, and stars are suspended, and by which the myriad things are sheltered? Supporting and bearing up like the earth is the ultimate breadth and thickness of the sage; covering and sheltering like heaven is the ultimate loftiness and brightness of the sage. As for taking office or declining it, remaining long or departing quickly, each according to what is fitting, this is no different from the alternating revolutions of spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and as for benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom issuing forth at their proper times, this is no different from the sun and moon alternating in brightness through day and night. Alternating in their courses like the four seasons and alternating in brightness like the sun and moon—this is the ultimate endurance of the sage. Yet while comparing the sage to the creative transformations is indeed sufficient to show the greatness of the sage's virtue, without drawing directly upon the greatness of heaven and earth, how could one see why the sage's virtue is great? Therefore, heaven covers and earth supports, and creatures that fly, dive, wriggle, and move each rectify their allotted nature and destiny: this is the myriad things being nourished together without ever harming one another. The four seasons and the sun and moon alternate in their courses and alternate in brightness, revolving in an endless cycle: this is their ways proceeding together without ever coming into conflict with one another. That by which they do not harm or conflict with one another is the lesser virtues flowing like river currents; that by which they are nourished together and proceed together is the great virtue thickening the transformations. The lesser virtues are the divisions of the whole substance; the great virtue is the root of the myriad differentiations. "Flowing like river currents" means being like the flow of rivers, with distinct channels moving onward without cease, wherein each of the myriad things possesses a Supreme Ultimate (Taiji 太極) of its own; "thickening the transformations" means making the transformations generous and thick, with a flourishing and great root issuing forth inexhaustibly, wherein the myriad things as a unified whole share one Supreme Ultimate. This is why heaven and earth are great. Once one knows the greatness of heaven and earth, the greatness of the sage can be known. When we observe how in his seamless unity of a single principle, the Four Beginnings and Five Canons are all encompassed within it, this shares the very same mechanism as being nourished together and proceeding together; and when in his broad responses and intricate appropriateness, none of the myriad things or myriad affairs fails to proceed from this, it is no different in effect from not harming and not conflicting with one another. Broad responses and intricate appropriateness are likewise the lesser virtues flowing like river currents; the seamless unity of a single principle is likewise the great virtue thickening the transformations. Ah! Great indeed is the Way of heaven and earth! Ultimate indeed is the virtue of the sage! Without the Way of heaven and earth, it would truly be insufficient to illuminate the sage's…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
人之盛德非聖人之德之盛又烏足以擬諸天地哉雖然天能覆而不能載地
能載而不能覆春夏之生長秋冬之斂藏日明乎晝月明乎夜各得其一偏
而聖人之德則會夫陰陽之全然則夫子其太極乎
易六名林渭
聖人立象以盡意設卦以盡情偽繫辭焉以盡其言變而通
之以盡利鼓之舞之以盡神
考試官教諭邵批〔立象設卦繫辭三盡字聖人作易之事变通鼓舞二盡字聖人用易之事此篇以經註經能〕
〔節節發明非熟於是經者不能也〕
考試官前侍講余批此篇行文詳整析理明净
===
知聖人備易書以具衆理當知聖人妙易道以應萬事夫大易之作固將以
前民用也自非聖人備物致用之功則易書之設天下之理為有限易道之應天下
之事為有窮矣自今觀之易之未作象卦言辭之未立而意言情偽曷從而
盡之變通鼓舞之未見而日用神利又曷從而盡之是則易書之作不能不
有賴於聖人焉聖人作易於是畫一竒以象陽畫一耦以象陰竒而加竒耦而加耦
以立太陰太陽之象竒而加耦耦而加竒以立少陰少陽之象天地水火乾坤坎
離之象立焉雷風山澤而震巽艮兌之象立焉聖人之意寧不於此而盡乎
泰卦既設則有以見內君子外小人之情否卦既設則有以見內小人外君
子之偽七日來復朋來無咎其情於復見之一陰方長勿用取女其偽於
punctuated:
人之盛德；非聖人之德之盛，又烏足以擬諸天地哉？雖然，天能覆而不能載，地能載而不能覆；春夏之生長，秋冬之斂藏；日明乎晝，月明乎夜，各得其一偏，而聖人之德則會夫陰陽之全。然則夫子其太極乎！

易：六名林渭。
「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭焉以盡其言，變而通之以盡利，鼓之舞之以盡神。」
考試官教諭邵批：〔立象、設卦、繫辭三「盡」字，聖人作《易》之事；变通、鼓舞二「盡」字，聖人用《易》之事。此篇以經註經，能〕〔節節發明，非熟於是經者不能也。〕
考試官前侍講余批：此篇行文詳整，析理明净。

知聖人備《易》書以具衆理，當知聖人妙《易》道以應萬事。夫大《易》之作，固將以前民用也。自非聖人備物致用之功，則《易》書之設，天下之理為有限；《易》道之應，天下之事為有窮矣。自今觀之，《易》之未作，象、卦、言、辭之未立，而意、言、情、偽曷從而盡之？變通、鼓舞之未見，而日用神、利又曷從而盡之？是則《易》書之作，不能不有賴於聖人焉。聖人作《易》，於是畫一竒以象陽，畫一耦以象陰；竒而加竒，耦而加耦，以立太陰、太陽之象；竒而加耦，耦而加竒，以立少陰、少陽之象。天、地、水、火，乾、坤、坎、離之象立焉；雷、風、山、澤，而震、巽、艮、兌之象立焉。聖人之意，寧不於此而盡乎？《泰》卦既設，則有以見「內君子外小人」之情；《否》卦既設，則有以見「內小人外君子」之偽。「七日來復」、「朋來無咎」，其情於《復》見之；一陰方長、「勿用取女」，其偽於
translation_en:
…the flourishing virtue of the sage; and were it not for the flourishing of the sage's virtue, how could he be compared to Heaven and Earth? Even so, Heaven can cover from above but cannot sustain from below, while Earth can sustain from below but cannot cover from above; spring and summer give birth and growth, while autumn and winter gather and store; the sun shines by day, while the moon shines by night—each attains only one partial aspect, whereas the virtue of the sage unites the entirety of yin and yang. If so, is not the Master himself the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji)?

Book of Changes (Yi): Sixth-ranked, Lin Wei 林渭.
"The sages established the images in order to express their ideas exhaustively; they set up the hexagrams in order to treat the true and false exhaustively; they appended the judgements in order to speak their words exhaustively; they changed and adapted them in order to secure the benefit exhaustively; they drummed and danced them in order to realize the spirit-like power exhaustively."
Comment by Examiner Instructor Shao: [The three occurrences of the word "exhaustively" (jin) with "establishing images," "setting up hexagrams," and "appending judgements" refer to the sages' work of creating the Book of Changes; the two occurrences of the word "exhaustively" with "changing and adapting" and "drumming and dancing" refer to the sages' work of applying the Book of Changes. This essay uses the Classic to annotate the Classic and is able to] [elucidate it step by step; no one who is not thoroughly versed in this Classic could have written it.]
Comment by Examiner Former Expositor-in-waiting Yu: This essay's composition is detailed and well-ordered, and its analysis of principles is clear and pure.

When one understands that the sages perfected the Book of Changes to encompass the multitude of principles, one ought also to understand that the sages wondrously enacted the Way of the Changes to respond to the myriad affairs. Now, the creation of the Great Changes was assuredly intended to prepare the way for the people's practical use. Without the achievement of the sages in providing things for practical application, in the setting up of the Book of Changes, the principles of the world would have remained limited, and in the responsiveness of the Way of the Changes, the affairs of the world would have been exhausted. Looking at it today, before the Changes was created and before the images, hexagrams, words, and judgements were established, how could ideas, words, the true, and the false be exhaustively expressed? Before changing, adapting, drumming, and dancing were manifested, how could the spirit-like power and benefit of daily use be exhaustively realized? Thus, the creation of the Book of Changes could not but depend upon the sages. When the sages created the Changes, they thereupon drew a single undivided line to symbolize yang, and drew a single divided line to symbolize yin; to an undivided line they added another undivided line, and to a divided line they added another divided line, in order to establish the images of Greater Yin and Greater Yang; to an undivided line they added a divided line, and to a divided line they added an undivided line, in order to establish the images of Lesser Yin and Lesser Yang. For heaven, earth, water, and fire, the images of the trigrams Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li were established; for thunder, wind, mountain, and marsh, the images of the trigrams Zhen, Xun, Gen, and Dui were established. Were not the ideas of the sages exhaustively expressed herein? Once the hexagram Tai (Peace) was set up, there was a means to see the true condition of "the gentleman within and the petty man without"; once the hexagram Pi (Obstruction) was set up, there was a means to see the false condition of "the petty man within and the gentleman without." title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
始見之則事之情偽寧不於此而盡乎乾之彖則繫以元亨利貞之辭乾之
初九則繫以潜龍勿用之辭坤之彖則繫以元亨利牝馬之貞坤之初六則繫
以履霜堅氷至之辭聖人之言又寧不於此而盡之乎象卦言辭之既立則易
書備而天下之理皆在其中矣易書既備不可無變通鼓舞之功也變通趣
時因時制宜此利之所在也而聖人則有以盡其利焉如卦至於蹇難之時吾
則變蹇為解而通解之道焉卦至於否塞之極吾則變否為泰而通泰之
道焉而凡窮則變變則通皆所以盡其利也利用出入民咸用之此神之所
在也而聖人則有以盡其神焉如屯難之世宜立君也吾則以利建侯之辭以
鼓舞之需待之道可濟險也吾則以利渉大川之辭以鼓舞之凡神而化之
===
使民宜之皆所以盡其神也變通鼓舞之既見而易道周矣易道之周易書
之備尤可見矣愚故曰云云者此也抑考之下文有曰極天下之賾者存乎卦
鼓天下之動者存乎辭即此盡意盡情偽盡言之意也又曰化而裁之存乎
變推而行之存乎通即此盡利盡神之道也讀者合而觀之則知聖人教人
之㫖益深切而著明矣
觀變於陰陽而立卦發揮於剛柔而生爻和順於道德而理
於義窮理盡性以至於命 十名陳康
考試官教諭邵 批〔此篇理明而辭暢言簡而意盡龍用朱子本義為講尤合經㫖必有本之士也〕
考試官前侍講余 批〔四書本經皆平順此篇不冗不泛文辭簡净宜在所選〕
punctuated:
始見之，則事之情偽寧不於此而盡乎？乾之彖，則繫以「元亨利貞」之辭；乾之初九，則繫以「潜龍勿用」之辭；坤之彖，則繫以「元亨利牝馬之貞」；坤之初六，則繫以「履霜堅氷至」之辭，聖人之言又寧不於此而盡之乎？象、卦、言、辭之既立，則《易》書備而天下之理皆在其中矣。《易》書既備，不可無變通鼓舞之功也。變通趣時，因時制宜，此利之所在也，而聖人則有以盡其利焉。如卦至於蹇難之時，吾則變蹇為解，而通解之道焉；卦至於否塞之極，吾則變否為泰，而通泰之道焉。而凡窮則變，變則通，皆所以盡其利也。利用出入，民咸用之，此神之所在也，而聖人則有以盡其神焉。如屯難之世，宜立君也，吾則以「利建侯」之辭以鼓舞之；需待之道，可濟險也，吾則以「利渉大川」之辭以鼓舞之。凡神而化之，使民宜之，皆所以盡其神也。變通鼓舞之既見，而《易》道周矣。《易》道之周，《易》書之備，尤可見矣。愚故曰云云者，此也。抑考之下文有曰：「極天下之賾者存乎卦，鼓天下之動者存乎辭。」即此盡意、盡情偽、盡言之意也。又曰：「化而裁之存乎變，推而行之存乎通。」即此盡利、盡神之道也。讀者合而觀之，則知聖人教人之㫖，益深切而著明矣。
「觀變於陰陽而立卦，發揮於剛柔而生爻，和順於道德而理於義，窮理盡性以至於命。」十名陳康
考試官教諭邵 批〔此篇理明而辭暢，言簡而意盡，龍用朱子《本義》為講，尤合經㫖，必有本之士也。〕
考試官前侍講余 批〔《四書》本經皆平順，此篇不冗不泛，文辭簡净，宜在所選。〕
translation_en:
…is seen in the Gou [? 始 for 姤] hexagram—so is the genuine or spurious nature of affairs not fully exhausted here? To the Judgment (tuan) of the Qian hexagram were appended the words "supreme success,貞 [beneficial to be persevering]"; to the Initial Nine line of Qian were appended the words "submerged dragon, do not act"; to the Judgment of the Kun hexagram were appended the words "supreme success, beneficial through the perseverance of a mare"; and to the Initial Six line of Kun were appended the words "treading on hoarfrost, solid ice will come"—so are the words of the sages not also fully exhausted in this? Once images, hexagrams, words, and appended phrases were established, the Book of Changes was complete, and all principles under heaven were contained within it. Once the Book of Changes was complete, it could not lack the efficacy of alternation, transformation, and inspiring action. Alternating and transforming to meet the times, and adapting measures to the moment—this is where benefit lies, and the sages had the means to fully exhaust its benefit. For instance, when a hexagram reaches a time of obstruction and difficulty (Jian), we transform Obstruction (Jian) into Deliverance (Jie) and carry through the way of Deliverance; when a hexagram reaches the extreme of stagnation (Pi), we transform Stagnation (Pi) into Peace (Tai) and carry through the way of Peace. In general, whenever things reach an impasse they change, and once changed they pass through smoothly—all of this is how they fully exhaust its benefit. Making use of it in going out and coming in, so that the common people all employ it—this is where the inscrutable spirit lies, and the sages had the means to fully exhaust its spirit. For instance, in an age of nascent difficulty (Zhun), when it is fitting to establish a ruler, we inspire them to action with the phrase "beneficial to establish a feudal lord"; when the way of waiting (Xu) can carry one across danger, we inspire them to action with the phrase "beneficial to cross the great river." In general, spiritually transforming things so as to make them fitting for the people—all of this is how they fully exhaust its spirit. Once alternation, transformation, and inspiring action are manifest, the Way of the Changes is comprehensive. Through the comprehensiveness of the Way of the Changes, the completeness of the Book of Changes can be seen all the more clearly. This is why I stated what I did at the beginning. Furthermore, if we examine the text below, it says: "Exploring the most complex phenomena under heaven depends on the hexagrams; inspiring all movements under heaven depends on the appended phrases." This expresses the very meaning of exhausting ideas, exhausting the genuine and the spurious, and exhausting words. It also says: "Transforming and tailoring it depends on alternation; extending and practicing it depends on carrying through." This is the very way of exhausting benefit and exhausting the spirit. If the reader combines and contemplates these passages together, it will be known that the sages' purpose in instructing people is all the more profound, earnest, and clearly manifest.

"They observed the changes in yin and yang and established the hexagrams; they gave full play to the firm and the yielding and generated the lines; they harmonized and complied with the Way and its Virtue and ordered what is right; they exhausted principle and fulfilled nature, so as to arrive at destiny."
10th-ranked: Chen Kang 陳康.

Comment by Examiner Instructor Shao 邵: 〔In this essay the reasoning is clear and the phrasing fluent; the words are concise yet the meaning is fully expressed. Able [? 龍 for 能] to use Master Zhu's [Zhu Xi 朱熹] Original Meaning (Benyi) for its exposition, it especially accords with the classic's purport. He must be a scholar of solid foundation.〕
Comment by Examiner Former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余: 〔His essays on the Four Books and his specialized classic are all smooth and coherent. This piece is neither prolix nor vague; its diction is concise and clean. He deserves to be among those selected.〕

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
觀聖人之作易既有以備至著之象尤有以盡至微之理夫卦爻者象之至著者
也道德義理性命者理之至微者也非聖人作易之功又焉能備夫象而盡乎
理哉自今觀之陰陽者天地之氣也聖人觀變於陽而立乾坎艮震之卦觀變
於陰而立巽离坤兌之卦剛柔者陰陽之質也聖人發揮乎剛而生竒之爻
發揮於柔而生耦之爻卦與爻有形之可擬也豈非聖人作易有以備至著
之象乎若夫道德者事理之當然人心之所以為德者也義者事之宜也於
道德則和順從容無所乖逆統言之也於義則隨事得其條理析言之也
理者事物之理性者人之所受於天命者天之所賦於人窮天下之理盡人物
之性則與天道昭合而無間焉此聖人作易之極功也夫道德義理性命無
===
迹之可見也又非聖人作易有以盡至微之理乎抑又論之易之為書貫通
乎三才者也有天道焉有地道焉有人道焉所謂天道非卦之立於陰陽乎
所謂地道非爻之生於剛柔乎所謂人道又非和順於道德而理於義窮
理盡性以至於命之謂乎學易君子其可不盡心歟
書〔一名林特望〕
詢于四岳闢四門明四目達四聰咨十有二牧曰食哉惟時
同考試官進士方批〔四書經義筆力滂沛文詞豐贍此篇發越帝舜詢咨岳牧之意虞廷雍容氣象藹然可見〕
〔終以圖治不自足之心結之尤佳後二場論策俱優誠有本有識之士也宜冠本經〕
考試官教諭邵批〔此篇以內臣外臣分講說理俱到聖人圖治之心藹然見於言意之表〕
punctuated:
觀聖人之作《易》，既有以備至著之象，尤有以盡至微之理。夫卦爻者，象之至著者也；道德、義理、性命者，理之至微者也。非聖人作《易》之功，又焉能備夫象而盡乎理哉？自今觀之，陰陽者，天地之氣也。聖人觀變於陽，而立乾、坎、艮、震之卦；觀變於陰，而立巽、离、坤、兌之卦。剛柔者，陰陽之質也。聖人發揮乎剛，而生竒之爻；發揮於柔，而生耦之爻。卦與爻，有形之可擬也，豈非聖人作《易》有以備至著之象乎？若夫道德者，事理之當然，人心之所以為德者也；義者，事之宜也。於道德則和順從容，無所乖逆，統言之也；於義則隨事得其條理，析言之也。理者，事物之理；性者，人之所受於天；命者，天之所賦於人。窮天下之理，盡人物之性，則與天道昭合而無間焉，此聖人作《易》之極功也。夫道德、義理、性命，無迹之可見也，又非聖人作《易》有以盡至微之理乎？抑又論之，《易》之為書，貫通乎三才者也。有天道焉，有地道焉，有人道焉。所謂天道，非卦之立於陰陽乎？所謂地道，非爻之生於剛柔乎？所謂人道，又非「和順於道德而理於義，窮理盡性以至於命」之謂乎？學《易》君子，其可不盡心歟？

《書》〔一名林特望〕
「詢于四岳，闢四門，明四目，達四聰。咨十有二牧，曰：『食哉惟時！』」
同考試官進士方批：〔四書、經義筆力滂沛，文詞豐贍。此篇發越帝舜詢咨岳牧之意，虞廷雍容氣象藹然可見；終以圖治不自足之心結之，尤佳。後二場論、策俱優，誠有本有識之士也，宜冠本經。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔此篇以內臣、外臣分講，說理俱到，聖人圖治之心，藹然見於言意之表。〕
translation_en:
Observing how the sages created the Book of Changes (Yi), we see that not only did they thereby provide in full the most manifest of emblems, they even more so exhausted the most subtle of principles. For the hexagrams and lines are the most manifest of emblems, while the Way and virtue, rightness and principle, human nature and the Mandate are the most subtle of principles. Were it not for the achievement of the sages in creating the Book of Changes, how could one provide in full the emblems and exhaust the principles? Viewed from the present: yin and yang are the vital forces of Heaven and Earth. The sages observed the transformations in yang and established the trigrams Qian, Kan, Gen, and Zhen; they observed the transformations in yin and established the trigrams Xun, Li, Kun, and Dui. The firm and the yielding are the substantial natures of yin and yang. The sages drew out the firm and generated the undivided lines; they drew out the yielding and generated the divided lines. Hexagrams and lines have forms that can be simulated—is this not how the sages, in creating the Book of Changes, had the means to provide in full the most manifest of emblems? As for the Way and virtue, they are what is naturally right in the principles of affairs and that whereby the human mind constitutes virtue; rightness is what is appropriate in affairs. With respect to the Way and virtue, to be harmonious, compliant, and unhurried, without anything contrary or refractory—this is to speak of it as a whole; with respect to rightness, to attain its orderly pattern in accordance with each affair—this is to speak of it analytically. Principle is the principle of affairs and things; nature is what man receives from Heaven; the Mandate is what Heaven endows in man. To investigate to the utmost the principles of all under Heaven and to fulfill completely the natures of men and things, so as to be in luminous accord with the Way of Heaven without the slightest gap—this is the ultimate achievement of the sages in creating the Book of Changes. Now the Way and virtue, rightness and principle, human nature and the Mandate have no trace that can be seen—is this not, moreover, how the sages, in creating the Book of Changes, had the means to exhaust the most subtle of principles? Furthermore, if we discuss it further, the Book of Changes as a book penetrates through the Three Powers. There is the Way of Heaven therein, there is the Way of Earth therein, and there is the Way of Man therein. What is called the Way of Heaven—is it not the establishment of the hexagrams from yin and yang? What is called the Way of Earth—is it not the generation of the lines from the firm and the yielding? And what is called the Way of Man—is it not what is meant by "harmonizing with and obeying the Way and its virtue and ordering according to rightness, investigating principle to the utmost and fulfilling nature completely so as to arrive at the Mandate"? How could the noble man who studies the Book of Changes fail to devote his whole mind to it?

Book of Documents (Shu) 〔1st place, Lin Tewang 林特望〕
"He consulted the Four Mountains, to throw open the doors of the four quarters, to see clearly with the eyes of the four quarters, and to hear distinctly with the ears of the four quarters. He consulted the Twelve Pastors, saying: 'Food! Everything depends on the seasons!'"
Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang comments: 〔His essays on the Four Books and the Classics are surging in brushwork and rich in diction. This essay brings out the meaning of Emperor Shun's consulting the Four Mountains and the Pastors, so that the poised and harmonious atmosphere of the court of Yu can be benignly seen; and concluding at the end with a mind intent on good governance without self-satisfaction is especially fine. In the latter two sessions, his discourses and policy essays are all excellent. Truly a scholar of substance and insight, he deserves to head the list in his Classic.〕
Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao comments: 〔This essay expounds the topic by dividing it between inner ministers and outer ministers, and its explanation of principle is thorough throughout. The sage's mind intent on seeking good governance benignly appears beyond the words and ideas.〕

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
考試官前侍講余批〔初場七篇皆豐整純潔無疵可指此篇於求賢養民之意尤有發越當時明良交會之盛可以〕
想見於千載之上後場俱稱宜在首選
觀聖君謀治於內臣欲其開賢路而廣視聽當觀聖君咨治於外臣欲其足民
食而重農時蓋謀治莫先於四岳而養民尤切於州牧聖君於即位之初安
得不舉其職而詢命之哉昔者帝舜謀治於四岳意蓋若曰圖治莫急於
用賢材而進賢莫善於開賢路彼其蘊經邦濟世之材者孰無願仕之心
佩仁義道德之懿者孰無帝臣之願但衒玉求售賢才所耻爾為四岳者
可不闢四門以來天下之賢俊乎必也旁求俊乂使空谷無白駒之歎可也敷
求哲人俾考槃無碩人之歌可也四門既闢而賢俊登庸矣彼鰥寡孤獨者
===
又孰不欲得其生疲癃殘疾者孰不欲遂其願但民情幽遠未易上達爾
為四岳者可不明目達聰以决天下之壅蔽乎必也視遠惟明使四方之目為
己之目而生民之休戚無不周知可也聽德惟聰使四方之聰為己之聰而天下
之利病無不上達可也夫既有以來賢俊而决壅蔽則四岳之職無不盡矣而
養民之政又豈可緩乎於是又命十二州之牧以養夫民焉蓋州牧以養民為
職養民之道以足食為先爾為州牧者必使林生總聚之民飢者得食
寒者得衣有含哺鼓腹之樂無艱鮮阻飢之憂而民食無不足可也然
足食之道不在乎他惟在乎不違農時也爾欲足民之食必也勿奪其耕耘之
時使民得盡力於畝畝不失其歛穫之候使民得務本於農工凡有興作不違
punctuated:
考試官前侍講余批：〔初場七篇皆豐整純潔，無疵可指。此篇於求賢養民之意，尤有發越。當時明良交會之盛，可以〕想見於千載之上。後場俱稱，宜在首選。

觀聖君謀治於內臣，欲其開賢路而廣視聽；當觀聖君咨治於外臣，欲其足民食而重農時。蓋謀治莫先於四岳，而養民尤切於州牧。聖君於即位之初，安得不舉其職而詢命之哉？昔者帝舜謀治於四岳，意蓋若曰：「圖治莫急於用賢材，而進賢莫善於開賢路。彼其蘊經邦濟世之材者，孰無願仕之心？佩仁義道德之懿者，孰無帝臣之願？但衒玉求售，賢才所耻。爾為四岳者，可不闢四門以來天下之賢俊乎？必也旁求俊乂，使空谷無《白駒》之歎可也；敷求哲人，俾考槃無《碩人》之歌可也。四門既闢，而賢俊登庸矣。彼鰥寡孤獨者，又孰不欲得其生？疲癃殘疾者，孰不欲遂其願？但民情幽遠，未易上達。爾為四岳者，可不明目達聰以决天下之壅蔽乎？必也視遠惟明，使四方之目為己之目，而生民之休戚無不周知可也；聽德惟聰，使四方之聰為己之聰，而天下之利病無不上達可也。」夫既有以來賢俊而决壅蔽，則四岳之職無不盡矣，而養民之政又豈可緩乎？於是又命十二州之牧以養夫民焉。蓋州牧以養民為職，養民之道以足食為先。「爾為州牧者，必使林生總聚之民，飢者得食，寒者得衣，有含哺鼓腹之樂，無艱鮮阻飢之憂，而民食無不足可也。然足食之道不在乎他，惟在乎不違農時也。爾欲足民之食，必也勿奪其耕耘之時，使民得盡力於畝畝；不失其歛穫之候，使民得務本於農工。凡有興作，不違
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Yu, former Expositor-in-Waiting: [All seven essays of the first session are rich, well-structured, pure, and spotless, with no flaws to point out. This essay is especially expressive regarding the meaning of seeking the worthy and nourishing the people. The flourishing harmony between enlightened ruler and worthy ministers in those days can be] envisioned across a thousand years. The subsequent sessions all match in quality; he ought to be placed first among those selected.

When we observe the sage ruler taking counsel on governance with his inner ministers, we see that he wished them to open the path for the worthy and broaden his sight and hearing; we should also observe the sage ruler consulting on governance with his outer ministers, wishing them to make the people's food sufficient and value the agricultural seasons. Indeed, in taking counsel on governance nothing comes before the Four Peaks, and in nourishing the people nothing is more urgent than the Pastors of the provinces. When the sage ruler first ascended the throne, how could he not raise up their duties and consult and charge them?

In ancient times, Emperor Shun took counsel on governance with the Four Peaks, his meaning being as if to say: "In planning for governance, nothing is more urgent than employing worthy talents, and in advancing the worthy, nothing is better than opening the path for the worthy. Among those who harbor the talent to order the state and succor the world, who does not have the heart to wish to serve in office? Among those who wear at their belt the excellence of benevolence, righteousness, the Way, and virtue, who does not have the wish to be a minister to the Emperor? Yet to show off one's jade to seek a sale is what worthy talents are ashamed of. You who serve as the Four Peaks, how can you not throw open the gates of the four quarters to draw in the worthy and eminent men of the realm? You must search far and wide for the eminent and able, so that in the empty valleys there is no sighing over the 'White Colt' (Baiju); you must broadly seek out wise men, so that in secluded retreats there is no singing of the 'Stalwart Man' (Shiren). Once the four gates are thrown open, the worthy and eminent will be elevated and employed. And as for those who areers, widows, orphans, and childless, who among them does not wish to sustain their life? Among the exhausted, decrepit, crippled, and infirm, who does not wish to fulfill their desires? Yet the circumstances of the people are obscure and distant, and not easily communicated upward. You who serve as the Four Peaks, how can you not clarify my sight and extend my hearing in order to clear away the obstructions and concealments in the realm? You must see far with clarity, making the eyes of the four quarters my own eyes, so that the joys and sorrows of the common people are all thoroughly known; you must listen to virtue with acuity, making the ears of the four quarters my own ears, so that the benefits and ills of the realm are all communicated upward."

Now, once there is the means to draw in the worthy and eminent and to clear away obstructions and concealments, the duties of the Four Peaks are completely fulfilled. Yet how could the administration of nourishing the people be delayed? Thereupon he also charged the Pastors of the twelve provinces to nourish the people. Indeed, the Pastors of the provinces take nourishing the people as their duty, and in the way of nourishing the people, making food sufficient comes first. "You who serve as Pastors of the provinces must ensure that among the multitudes of people gathered like a forest, the hungry obtain food and the cold obtain clothing, having the joy of holding food in their mouths and drumming their bellies, without the worry of scarcity and famine, so that the people's food is never insufficient. Yet the way to make food sufficient lies in nothing else than not violating the agricultural seasons. If you wish to make the people's food sufficient, you must not rob them of their times for plowing and weeding, allowing the people to exert their full strength in the fields; and you must not miss the periods for harvesting and gathering, allowing the people to attend to the fundamental occupation of farming. Whenever there are public works, do not violate…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
此時至冬乃役之則穀不可勝食而民食足矣夫既重農時以足民食則州
牧之職無不修矣噫四岳之職舉則内治有其人州牧之職盡則外治有其
人内外兼舉而治道無餘蘊矣抑又考之帝舜之時野無遺賢人路非不
開也鰥寡無蓋民情非不達也烝民乃粒則民食未嘗不足也而帝舜方且
拳拳於岳牧之命何耶盖治雖盛矣而聖人之心不自足故視治猶未治焉若曰
吾治已足則非所謂聖人矣故曰博施濟衆堯舜其猶病諸其以此歟
其難其慎惟和惟一 林特望
同考試官進士方 批 理明文贍深得本旨佳作也
考試官教諭邵 批 〔題目分截簡短難於措辭此篇以防小人任君子立意組織成文詳贍縝密誠有本之士也〕
===
考試官前侍講余 批 文理簡嚴超於衆作
既遴選之必嚴復信任之六道此大臣告君用人之要也盖遴選之不嚴則小
人得以逞其奸信任之無道則君子不得以行其志大臣告君用人之要其
至矣乎昔者伊尹告老而歸恐太甲任用非人故告之以此意盖若曰人臣
之職為上為德為下為民其職任所係不為不重人君於未任之先可
不其難其慎乎謂之難者難於任用使不才者無倖進之門而布列庶
位者皆有為有守之人可也謂之慎者慎於聽察使不肖者無以售奸
邪之志而有服在大僚者皆碩德鉅才之士可也夫既難於任用而又謹
於聽察則防小人也嚴矣小人既去則君子在位人君於已用之後可不
punctuated:
此時，至冬乃役之，則穀不可勝食，而民食足矣。夫既重農時以足民食，則州牧之職無不修矣。噫！四岳之職舉，則内治有其人；州牧之職盡，則外治有其人。内外兼舉，而治道無餘蘊矣。抑又考之，帝舜之時，野無遺賢，人路非不開也；鰥寡無蓋，民情非不達也；烝民乃粒，則民食未嘗不足也。而帝舜方且拳拳於岳牧之命，何耶？盖治雖盛矣，而聖人之心不自足，故視治猶未治焉。若曰吾治已足，則非所謂聖人矣。故曰：「博施濟衆，堯、舜其猶病諸！」其以此歟？

《其難其慎，惟和惟一》 林特望
同考試官進士方 批：理明文贍，深得本旨，佳作也。
考試官教諭邵 批：〔題目分截簡短，難於措辭。此篇以防小人、任君子立意，組織成文，詳贍縝密，誠有本之士也。〕
考試官前侍講余 批：文理簡嚴，超於衆作。

既遴選之必嚴，復信任之六道，此大臣告君用人之要也。盖遴選之不嚴，則小人得以逞其奸；信任之無道，則君子不得以行其志。大臣告君用人之要，其至矣乎！昔者伊尹告老而歸，恐太甲任用非人，故告之以此。意盖若曰：人臣之職，為上為德，為下為民，其職任所係不為不重。人君於未任之先，可不其難其慎乎？謂之難者，難於任用，使不才者無倖進之門，而布列庶位者皆有為有守之人可也。謂之慎者，慎於聽察，使不肖者無以售奸邪之志，而有服在大僚者皆碩德鉅才之士可也。夫既難於任用，而又謹於聽察，則防小人也嚴矣。小人既去，則君子在位，人君於已用之後，可不
translation_en:
… this season, and only employ them in corvée labor when winter arrives; then there will be more grain than can be eaten, and the people's food will be sufficient. Once the agricultural seasons are respected so as to make the people's food sufficient, there is nothing in the duties of the Twelve Pastors that goes unfulfilled. Ah! When the duties of the Four Peaks are upheld, domestic governance has the right men; when the duties of the Twelve Pastors are fulfilled, regional governance has the right men. With both inner and outer governance upheld together, nothing remains unaccomplished in the Way of rule. Yet if we examine the matter further: in the time of Emperor Shun, no worthy men were left neglected in the countryside, so the path of advancement for men was not unopened; widowers and widows were not prevented from voicing their grievances, so the conditions of the people were not uncommunicated; and the multitude of the people had grain to eat, so the people's food was never insufficient. Why, then, was Emperor Shun still so earnestly concerned with his charges to the Four Peaks and Twelve Pastors? It is because even when governance is flourishing, the mind of a sage is never self-satisfied, and therefore he regards a state of order as though it were not yet ordered. Were he to say, "My governance is already sufficient," he would not be what is called a sage. Thus it is said: "To bestow benefits widely and bring relief to the multitude—even Yao and Shun would still find themselves deficient in this!" Is it not for this reason?

"Be Hesitant, Be Cautious; Be Harmonious, Be Undivided" [from the Book of Documents, "Both Possessed Pure Virtue"] — by Lin Tewang 林特望
Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate Fang, comments: The reasoning is clear and the writing rich; it deeply grasps the essential purport. A fine piece!
Examiner, Instructor Shao, comments: [The examination topic is broken into short segments, making it difficult to phrase an essay. This piece establishes its central idea around guarding against petty men and employing noble men, weaving them into a composition that is detailed, rich, and closely reasoned. Truly a scholar of solid learning!]
Examiner, Former Expositor-in-Waiting Yu, comments: The composition and reasoning are concise and rigorous, surpassing the other essays.

First, selecting them must be strict; second, trusting and employing them must follow the proper way [reading 有道 for 六道 (?)]—this is the essential principle by which a great minister counsels his ruler on employing men. For if selection is not strict, petty men will be able to indulge their wickedness; and if trust and employment lack the proper way, noble men will be unable to carry out their aspirations. How consummate is the essential principle by which the great minister counsels his ruler on employing men! In antiquity, when Yi Yin 伊尹 requested leave to retire on account of old age, he feared that Tai Jia 太甲 might employ the wrong men, and therefore counseled him with these words. His meaning was to say: The duty of a minister is, above, to promote the ruler's virtue, and below, to care for the people; the responsibilities attached to his office are by no means light. Before appointing someone, how can a ruler not be hesitant and cautious? What is meant by "hesitant" is being hesitant in making appointments, ensuring that those without talent have no door foropportunistic advancement, and that all who are arrayed in the various offices are men of capability and integrity. What is meant by "cautious" is being cautious in listening and observing, ensuring that the unworthy have no means to peddle their treacherous and evil designs, and that all who hold office among the high dignitaries are scholars of great virtue and immense talent. Once one is both hesitant in making appointments and careful in listening and observing, then the defense against petty men is strict indeed. Once petty men have been removed and noble men are in office, after the ruler has employed them, how can he not…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
惟和惟一乎謂之和者可以濟否如麴蘗之於酒塩梅之於羹可也謂之一者則任
之勿貳信之勿疑不以始之諫而聽從終之言而不受可也夫既可否相濟而
又始終如一則任君子也誠矣於乎賢才者國家之利器而資之以為德為
民者也始之防小人而察之不明則論篤色莊者有矣而有以害吾之治終之
任君子也信之不誠則賢者無願仕之心孰與之以安民哉此伊尹所以拳拳為
太甲告也抑又考之咸有一德之書伊尹告老而歸恐太甲德不純一及任用非
人而作也此章則言用人之道先以任官惟賢才左右惟其人以見用人當隨其
才繼言為上為德為民為下以見職任係上下之重至此則言所以任用之
道在於防小人而任君子也噫大臣之忠愛何其至歟
===
詩
篤公劉逝彼百泉瞻彼溥原迺陟南岡乃覯于京京師之野于
時處處于時廬旅于時言言于時語語
同考試官敎授陳批〔此篇講公劉審地安民篤厚之意逐節詳明必魁於詩者一薦何忝〕
考試官敎諭邵批〔理明詞暢深見古人篤厚之意〕
考試官前侍講余批〔四書詞理通暢本經雍容詳雅此篇於公劉相地作邑處善於形容可謂得溫柔敦厚之旨矣後二塲俱優宜冠本經〕
四名陳昊
賢君之厚於民也既能審地利而各得其宜斯能奠民居而各得其所夫民居
punctuated:
惟和惟一乎？謂之和者，可以濟否，如麴蘗之於酒，塩梅之於羹，可也；謂之一者，則任之勿貳，信之勿疑，不以始之諫而聽從，終之言而不受，可也。夫既可否相濟，而又始終如一，則任君子也誠矣。於乎！賢才者，國家之利器，而資之以為德為民者也。始之防小人而察之不明，則論篤色莊者有矣，而有以害吾之治；終之任君子也信之不誠，則賢者無願仕之心，孰與之以安民哉？此伊尹所以拳拳為太甲告也。抑又考之，《咸有一德》之書，伊尹告老而歸，恐太甲德不純一及任用非人而作也。此章則言用人之道：先以「任官惟賢才，左右惟其人」，以見用人當隨其才；繼言「為上為德，為民為下」，以見職任係上下之重；至此則言所以任用之道，在於防小人而任君子也。噫！大臣之忠愛何其至歟！

詩

「篤公劉，逝彼百泉，瞻彼溥原；迺陟南岡，乃覯于京。京師之野，于時處處，于時廬旅，于時言言，于時語語。」

同考試官敎授陳批：〔此篇講公劉審地安民篤厚之意，逐節詳明，必魁於《詩》者，一薦何忝！〕
考試官敎諭邵批：〔理明詞暢，深見古人篤厚之意。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔《四書》詞理通暢，本經雍容詳雅。此篇於公劉相地作邑處善於形容，可謂得溫柔敦厚之旨矣。後二塲俱優，宜冠本經。〕

四名陳昊

賢君之厚於民也，既能審地利而各得其宜，斯能奠民居而各得其所。夫民居
translation_en:
… be harmonious and single-minded? What is meant by "harmonious" is using the acceptable to remedy the unacceptable, just as leaven is to wine and salt and sour plums are to soup; that is how it should be. What is meant by "single-minded" is to employ them without duplicity and trust them without doubt, not heeding and following their remonstrances at the beginning only to reject their words at the end; that is how it should be. Now, when the acceptable and unacceptable mutually complement each other, and there is consistency from beginning to end, then the employment of gentlemen is truly sincere. Alas! Worthies and men of talent are the sharp instruments of the state, upon whom the ruler relies to cultivate virtue for his own sake and to care for the people below. If at first, in guarding against petty men, one does not examine them clearly, then there will be those whose words sound sincere and whose countenances appear dignified, and they will bring harm to our governance. If in the end, in employing gentlemen, one does not trust them sincerely, then worthy men will have no desire to serve in office—and with whom, then, can one bring peace to the people? This is why Yi Yin so earnestly admonished Tai Jia. Furthermore, if we examine the chapter "Both Possessed Pure Virtue" (Xian you yi de) in the Book of Documents, it was composed when Yi Yin requested leave to retire on account of age, fearing that Tai Jia’s virtue was not pure and single-minded and that he might employ the wrong men. This passage speaks of the way of employing men: first, with "In appointing to office, use only the worthy and talented; for your close attendants, choose only the right men," it shows that employing men ought to accord with their talents; next, it says "Their duty is to help the sovereign cultivate his virtue, and to benefit the people below," [?] to show that official responsibilities are tied to the weighty concerns of both above and below; and arriving at this point, it states that the way to employ them lies in guarding against petty men and trusting gentlemen. Ah! How supreme is the loyalty and devotion of a great minister!

Classic of Poetry (Shi)

"Devoted was Duke Liu! He went to that Hundred Springs, and gazed upon that vast plain; then he ascended the southern ridge, and looked upon the great hill—a region for a capital, where they could dwell, where strangers could lodge, where they could speak out, where they could converse."

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Chen: [This essay explains the devoted kindness of Duke Liu in surveying the land and settling the people. Every section is detailed and clear. He is surely a top candidate in the Classic of Poetry—what shame could there be in recommending him!]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao: [The reasoning is clear and the diction fluent; it deeply reveals the devoted kindness of the ancients.]
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-waiting Yu: [His essays on the Four Books are fluent in both diction and reasoning, and those on his specialized Classic are poised, detailed, and elegant. This piece excels at describing how Duke Liu surveyed the land and built a settlement; it may be said to have grasped the teaching of gentle and sincere kindness. His second and third sessions were both superior; he ought to be placed first in his Classic.]

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
之得其所者正由地利之得其宜也賢君遍觀而審度之其厚民之心為何如哉
思昔召康公以成王將涖政當戒以民事欲咏公劉之事以告之其意若曰厚
哉公劉之於民也當國家創建之初土地不可以不審人民不可以不安於是相
其陰陽而必擇其地之宜跋涉上下而不知其已之勞是故百泉之往非徒往
也亦惟相其廣平之原焉高岡之陟非徒陟也亦惟望其高丘之地焉謂之曰
百泉則衆川之所會下流之所鍾而有以備夫灌漑之利也可知謂之曰溥原則
向背之得宜陰陽之得所而有以獲夫地勢之宜也可見由是驗其京師之野則
山川回合風氣所萃前朝後市之規由此而立左祖右社之制由此而成此公
劉度之詳而慮之審者豈徒為一已之謀哉盖欲安乎衆民之居也越是于
===
時處處皆為之居室而各得安於所止矣於是廬其實旅則行者亦願出於
其途矣自言曰言其所言者豈為無事而空言哉吾知其無非農桑衣食
之言也論難曰語其所語者豈無實之虛語哉吾知其無非篤厚艱難之
語也既有以安其居又得以遂其性又豈有一夫之不得其所哉自非公劉慮
度之審疇克臻是耶抑攷是詩凡六章首章既言自西戎而迁於邠二章則
言其至邠焉至是章乃言營度邑居以安民下章又言宮室成而落之五章
則辨土宜而定賦稅六章則総序其始終言其民日衆而地日廣一詩之中拳拳
乎篤厚之意諄諄乎艱難之詞無非所以戒成王而欲其知創業之艱也厥後成王
果為繼體守文之令主以成鳧鷖既醉之太平謂非康公告戒之力可乎
punctuated: 之得其所者，正由地利之得其宜也。賢君遍觀而審度之，其厚民之心為何如哉！思昔召康公以成王將涖政，當戒以民事，欲咏公劉之事以告之。其意若曰：厚哉！公劉之於民也。當國家創建之初，土地不可以不審，人民不可以不安。於是相其陰陽，而必擇其地之宜；跋涉上下，而不知其已之勞。是故百泉之往，非徒往也，亦惟相其廣平之原焉；高岡之陟，非徒陟也，亦惟望其高丘之地焉。謂之曰「百泉」，則衆川之所會，下流之所鍾，而有以備夫灌漑之利也可知；謂之曰「溥原」，則向背之得宜，陰陽之得所，而有以獲夫地勢之宜也可見。由是驗其京師之野，則山川回合，風氣所萃，前朝後市之規由此而立，左祖右社之制由此而成。此公劉度之詳而慮之審者，豈徒為一已之謀哉？盖欲安乎衆民之居也。越是于時處處，皆為之居室，而各得安於所止矣；於是廬其實旅，則行者亦願出於其途矣。自言曰「言」，其所言者，豈為無事而空言哉？吾知其無非農桑衣食之言也。論難曰「語」，其所語者，豈無實之虛語哉？吾知其無非篤厚艱難之語也。既有以安其居，又得以遂其性，又豈有一夫之不得其所哉？自非公劉慮度之審，疇克臻是耶？抑攷是詩凡六章：首章既言自西戎而迁於邠，二章則言其至邠焉；至是章，乃言營度邑居以安民；下章又言宮室成而落之；五章則辨土宜而定賦稅；六章則総序其始終，言其民日衆而地日廣。一詩之中，拳拳乎篤厚之意，諄諄乎艱難之詞，無非所以戒成王，而欲其知創業之艱也。厥後成王果為繼體守文之令主，以成《鳧鷖》、《既醉》之太平，謂非康公告戒之力可乎？
translation_en:
… attaining their proper place is precisely because the advantages of the terrain have been properly secured. When a worthy ruler surveys everything thoroughly and measures it carefully, how profound is his mind to treat the people generously!

Reflecting on the past, Duke Kang of Shao (Shao Kanggong 召康公), considering that King Cheng (Chengwang 成王) was about to assume the reins of government and ought to be admonished regarding the affairs of the people, wished to sing of the deeds of Duke Liu (Gong Liu 公劉) in order to instruct him. His meaning was as if to say: How generous was Duke Liu toward the people! At the very beginning of the founding of the state, the land could not but be carefully examined, and the people could not but be settled in peace. Thereupon he inspected the yin and yang aspects, обязательно choosing what was suitable in the terrain; he trudged up and down without minding his own toil. Therefore, his going to the Hundred Springs (Baiquan 百泉) was not merely going for its own sake, but solely to inspect that broad and level plain; his ascending the southern ridge was not merely ascending for its own sake, but solely to gaze upon that land of the high mound. That it is called the "Hundred Springs" lets us know that it was where the many streams converged and where the lower reaches gathered, thus providing the benefit of irrigation. That it is called the "Broad Plain" (Puyuan 溥原) lets us see that its orientation was suitable and its sunlit and shaded sides were properly situated, thus securing the advantages of the topography. 

From this, examining the wilderness of his capital city (Jingshi 京師), the mountains and rivers encircled and met, and the vital influences of wind and air gathered there; from this the layout of the court in front and the market in back was established, and from this the system of the ancestral temple on the left and the altars of soil and grain on the right was completed. In measuring so thoroughly and deliberating so carefully, was Duke Liu planning merely for himself alone? Rather, he wished to settle the dwellings of the multitude of the people. Thereupon, here and there they resided, all making their dwelling houses so that each was able to rest peacefully in his abode; and thereupon he lodged his guests and travelers [reading 賓 for 實], so that wayfarers too wished to travel upon his roads. Speaking by oneself is called "talking" (yan 言); could what was talked about be idle talk over nothing? I know that it was nothing other than talk of farming, mulberry cultivation, clothing, and food. Discussing and debating is called "conversing" (yu 語); could what was conversed about be empty words devoid of substance? I know that it was nothing other than conversation about generous devotion and hardship. Having both settled their dwellings and enabled them to fulfill their natures, how could there be even a single man who failed to find his proper place? Had it not been for the carefulness of Duke Liu's deliberations and measurements, who could have achieved this?

Moreover, if we examine this ode as a whole, it has six stanzas: the first stanza speaks of migrating from the Western Rong (Xirong 西戎) to Bin (邠); the second stanza speaks of his arrival in Bin; coming to this stanza, it speaks of laying out and measuring the settlement and dwellings in order to give peace to the people; the next stanza goes on to speak of the completion of the halls and chambers and their inaugural feast; the fifth stanza distinguishes the suitability of the soil and fixes the land taxes; and the sixth stanza summarizes the entire process from beginning to end, saying that his people grew daily more numerous and his territory daily more expansive. Throughout the single ode, there is an earnest expression of generous devotion and a tireless repetition of words about hardship—all of which served as a means to admonish King Cheng and to make him understand the difficulties of founding a dynasty. Afterward, King Cheng indeed became an admirable ruler who succeeded to the line and upheld the civil order, thereby achieving the great peace celebrated in the odes "Wild Ducks" (Fuyi 鳧鷖) and "Already Drunk" (Jizui 既醉). How could one say that this was not due to the power of Duke Kang's admonitions?

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
作召公考天子萬壽　　十五名陳俞
同考試官教授陳　批〔行文縝密經旨明白講穆公報稱之誠藹然見於言外深得詩体〕
考試官教諭邵　批〔義理昭融文辭豐贍非深体臣子感恩祝愿之至情者不能如此形容之〕
考試官前侍講余　批〔此題場中作者不失之窘則失之泛獨此篇詞婉而意周有一倡三嘆之遺音可謂熟於說經者矣况經義四書俱優後兩場皆有發越高薦何忝〕
勒君命於廟器祝君壽於悠乆此大臣愛君之誠也夫勒廟器而考其功之成者
固臣子之深意祝君壽於悠乆者又臣子之至情古之人有能然者吾於江漢之
詩見之矣是詩也說者以為宣王命召穆公平淮南之夷有功而歸故詩人作
是以美之然則穆公有非常之功為宣王者盍亦錫之以非常之典歟今也釐爾
===
圭瓚秬鬯一卣則宣王錫予召虎之禮至矣告于文人錫山土田則宣王寵異召
虎之禮為有加矣穆公受君之賜感君之恩安得自已於言哉固必作我康
公之廟器而勒王策命之詞以考其成功焉意其着曰向也宣王之命有曰
無曰予小子召公是以今則勒之於廟器果能以召公之是似否乎向也宣王
之命有曰肇敏戎功用錫爾祉今則考之於廟器果能以召公之肇敏否
乎然不惟考成功而已抑且祝君以萬壽焉壽而謂之萬壽則萬有千歲
眉壽無有害不足以方其乆也黃髮台背壽胥與試不足以喻其永也作
康公之廟器而祝天子以萬壽意謂吾君之壽考無窮而廟器之作亦與
之悠乆而無窮而後世之子孫觀康公之廟器者又安得不感君恩於無
punctuated:
「作召公考，天子萬壽」　　十五名陳俞
同考試官教授陳　批〔行文縝密，經旨明白，講穆公報稱之誠，藹然見於言外，深得詩体。〕
考試官教諭邵　批〔義理昭融，文辭豐贍，非深体臣子感恩祝愿之至情者，不能如此形容之。〕
考試官前侍講余　批〔此題場中作者，不失之窘，則失之泛，獨此篇詞婉而意周，有一倡三嘆之遺音，可謂熟於說經者矣。况經義、四書俱優，後兩場皆有發越，高薦何忝！〕
勒君命於廟器，祝君壽於悠乆，此大臣愛君之誠也。夫勒廟器而考其功之成者，固臣子之深意；祝君壽於悠乆者，又臣子之至情。古之人有能然者，吾於《江漢》之詩見之矣。是詩也，說者以為宣王命召穆公平淮南之夷，有功而歸，故詩人作是以美之。然則穆公有非常之功，為宣王者，盍亦錫之以非常之典歟？今也，「釐爾圭瓚，秬鬯一卣」，則宣王錫予召虎之禮至矣；「告于文人，錫山土田」，則宣王寵異召虎之禮為有加矣。穆公受君之賜，感君之恩，安得自已於言哉？固必作我康公之廟器，而勒王策命之詞，以考其成功焉。意其着曰：向也宣王之命有曰：「無曰予小子，召公是似。」今則勒之於廟器，果能以召公之是似否乎？向也宣王之命有曰：「肇敏戎功，用錫爾祉。」今則考之於廟器，果能以召公之肇敏否乎？然不惟考成功而已，抑且祝君以萬壽焉。壽而謂之萬壽，則「萬有千歲，眉壽無有害」不足以方其乆也；「黃髮台背，壽胥與試」不足以喻其永也。作康公之廟器，而祝天子以萬壽，意謂吾君之壽考無窮，而廟器之作亦與之悠乆而無窮；而後世之子孫觀康公之廟器者，又安得不感君恩於無
translation_en:
"Therefore I make for my ancestor Duke Shao this sacral vessel, and may the Son of Heaven live for ten thousand years!" — 15th place, Chen Yu 陳俞.

Associate Examiner, Confucian School Professor Chen 陳, comments: [The composition is meticulous and the meaning of the Classic is clear. In explaining Duke Mu's 穆公 sincerity in repaying his sovereign's favor, a warm reverence shines forth beyond the words themselves, deeply capturing the spirit of the *Odes*.]

Examiner, Confucian School Instructor Shao 邵, comments: [The moral principles are bright and harmonious, and the diction is rich and abundant. None who had not deeply entered into a subject's utmost feelings of gratitude and prayerful well-wishing could have depicted it like this.]

Examiner, former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余, comments: [Among the candidates in the examination hall writing on this topic, those who did not err on the side of crampedness erred on the side of vagueness. This essay alone is gentle in expression yet comprehensive in meaning, possessing the lingering resonance of "one leading the song and three joining in sighing admiration." He may truly be called well-versed in expounding the Classics! Moreover, his essays on the Five Classics and Four Books are all excellent, and his work in the latter two sessions also shows brilliant insight—how could a high recommendation bring any shame?]

To engrave the sovereign's charge upon a temple vessel and to pray for the sovereign's longevity into the distant future—this is a great minister's sincere love for his ruler. Indeed, engraving a temple vessel to commemorate the completion of his achievement is the profound intent of a subject; praying for the sovereign's longevity into the distant future is furthermore the utmost sentiment of a subject. That there were men of antiquity capable of this, I see in the ode "Jiang Han" 江漢. Regarding this ode, commentators hold that King Xuan 宣王 commanded Duke Mu of Shao 召穆公 to pacify the Yi 夷 tribes south of the Huai 淮 River; when he returned with merit, the poet composed this to praise him. Since Duke Mu had achieved extraordinary merit, why would one acting as King Xuan not also bestow upon him extraordinary honors? Now, "I bestow on you a jade-handled libation ladle, and a jar of aromatic black-millet wine"—thus the rites with which King Xuan rewarded Shao Hu 召虎 reached the utmost; "Report to my accomplished ancestors, and bestow on you hills, lands, and fields"—thus the rites with which King Xuan favored and distinguished Shao Hu were augmented even further. Receiving his sovereign's gifts and moved by his sovereign's grace, how could Duke Mu keep himself from speaking out? Surely he had to cast a temple vessel for his ancestor Duke Kang 康公, engraving upon it the words of the King's brevet of appointment so as to commemorate the completion of his success. One may imagine his thought [?] to be: Earlier, King Xuan's charge said, "Do not say, 'I am but a young child'; take Duke Shao as your model!" Now that I engrave this upon the temple vessel, have I truly been able to model myself upon Duke Shao or not? Earlier, King Xuan's charge said, "You have been diligent and swift in military merit, and therefore I bestow blessings upon you." Now that I commemorate this upon the temple vessel, have I truly been able to match Duke Shao's diligence and swiftness or not? Yet he did not merely commemorate his completed achievement; he also prayed that his sovereign enjoy ten thousand years of life. When longevity is called "ten thousand years of life," then even "ten thousand and a thousand years, bushy-browed longevity without harm" is not enough to compare with its duration; even "yellow hair and wrinkled back, in old age helping and serving one another" is not enough to illustrate its permanence. In making a temple vessel for Duke Kang and praying that the Son of Heaven enjoy ten thousand years of life, his meaning was that our sovereign's long life should be endless, and the making of this temple vessel should likewise endure alongside it endlessly into the distant future; and among the descendants of later generations who behold the temple vessel of Duke Kang, how could they not feel gratitude for the sovereign's grace without…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
窮也哉報稱之意見於廟器之作祝頌之誠形於咏歌之表古人感恩圖報
之情若此自非忠愛之至能若是哉不特此也下文又曰明明天子令聞不已
矢其文德洽此四國則是不徒祝其君之福而又勉其君之德也若穆公者
可謂忠愛其君之至矣猗歟盛哉
自天降豐年穰穰來假來饗降福無疆顧予烝嘗湯孫之
將
四名陳昊
同考試官教諭柴批〔破講詳明發越期望眷顧之意一唱三嘆無餘蘊矣深得詩人之旨佳作也〕
考試官教諭邵批〔場中作者於湯孫之將一段多遺漏不講此篇一破能包括題意通篇明暢令人愛羡不已〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此題於下截語簡而意深難於發越而此卷獨佳於顧予烝嘗形容最為精切非〕
深於六義者不能也尚薦何沗
===
人君得天時以奉祭不惟感先王錫福之久尤必望先王眷顧之深夫奉祭者人
君報本之心也然非獲夫豐年之利則何以備祀事而感先王之錫福兾先
王之眷顧哉是詩說者謂祀成湯之樂歌也吾想夫詩人之意若曰我之所
以得奉祭於宗廟者實賴乎自天降康而獲豐年之利也降康而謂之自天
必其天時恊和而雨暘時若也豐年而謂之穰々必其多黍多稌而萬億及
秭也於斯時而獲有年於斯時而行祀禮為酒為醴無一禮之不具維羊
維牛無一物之不將豈非豐年之所致乎但見昭格之時對越之頃祖考有
靈洋々在上不徒格之而來格而且惠我以無窮之福綿々而不已有如日之方
punctuated:
窮也哉！報稱之意見於廟器之作，祝頌之誠形於咏歌之表。古人感恩圖報之情若此，自非忠愛之至，能若是哉？不特此也，下文又曰：「明明天子，令聞不已，矢其文德，洽此四國。」則是不徒祝其君之福，而又勉其君之德也。若穆公者，可謂忠愛其君之至矣。猗歟盛哉！

「自天降，豐年穰穰。來假來饗，降福無疆。顧予烝嘗，湯孫之將。」
四名陳昊
同考試官教諭柴批：〔破講詳明發越，期望眷顧之意，一唱三嘆，無餘蘊矣。深得詩人之旨，佳作也。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔場中作者於「湯孫之將」一段多遺漏不講，此篇一破能包括題意，通篇明暢，令人愛羡不已。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔此題於下截語簡而意深，難於發越，而此卷獨佳，於「顧予烝嘗」形容最為精切，非〕深於六義者不能也。尚薦何沗！

人君得天時以奉祭，不惟感先王錫福之久，尤必望先王眷顧之深。夫奉祭者，人君報本之心也。然非獲夫豐年之利，則何以備祀事而感先王之錫福、兾先王之眷顧哉？是詩，說者謂祀成湯之樂歌也。吾想夫詩人之意，若曰：我之所以得奉祭於宗廟者，實賴乎自天降康而獲豐年之利也。降康而謂之「自天」，必其天時恊和而雨暘時若也；豐年而謂之「穰々」，必其多黍多稌而萬億及秭也。於斯時而獲有年，於斯時而行祀禮，為酒為醴，無一禮之不具；維羊維牛，無一物之不將。豈非豐年之所致乎？但見昭格之時、對越之頃，祖考有靈，洋々在上，不徒格之而來格，而且惠我以無窮之福，綿々而不已，有如日之方
translation_en:
… end! The intention to repay in full measure is seen in the making of the ancestral temple vessels, and the sincerity of his prayers and praises takes form on the surface of his chanted songs. Such were the feelings of gratitude for grace and desire to repay it among the ancients; if it did not stem from the utmost loyalty and affection, how could it be like this? Not only this, the text below also says: "Resplendent is the Son of Heaven, his fine reputation never ceases; he displays his civil virtue, permeating these quarters of the realm." Thus he not only prays for his ruler's good fortune, but also encourages his ruler's virtue. One such as Duke Mu may be called possessing the utmost loyalty and affection toward his ruler. Oh, how magnificent!

"[Peace] is sent down from Heaven [Note: '康' (peace) is omitted in the woodblock transcription], and the abundant year is rich and plentiful. He comes, he accepts the offering, and sends down blessings without limit. Look with favor upon our winter and autumn sacrifices, offered by the descendant of Tang."
Fourth place: Chen Hao 陳昊.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Chai 柴: 〔The opening analysis and exposition are detailed, clear, and expressive. The sentiment of hoping for favored regard is chanted with lingering resonance, leaving nothing unexpressed. It deeply grasps the intent of the poet; a fine piece of work.〕
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao 邵: 〔Writers in the examination hall mostly omitted and failed to expound upon the section "offered by the descendant of Tang." This essay, in its very opening analysis, is able to encompass the meaning of the theme, and the entire piece is lucid and fluent, making one admire it endlessly.〕
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-Waiting Yu 余: 〔In the latter half of this theme, the words are brief yet the meaning is profound, making it difficult to bring out fully. Yet this paper alone excels; its depiction of "Look with favor upon our winter and autumn sacrifices" is most precise and fitting. None〕 who is not deeply versed in the Six Principles of the Odes could achieve this. What shame could there be in recommending it for success!

When a ruler obtains seasonable weather from Heaven in order to perform the sacrifices, he not only feels gratitude for the enduring blessings bestowed by the former kings, but even more must he hope for the deep and favored regard of the former kings. Now, performing sacrifices stems from the ruler's heart of repaying his origins. Yet without obtaining the benefit of an abundant year, wherewith could he prepare the sacrificial affairs, feel gratitude for the blessings bestowed by the former kings, and hope for the favored regard of the former kings? Commentators say that this ode is a musical song for sacrificing to Cheng Tang 成湯. I imagine that the meaning of the poet is as if to say: The reason why I am able to perform sacrifices in the ancestral temple truly depends upon peace being sent down from Heaven and our obtaining the benefit of an abundant year. That sending down peace is said to be "from Heaven" surely means that the heavenly seasons are in harmony and rain and sunshine are timely; that the abundant year is called "rich and plentiful" surely means that there is much millet and much rice, reaching into the billions and trillions. Obtaining a bountiful harvest at this time, and performing the sacrificial rites at this time: making spirits and making sweet wine, not a single rite is unprovided for; offering sheep and offering oxen, not a single item goes unpresented. Is this not brought about by the abundant year? One only sees that at the time of bright arrival, at the moment of standing in solemn presence, the ancestral spirits are numinous, vast and omnipresent above. Not only are they summoned to come and do they come, they moreover favor us with endless blessings, continuous and unceasing, like the sun just…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
升也不徒享之而來享而且錫我以無疆之休繩繩而不替有如川之方至也
此所以致其丁寧之詞於昭昭之際而望其感格之意於冥冥之中故曰湯
其尚顧我烝嘗哉盖烝嘗秋冬之祭名也四時之祭各有其名舉烝嘗則其
餘可知此烝嘗之禮所以為湯孫之所將也以成湯之孫奉成湯之祭不必臭
陽達於墻屋臭陰達於淵泉以求之盖吾身之精神即祖考之精神也吾
身之精神既交會於奉祭之頃祖考其有不享吾烝嘗之祭乎奉祭之
物既有以得乎豐年享祭之効又有以望于先王宗廟之祭孝思之誠為何
如哉抑又論之豐年者祭祀之本祭祀者獲福之源茍或年之不豐則
穡事不成尚何以備其祭祀之禮哉觀楚茨之祀事孔明而必先之黍稷與
===
翼載芟之以洽百禮而必繼之以振古如茲是則不惟商人賴豐年而奉祭
而周人亦莫不賴豐年而奉祭也故併及之
春秋
齊侯宋人陳人蔡人邾人會于北杏〔莊公十三年〕公會齊侯宋公陳
侯鄭伯同盟于幽〔莊公二十七年〕
五名楊永
考試官教諭邵批〔春秋之旨重在於尊王抑伯北杏之會于幽之盟一則為王道憂聖人公天下之本心一則為世道慮聖人不得已之意也此篇首舉憂伯圖之啓喜伯業之成深得夫筆削之旨高薦何忝〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此篇寓意措辭縝嚴而融暢况初場俱優三策論議滔滔略無窘滯宜冠本經〕
春秋憂伯圖之始啓而喜伯業之已成夫伯圖啓則王道微伯業成則王室
punctuated:
升也，不徒享之而來享，而且錫我以無疆之休，繩繩而不替，有如川之方至也。此所以致其丁寧之詞於昭昭之際，而望其感格之意於冥冥之中，故曰：「湯其尚顧我烝嘗哉！」盖烝嘗，秋冬之祭名也。四時之祭各有其名，舉烝嘗則其餘可知，此烝嘗之禮所以為湯孫之所將也。以成湯之孫，奉成湯之祭，不必臭陽達於墻屋、臭陰達於淵泉以求之，盖吾身之精神即祖考之精神也。吾身之精神既交會於奉祭之頃，祖考其有不享吾烝嘗之祭乎？奉祭之物，既有以得乎豐年；享祭之効，又有以望于先王。宗廟之祭，孝思之誠為何如哉！抑又論之，豐年者，祭祀之本；祭祀者，獲福之源。茍或年之不豐，則穡事不成，尚何以備其祭祀之禮哉？觀《楚茨》之「祀事孔明」，而必先之「黍稷與翼」；《載芟》之「以洽百禮」，而必繼之以「振古如茲」。是則不惟商人賴豐年而奉祭，而周人亦莫不賴豐年而奉祭也，故併及之。

《春秋》
齊侯、宋人、陳人、蔡人、邾人會于北杏〔莊公十三年〕；公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、鄭伯同盟于幽〔莊公二十七年〕。
五名楊永
考試官教諭邵批〔《春秋》之旨，重在於尊王抑伯。北杏之會、于幽之盟，一則為王道憂，聖人公天下之本心；一則為世道慮，聖人不得已之意也。此篇首舉憂伯圖之啓、喜伯業之成，深得夫筆削之旨，高薦何忝。〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此篇寓意措辭，縝嚴而融暢。况初場俱優，三策論議滔滔，略無窘滯，宜冠本經。〕

《春秋》憂伯圖之始啓，而喜伯業之已成。夫伯圖啓則王道微，伯業成則王室
translation_en:
… rising; not only do we offer them sacrifices and they come to enjoy them, but they also bestow upon us boundless blessings, continuous and unceasing like a river just arriving at full flow. This is why he expresses his earnest words in the bright light of the ceremony and hopes for their responsive presence out of the unseen realm, saying: "May Tang still look with favor upon our winter and autumn sacrifices!" Now zheng and chang are the names of the winter and autumn sacrifices. Each of the sacrifices of the four seasons has its own name; by mentioning the winter and autumn sacrifices, the rest may be known. This is why the rites of the winter and autumn sacrifices are performed by the descendant of Tang. When the descendant of Cheng Tang performs the sacrifices to Cheng Tang, he need not seek him by causing the rising scent of burnt fat to reach the walls and roof, or the sinking libation to reach the deep springs, for the spirit of my own person is the very spirit of my ancestors. Since the spirit of my own person already communes with theirs at the moment of offering sacrifice, how could my ancestors fail to enjoy my winter and autumn sacrifices? The offerings for the sacrifice have already been obtained through a bountiful year, and the efficacy of their enjoying the sacrifice is furthermore hoped for from the former kings. In the sacrifices of the ancestral temple, how profound is the sincerity of filial devotion! Moreover, if we consider it further: a bountiful year is the foundation of sacrifice, and sacrifice is the source of obtaining blessings. If the year were not bountiful, the harvest would not be accomplished; how then could one prepare the rites of sacrifice? Observe how in the ode "Thick Tribulus" (Chuci), "the sacrificial service is grandly illustrious" is necessarily preceded by "our glutinous and panicledih millet is luxuriant" [reading 翼翼 for 與翼]; and how in the ode "Clearing the Grass" (Zaishan), "to fulfill all the hundred rites" is necessarily followed by "from of old it has been thus." Thus not only did the people of Shang rely on bountiful years to perform their sacrifices, but the people of Zhou likewise without exception relied on bountiful years to perform their sacrifices; therefore I mention this together here.

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"The Marquis of Qi, a man of Song, a man of Chen, a man of Cai, and a man of Zhu met at Beixing" [thirteenth year of Duke Zhuang]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and together made a covenant at You" [twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhuang].
Fifth-placed candidate: Yang Yong 楊永
Comment by Examiner Shao, Instructor (jiaoyu): [The purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals lies chiefly in honoring the King and restraining the hegemons. As for the meeting at Beixing and the covenant at You, the former sorrows over the Kingly Way, reflecting the Sage's fundamental mind of impartiality toward all under Heaven; the latter takes thought for the way of the world, reflecting the Sage's reluctant resort when there was no alternative. This essay begins by raising the sorrow over the opening of hegemonic ambitions and the joy over the accomplishment of the hegemonic enterprise, deeply grasping the purport of the Sage's brush in recording and deleting. How could a high recommendation be undeserved?]
Comment by Examiner Yu, former Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang): [The underlying meaning and phrasing of this essay are rigorous yet smooth and fluent. Moreover, his first-session papers were all excellent, and his three policy essays argued in a surging flow without the slightest stiffness or obstruction; he ought to head the list for his classic.]

The Spring and Autumn Annals sorrows over the initial opening of hegemonic ambitions, yet rejoices that the hegemonic enterprise has been accomplished. Now when hegemonic ambitions open, the Kingly Way declines; when the hegemonic enterprise is accomplished, the Royal House…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
尊春秋為尊王而作安得不憂之於前而喜之於後乎思昔岐豐盛時侯伯
受職古未始有伯也迨夫東遷以來王澤微而力政起伯者之名所由立也
有如齊桓以賜履建侯之裔踵齊僖小伯之襲因宋有蒙澤之變會北杏以
平之寔圖伯之始事也然向為王道而今為伯圖安攘之功未著會盟之政已
專大而宋陳既俯首而偕來小而蔡邾咸帖耳而聽命自是天下知有伯而不
知有王矣春秋於齊雖書爵而猶人四國者所以憂伯圖之始啓也然伯圖啓
固春秋之所憂伯業成又春秋之所喜何哉夫以周室既微之日人心渙散之
秋桓公并合諸侯而為于幽之盟衣冠萃聚既莫不以尊王為心玉帛來臨亦
莫不以尊王為事人心已離而復合王室既微而復尊向也始盟于幽尚有内
===
外寮一之疑今則同心聽命無敢二三其德於是授之諸侯而齊侯遂得衆矣
春秋於會而書公於盟而書同者所以喜伯業之已成也吁謹伯圖之始啓
聖人扶持王道之本心喜伯業之已成聖人惓惓於世道不得已之意也以王道
而論固不可以有伯以世道而觀安可以無伯乎雖然齊桓創伯盛衰凡三變
焉自北杏以至于幽而伯業始成自于幽以至葵丘而伯業極盛自葵丘以至
會淮則伯業終衰其盛也為甚難而衰也為甚易良由伯者假仁義之所
致抑亦管仲之器量褊淺而然歟不然則桓有王德管仲為王佐矣
遂伐楚公至自伐楚〔僖公四年〕公會齊侯于夾谷公至自夾
谷〔定公十年〕五名楊永
punctuated:
尊，《春秋》為尊王而作，安得不憂之於前而喜之於後乎？思昔岐、豐盛時，侯伯受職，古未始有伯也。迨夫東遷以來，王澤微而力政起，伯者之名所由立也。有如齊桓，以賜履建侯之裔，踵齊僖小伯之襲，因宋有蒙澤之變，會北杏以平之，寔圖伯之始事也。然向為王道，而今為伯圖，安攘之功未著，會盟之政已專。大而宋、陳，既俯首而偕來；小而蔡、邾，咸帖耳而聽命。自是天下知有伯而不知有王矣。《春秋》於齊雖書爵，而猶人四國者，所以憂伯圖之始啓也。然伯圖啓，固《春秋》之所憂，伯業成，又《春秋》之所喜，何哉？夫以周室既微之日，人心渙散之秋，桓公并合諸侯而為于幽之盟。衣冠萃聚，既莫不以尊王為心；玉帛來臨，亦莫不以尊王為事。人心已離而復合，王室既微而復尊。向也始盟于幽，尚有內外寮一之疑；今則同心聽命，無敢二三其德。於是授之諸侯，而齊侯遂得衆矣。《春秋》於會而書「公」，於盟而書「同」者，所以喜伯業之已成也。吁！謹伯圖之始啓，聖人扶持王道之本心；喜伯業之已成，聖人惓惓於世道不得已之意也。以王道而論，固不可以有伯；以世道而觀，安可以無伯乎？雖然，齊桓創伯，盛衰凡三變焉：自北杏以至于幽，而伯業始成；自于幽以至葵丘，而伯業極盛；自葵丘以至會淮，則伯業終衰。其盛也為甚難，而衰也為甚易，良由伯者假仁義之所致，抑亦管仲之器量褊淺而然歟？不然，則桓有王德，管仲為王佐矣。

「遂伐楚」「公至自伐楚」〔僖公四年〕；「公會齊侯于夾谷」「公至自夾谷」〔定公十年〕。
五名楊永。
translation_en:
… [when the hegemony is accomplished, the royal house is] revered. Since the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) was composed to revere the King, how could it not lament the former earlier on and rejoice over the latter afterward?

When we reflect upon the flourishing era of Qi and Feng in antiquity, the marquises and earls received their appointed offices, and in ancient times there had never been any hegemon (ba). Yet following the eastern relocation of the capital, royal beneficence waned and rule by force arose; from this the title of hegemon came to be established. Take Duke Huan of Qi: as a descendant of a line granted territorial bounds and enfeoffed as marquises, he followed in the footsteps of the minor hegemony of Duke Xi of Qi. Taking advantage of the upheaval at Mengze in Song, he convened a meeting at Beixing to pacify it—this was truly the inaugural enterprise of his design for hegemony. Yet what had formerly been the Kingly Way now became a scheme for hegemony; before the merits of pacifying the realm and repelling the barbarians had been made manifest, he already monopolized the administration of meetings and covenants. Great states like Song and Chen bowed their heads and came together; small states like Cai and Zhu all drooped their ears in submissive obedience. From this point onward, the world knew only that there was a hegemon, and no longer knew that there was a King. Although the Spring and Autumn Annals records the noble rank of Qi, it still refers to the participants of the four other states merely as "men" (ren); this was how it lamented the initial opening of designs for hegemony.

Yet if the opening of designs for hegemony was indeed what the Spring and Autumn Annals lamented, why was the accomplishment of the hegemonic enterprise in turn what the Spring and Autumn Annals rejoiced over? At a time when the house of Zhou had already grown weak and in a season when people's hearts were scattered, Duke Huan united the feudal lords and forged the covenant at You. As caps and robes gathered together, there were none who did not take revering the King as their mind; as jade and silk arrived at the assembly, there were likewise none who did not take revering the King as their business. People's hearts, having drifted apart, were reunited; the royal house, having grown weak, was once again revered. Earlier, at the first covenant at You, there had still been doubts of division between inner and outer [?]; now, however, all obeyed commands with a single heart, none daring to be wavering in their virtue. Thus authority over the feudal lords was accorded to him, and the Marquis of Qi consequently won the multitude. That the Spring and Autumn Annals records "the Duke" (gong) at the meeting and records "together" (tong) at the covenant is how it rejoices that the hegemonic enterprise had been accomplished.

Alas! Being guarded about the initial opening of designs for hegemony was the Sage's original mind in upholding the Kingly Way; rejoicing over the accomplishment of the hegemonic enterprise was the Sage's reluctant intent out of earnest concern for the state of the world. Judged in terms of the Kingly Way, there certainly ought not to be a hegemon; viewed in terms of the state of the world, how could one do without a hegemon? Even so, in Duke Huan of Qi's founding of the hegemony, its rise and decline underwent three transformations in all: from Beixing to You, the hegemonic enterprise was first accomplished; from You to Kuiqiu, the hegemonic enterprise reached its peak of flourishing; and from Kuiqiu to the meeting at Huai, the hegemonic enterprise finally declined. That its flourishing was so difficult and its decline so easy—was this truly brought about because a hegemon merely borrows benevolence and righteousness, or was it also because Guan Zhong's capacity and measure were narrow and shallow? Had it not been so, Duke Huan would have possessed kingly virtue, and Guan Zhong would have been a kingly coadjutor.

"Thereupon they invaded Chu"; "The Duke arrived from invading Chu" 〔Fourth year of Duke Xi〕; "The Duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu"; "The Duke arrived from Jiagu" 〔Tenth year of Duke Ding〕.
5th place, Yang Yong 楊永.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭邵批〔此篇一則序齊桓之服楚一則著大國之感化題本正大場中佳者絕不多得獨此篇叙事詳明行文嚴整非孰於是經者不能也三塲俱稱宜魁本經〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此篇筆力雄健有斷制有發明麟經之傑然者也〕
義以攘外夷春秋旣托望國之至以大其功禮以服大國春秋復托望國之至以
著其美此齊桓服楚之功聖人變齊之效春秋安得不於我公之至屢書而致
其意焉夫膺懲之訓無聞蠻夷之勢駸駸乎中國今年以荆敗蔡書明年以荆
伐鄭書則楚之蚕食我諸姬者其患未有紀極也吁不有齊桓中國且奈之何
哉廼今伐楚之役齊桓之意盖曰荆楚暴橫非義不足以格其心蠻夷陸梁
非義不足以折其勇故不以兵力為武不以攻戰為威唯以義而服之使兵無
===
血刄之虞民無暴骨之慘責以苞茅之不貢問以昭王之不復卒之不待兵交
而楚人帖服二百四十二年之間伯功之盛惟此時為最春秋於我公反行告廟之
際特書曰公至自伐楚豈非義以攘外夷春秋托望國之至以大其功乎迨夫
夾輔之誓陵夷齊景之患駸駸乎我魯今日以齊國夏伐我北鄙書明日
以齊國夏伐我西鄙書則齊之揺蕩我邊鄙者其患未有遏止也吁不
有聖人魯且奈之何哉廼今夾谷之會聖人之意盖曰大敵恣睢非禮不足以
服其心強國憑凌非禮不足以格其志故不千之以盟不逼之以好唯以禮而
化之一言之出却萊人之兵罷野享之設以衣冠而化強暴以禮義而為干
櫓卒之齊景愧悟而王道遂明二百四十二年之際聖化之行唯此時為然春秋
punctuated:
考試官敎諭邵批：〔此篇一則序齊桓之服楚，一則著大國之感化。題本正大，場中佳者絕不多得。獨此篇叙事詳明，行文嚴整，非孰於是經者不能也。三塲俱稱，宜魁本經。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔此篇筆力雄健，有斷制，有發明，《麟經》之傑然者也。〕
義以攘外夷，《春秋》旣托望國之至以大其功；禮以服大國，《春秋》復托望國之至以著其美。此齊桓服楚之功，聖人變齊之效，《春秋》安得不於我公之至屢書而致其意焉？夫膺懲之訓無聞，蠻夷之勢駸駸乎中國。今年以「荆敗蔡」書，明年以「荆伐鄭」書，則楚之蚕食我諸姬者，其患未有紀極也。吁！不有齊桓，中國且奈之何哉？廼今伐楚之役，齊桓之意盖曰：荆楚暴橫，非義不足以格其心；蠻夷陸梁，非義不足以折其勇。故不以兵力為武，不以攻戰為威，唯以義而服之，使兵無血刄之虞，民無暴骨之慘。責以苞茅之不貢，問以昭王之不復，卒之不待兵交而楚人帖服。二百四十二年之間，伯功之盛，惟此時為最。《春秋》於我公反行告廟之際，特書曰：「公至自伐楚。」豈非義以攘外夷，《春秋》托望國之至以大其功乎？迨夫夾輔之誓陵夷，齊景之患駸駸乎我魯。今日以「齊國夏伐我北鄙」書，明日以「齊國夏伐我西鄙」書，則齊之揺蕩我邊鄙者，其患未有遏止也。吁！不有聖人，魯且奈之何哉？廼今夾谷之會，聖人之意盖曰：大敵恣睢，非禮不足以服其心；強國憑凌，非禮不足以格其志。故不千之以盟，不逼之以好，唯以禮而化之。一言之出，却萊人之兵，罷野享之設，以衣冠而化強暴，以禮義而為干櫓，卒之齊景愧悟而王道遂明。二百四十二年之際，聖化之行，唯此時為然。《春秋》
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Instructor Shao: [This essay first recounts Duke Huan of Qi’s subjugation of Chu, and second sets forth the moral transformation of a great state. The topic itself is upright and grand, yet fine essays on it in the examination compound were exceedingly rare. This essay alone narrates events with detailed clarity and is composed with rigorous order—something only one thoroughly versed in this Classic could achieve. All three sessions of his examination are well-matched; he ought to rank first in his Classic.]
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-Waiting Yu: [This essay’s brushwork is vigorous and bold, possessing both decisive judgment and original elucidation; it is an outstanding piece on the Classic of the Unicorn (Spring and Autumn Annals).]
By using righteousness to repel foreign barbarians, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) seized upon the return of the ruler of our esteemed state [of Lu] to magnify that achievement; by using ritual propriety to subdue a great state, the Spring and Autumn Annals again seized upon the return of the ruler of our esteemed state to make manifest that excellence. Given such an achievement as Duke Huan of Qi’s subjugation of Chu, and such an effect as the Sage’s [Confucius’s] transformation of Qi, how could the Spring and Autumn Annals not repeatedly record our Duke’s return so as to convey its deeper meaning?
When the teachings of punishment and chastisement were no longer heard, the power of the southern barbarians encroached steadily upon the Central States. One year it was recorded that "Jing [Chu] defeated Cai," and the next year it was recorded that "Jing attacked Zheng"; thus Chu’s silkworm-like devouring of the states of our royal Ji clan was a menace that knew no bounds. Alas! Had there been no Duke Huan of Qi, what could the Central States have done? Now, in the campaign to attack Chu, Duke Huan’s intention was doubtless to say: "Jing-Chu is violent and overbearing—without righteousness, one cannot rectify its heart; the southern barbarians are unruly and rampant—without righteousness, one cannot break their bravado." Therefore, he did not take military force as martial virtue, nor offensive warfare as awe-inspiring might, but subdued them solely through righteousness, ensuring that soldiers suffered no peril of bloodied blades and the people knew no tragedy of exposed bones. He rebuked them for failing to send tribute of wrappedrush-grass, and interrogated them over King Zhao’s failure to return [from his southern campaign]; in the end, without waiting for armies to clash, the men of Chu submitted docilely. Across the span of two hundred and forty-two years, the flourishing of a hegemon’s achievement was at its very height at this moment. When our Duke returned from the expedition and reported to the ancestral temple, the Spring and Autumn Annals specially recorded: "The Duke arrived from attacking Chu." Was this not because he used righteousness to repel foreign barbarians, and the Spring and Autumn Annals seized upon the return of the ruler of our esteemed state to magnify his achievement?
Later, when the oath of mutual assistance and support fell into decay, the menace of Duke Jing of Qi encroached steadily upon our state of Lu. One day it was recorded that "Guo Xia of Qi attacked our northern border," and the next day it was recorded that "Guo Xia of Qi attacked our western border"; thus Qi’s shaking and disturbing of our frontier settlements was a menace that could not be halted. Alas! Had there been no Sage, what could Lu have done? Now, at the meeting of Jiagu, the Sage’s intention was doubtless to say: "A great enemy is willful and overbearing—without ritual propriety, one cannot subdue its heart; a powerful state bullies and encroaches—without ritual propriety, one cannot rectify its ambition." Therefore, he did not importune[?] them with covenants, nor press them for amity, but transformed them solely through ritual propriety. With the utterance of a single word, he drove back the soldiers of Lai and called off the arrangements for a rustic banquet; using ceremonial robes and caps to transform the violent and strong, and taking ritual propriety and righteousness as his shield and buckler, in the end Duke Jing of Qi was ashamed and awakened, and the Kingly Way was thereby made clear. Across the span of two hundred and forty-two years, the realization of sagely transformation occurred at this moment alone. The Spring and Autumn Annals…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
於我公舎爵策勲之日特書曰公至自夾谷豈非禮以服大國春秋托望國
之至以著其美乎雖然以一時之事功而論則其美或可以並稱以春秋之大法
律之則伯者之功豈可與聖人之化同日而語哉自夫伐楚之後召陵還師
而肆侵陳之忿葵丘震矜而致九國之叛則齊桓雖有其功不能無其過
矣自夫夾谷之後三田來歸既有得齊人之歸心墮郈墮費復有以致三
家之效順則聖人不唯能變齊而又能變魯矣旹伯者之功過不相掩不足
論也惜夫女樂魯庭聖轍汶上吾夫子之心不得直遂於魯可勝嘆哉
禮記
是故聖人之記事也慮之以大愛之以敬行之以禮脩之以孝養
===
紀之以義終之以仁是故古之人一舉事而衆皆知其德之
備也
十三名洪顯
同考試官訓導柴批〔禮經三篇經旨貫徹組織不凡此篇他卷破題於古人一舉處不能包括獨此一破尤妙中間講析節節詳整無隙可議真佳作也四書二篇皆得其旨後場論策善發明條答尤宜〕
前列
考試官教諭邵批〔此篇理明文贍可為程式三場俱優一薦何忝〕
考試官前侍講余批〔四書本經皆詳明此篇破題以篤近舉遠由此達彼為一篇之關鍵傑然超於他作後場〕
論策皆平順宜在前列
觀聖人之記大事篤近而舉遠者其義為甚詳則知古人之舉大事由此
punctuated:
於我公舎爵策勲之日，特書曰：「公至自夾谷。」豈非禮以服大國，《春秋》托望國之至以著其美乎？雖然，以一時之事功而論，則其美或可以並稱；以《春秋》之大法律之，則伯者之功豈可與聖人之化同日而語哉！自夫伐楚之後，召陵還師而肆侵陳之忿，葵丘震矜而致九國之叛，則齊桓雖有其功，不能無其過矣。自夫夾谷之後，三田來歸，既有得齊人之歸心；墮郈、墮費，復有以致三家之效順，則聖人不唯能變齊，而又能變魯矣。旹！伯者之功過不相掩，不足論也；惜夫女樂魯庭，聖轍汶上，吾夫子之心不得直遂於魯，可勝嘆哉！

禮記

是故聖人之記事也，慮之以大，愛之以敬，行之以禮，脩之以孝養，紀之以義，終之以仁。是故古之人一舉事，而衆皆知其德之備也。

十三名洪顯
同考試官訓導柴批：〔《禮經》三篇，經旨貫徹，組織不凡。此篇他卷破題於「古人一舉」處不能包括，獨此一破尤妙。中間講析，節節詳整，無隙可議，真佳作也。《四書》二篇，皆得其旨。後場論、策善發明，條答尤宜〕前列。
考試官教諭邵批：〔此篇理明文贍，可為程式。三場俱優，一薦何忝！〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔《四書》、本經皆詳明。此篇破題以「篤近舉遠，由此達彼」為一篇之關鍵，傑然超於他作。後場〕論、策皆平順，宜在前列。

觀聖人之記大事，篤近而舉遠者，其義為甚詳；則知古人之舉大事，由此
translation_en:
…on the day our Duke drank the cup of return and recorded merits in the ancestral temple, specifically wrote: "The Duke arrived from Jiagu." Is it not because ritual propriety was used to win the submission of a great state that the Spring and Autumn Annals entrusted the recording of the esteemed state's ruler's arrival to manifest its excellence? Even so, if discussed in terms of the practical achievements of a single moment, their merits might perhaps be mentioned together; yet if judged by the great principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals, how could the achievements of a hegemon be spoken of on the same day as the transformative influence of a sage!
