Following the campaign against Chu, when the army returned from Shaoling, he indulged his anger by invading Chen; and at Kuiqiu, his arrogant pride caused the rebellion of nine states—thus although Duke Huan of Qi had his achievements, he was not without his faults. Following the meeting at Jiagu, the lands of the three cities were returned, which already won the allegiance of the people of Qi; and the dismantling of the walls of Hou and Bi further brought about the obedience of the Three Huan families—thus the Sage was able not only to transform Qi, but also to transform Lu. Alas! A hegemon's achievements and faults do not cancel each other out and are not worth discussing; how regrettable that when female musicians entered the court of Lu, the Sage's carriage tracks turned toward the Wen River, and our Master's aspirations could not be directly fulfilled in Lu—how can one sigh enough over this!

Record of Rites (Liji)

"Therefore, when the sages recorded events, they planned them with greatness, loved them with reverence, carried them out with ritual propriety, cultivated them with filial nourishment, regulated them with righteousness, and concluded them with benevolence. Therefore, when the ancients undertook a single affair, all the multitude knew the completeness of their virtue."

13th place: Hong Xian
Comment by Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Chai: [In the three essays on the Classic of Rites, the meaning of the classic is thoroughly penetrated and the structure is extraordinary. In this essay, other papers failed to encompass the part about "when the ancients undertook a single affair" in their opening thesis, whereas this opening alone is especially marvelous. The exposition in the middle is detailed and orderly in every section, leaving no flaw to criticize—truly a fine piece. The two essays on the Four Books both grasp their main purport. In the later sessions, the discourse and policy essays are good at elucidating the themes, and his itemized responses place him particularly fittingly] in the top ranks.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor Shao: [In this essay, the principles are clear and the writing is rich; it can serve as a model answer. He excelled in all three sessions—what shame could there be in recommending him!]
Comment by Examiner, former Expositor-in-waiting Yu: [Both the Four Books and his specialized classic are detailed and clear. The opening thesis of this essay takes "devoting oneself to what is near in order to raise up what is distant, and proceeding from this to reach that" as the key to the whole piece, standing out brilliantly above other works. In the later sessions,] his discourse and policy essays are all smooth and coherent; he ought to be placed in the top ranks.

When we observe that in the sages' recording of great affairs, their devotion to what is near in order to raise up what is distant is most detailed in its meaning, we know that in the ancients' undertaking of great affairs, proceeding from this…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
而達彼者其德無不該夫養老之禮王道之大端也今也聖人篤近以舉遠者
其義無不詳則其推此而達彼者其德又豈有不該者哉記禮者知其然謂
夫虞夏商周皆有養老之禮後王亦皆記序前代之事也然天子莫重於養
老人道莫大於孝弟養老之禮無非謀慮此孝弟之大而推行之此所謂慮
之以大也孝弟莫先於愛愛而弗敬獸畜之也故設三老五更群老之席位
而敬無失焉此所謂愛之以敬也愛之而不以禮則失於徑情而直行故必親迎
肅入登歌合語而行之以禮焉徒禮之而不以養之則為無實而虛拘又必
適饌省醴作樂發咏而脩之以孝養焉孝養既脩又必下管象舞大武
以正君臣之位別貴賤之等而紀之以義焉然此篤近之禮而已又必命鄉
===
遂之群吏畿內之諸侯效法而舉行以及之於遠焉非終之以仁乎然始則
盡禮於一國終則推之於天下矣盖養老之禮孝弟之道也人同此心心同此
道今也一舉於此則孝弟之道達於彼是以衆皆知其德之備者悉由于我
之所以一舉夫大事也謂非篤近而舉遠者其義為甚詳由此以達彼者其
德無不該乎抑又論之養老者孝弟之本而孝弟又治天下之本也虞夏
商周天下之盛王也未有遺年者非天子重養老之禮乎夫以萬乘之尊
而躬行其禮何哉豈非以親親長長必自吾身始而天下人人親其親長其長
而成大同之世歟〔結語亦佳〕故曰立愛惟親立敬惟長始于家邦終于四海豈虛語哉
古之聖人內之為尊外之為樂少之為貴多之為美是故先王
punctuated:
而達彼者，其德無不該。夫養老之禮，王道之大端也。今也，聖人篤近以舉遠者，其義無不詳，則其推此而達彼者，其德又豈有不該者哉？記禮者知其然，謂夫虞、夏、商、周皆有養老之禮，後王亦皆記序前代之事也。然天子莫重於養老，人道莫大於孝弟。養老之禮，無非謀慮此孝弟之大而推行之，此所謂「慮之以大」也。孝弟莫先於愛，愛而弗敬，獸畜之也。故設三老、五更、群老之席位，而敬無失焉，此所謂「愛之以敬」也。愛之而不以禮，則失於徑情而直行，故必親迎、肅入、登歌、合語，而「行之以禮」焉。徒禮之而不以養之，則為無實而虛拘，又必適饌、省醴、作樂、發咏，而「脩之以孝養」焉。孝養既脩，又必下管《象》，舞《大武》，以正君臣之位，別貴賤之等，而「紀之以義」焉。然此篤近之禮而已，又必命鄉遂之群吏、畿內之諸侯效法而舉行，以及之於遠焉，非「終之以仁」乎？然始則盡禮於一國，終則推之於天下矣。盖養老之禮，孝弟之道也。人同此心，心同此道。今也一舉於此，則孝弟之道達於彼。是以衆皆知其德之備者，悉由于我之所以一舉夫大事也。謂非篤近而舉遠者其義為甚詳，由此以達彼者其德無不該乎？抑又論之，養老者，孝弟之本，而孝弟又治天下之本也。虞、夏、商、周，天下之盛王也，未有遺年者，非天子重養老之禮乎？夫以萬乘之尊而躬行其禮，何哉？豈非以親親、長長必自吾身始，而天下人人親其親、長其長，而成大同之世歟？〔結語亦佳〕故曰：「立愛惟親，立敬惟長，始于家邦，終于四海。」豈虛語哉！
古之聖人，內之為尊，外之為樂，少之為貴，多之為美。是故先王
translation_en:
… and extends to that, his virtue is all-encompassing. Now, the rite of nourishing the aged is a great fundamental of the Kingly Way. When the sages devote themselves to what is near in order to raise up what is distant, the meaning is in every respect detailed; when they push from this to reach that, how could their virtue fail to be all-encompassing? The recorder of the rites knew this to be so, stating that Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou all had the rite of nourishing the aged, and that later kings likewise recorded in order the affairs of preceding eras. Yet for the Son of Heaven, nothing is more important than nourishing the aged, and in the way of humanity, nothing is greater than filial piety and fraternal submission. The rite of nourishing the aged is nothing other than deliberating upon the greatness of filial piety and fraternal submission and putting them into practice; this is what is meant by "deliberating upon it with greatness." In filial piety and fraternal submission, nothing comes before love, yet to love without respect is to treat them as domestic animals. Therefore, one sets out the mat positions for the Three Aged, the Five Experienced, and the multitude of elders, so that respect is never lacking; this is what is meant by "loving them with respect." To love them without ritual is to err by giving rein to unmediated feeling and acting without restraint; therefore, one must personally welcome them, respectfully usher them in, have the singers ascend, and join in discourse, thus "carrying it out with ritual." Merely to show them ritual without nourishing them would be empty detention devoid of substance; therefore, one must also go to the food offerings, inspect the sweet wine, strike up music, and chant songs, thus "cultivating it with filial nourishment." Once filial nourishment is cultivated, one must further have the pipes play the Xiang below the hall and perform the dance of Dawu, in order to rectify the positions of ruler and minister, distinguish the grades of noble and base, and thus "regulate it with righteousness." Yet all this is merely the rite of devoting oneself to what is near. One must further command the various officials of the districts and outlying jurisdictions, as well as the feudal lords within the royal domain, to emulate and perform it so as to extend it to what is distant—is this not "consummating it with benevolence"? Thus, in the beginning one exhausts ritual within a single state, and in the end one extends it throughout the realm. For the rite of nourishing the aged is the way of filial piety and fraternal submission. All people share this mind, and all minds share this way. Now, once it is raised up here, the way of filial piety and fraternal submission reaches over there. Therefore, the multitude all know that the completeness of his virtue stems entirely from his raising up this great affair in a single act. Can it not be said that in devoting oneself to what is near and raising up what is distant, its meaning is exceedingly detailed, and in proceeding from this to reach that, its virtue is all-encompassing? Moreover, let us consider this further: nourishing the aged is the root of filial piety and fraternal submission, and filial piety and fraternal submission are in turn the root of governing the realm. Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou were theflourishing kings of the world, and none of them neglected age—was this not because the Son of Heaven attached great weight to the rite of nourishing the aged? Why is it that, with the majesty of the lord of ten thousand chariots, he personally performed this rite? Was it not because treating relatives as relatives and elders as elders must begin with one's own person, so that everyone in the world will treat their relatives as relatives and their elders as elders, thereby bringing about an era of Great Unity? [The concluding remarks are also fine.] Therefore it is said: "To establish love, begin with relatives; to establish respect, begin with elders; it starts in the family and state, and culminates throughout the four seas." How could these be empty words!

"The sages of antiquity esteemed what was internal and took joy in what was external; they valued paucity and admired abundance. Therefore, when the former kings…"…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
之制禮也不可多也不可寡也唯其稱也
同考試官訓導柴批〔四書三篇文理簡順禮經四篇皆熟於經文講習有素此篇發揮內外多寡之義粲〕
〔然可見如觀尺璧畧無纖玷場中礼經無出其右者論策俱有發越允稱前場〕
高薦何忝
考試官教諭邵批〔此篇經旨明白文辭簡浄必深於禮經者宜居前列〕
考試官前侍講余批〔初場七篇理明辭暢冠乎衆作此篇尤有發越場中所未及論策俱優誠有學之〕
士也賓之首選允愜輿論
三名鄭亮
觀聖人之行禮〔破得旨〕隨所寓而有不同當觀聖人之制禮隨所施而無不當夫禮貴
===
乎稱而已然聖人之禮雖有內外多少之不同又豈可過於中而不得其當哉且
夫古之聖人必有德有位之聖人也〔說得明白他卷言不及此〕其為禮者果何如耶盖致其敬而誠若者
心之寓於內者也心寓乎內則純誠之懿幽隱而難窮德產之致微妙而莫測
方寸之間惟精惟一豈不以內為尊乎有美而文而誠若者心之寓乎外者也
心寓乎外則發育萬物吾仁之形著大理物博吾德之發揚心與物交歡忻
悅懌豈不以外為樂乎心之所寓既有不同禮之所施豈無或異是故至
敬無文祭天特牲此禮之以少為貴也外盡其物儀文備舉此禮之以多為
美也其少者豈徒少哉一心之和足以備兩間之和一心之理足以該萬物之理
故不能不以少為貴焉其多者豈徒多哉三牲不備不足以盡祭祀之誠
punctuated:
之制禮也，不可多也，不可寡也，唯其稱也。
同考試官訓導柴批：〔四書三篇，文理簡順；禮經四篇，皆熟於經文，講習有素。此篇發揮內外多寡之義，粲〕〔然可見，如觀尺璧，畧無纖玷，場中礼經無出其右者。論策俱有發越，允稱前場。〕高薦何忝。
考試官教諭邵批：〔此篇經旨明白，文辭簡浄，必深於禮經者，宜居前列。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔初場七篇，理明辭暢，冠乎衆作。此篇尤有發越，場中所未及。論策俱優，誠有學之〕士也。賓之首選，允愜輿論。
三名鄭亮。
觀聖人之行禮，〔破得旨〕隨所寓而有不同；當觀聖人之制禮，隨所施而無不當。夫禮貴乎稱而已。然聖人之禮，雖有內外多少之不同，又豈可過於中而不得其當哉？且夫古之聖人，必有德有位之聖人也。〔說得明白，他卷言不及此〕其為禮者果何如耶？盖致其敬而誠若者，心之寓於內者也。心寓乎內，則純誠之懿，幽隱而難窮；德產之致，微妙而莫測。方寸之間，惟精惟一，豈不以內為尊乎？有美而文而誠若者，心之寓乎外者也。心寓乎外，則發育萬物，吾仁之形著；大理物博，吾德之發揚。心與物交，歡忻悅懌，豈不以外為樂乎？心之所寓既有不同，禮之所施豈無或異？是故至敬無文，祭天特牲，此禮之以少為貴也；外盡其物，儀文備舉，此禮之以多為美也。其少者豈徒少哉？一心之和，足以備兩間之和；一心之理，足以該萬物之理，故不能不以少為貴焉。其多者豈徒多哉？三牲不備，不足以盡祭祀之誠；
translation_en:
…in instituting rites, they may neither be too many nor too few, but only what is fitting.”

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Chai: [His three essays on the Four Books are concise and smooth in reasoning and style; his four essays on the Classic of Rites all show familiarity with the canonical text and well-practiced study. This essay expounds the meaning of internal and external, many and few, with] [brilliant clarity, like beholding a foot-wide jade disk without the slightest flaw; among the essays on the Classic of Rites in the examination hall, none surpasses it. His discourse and policy essays also show spirited insight, truly matching his performance in the first session.] What shame could there be in recommending him for high placement?

Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao: [In this essay, the meaning of the classic is clear and the language is concise and pure. He must be someone deeply versed in the Classic of Rites, and ought to be placed in the front ranks.]

Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-Waiting Yu: [His seven essays in the first session are clear in principle and fluent in expression, crowning all the other compositions. This essay is especially spirited and insightful, reaching what others in the hall did not attain. His discourse and policy essays are both excellent; he is truly a] scholar [of learning]. Welcoming him as a top selection truly satisfies public opinion.

3rd Place: Zheng Liang 鄭亮.

When we observe how the sages practiced rites, [The opening captures the main theme.] they varied according to where the mind was lodged; we ought to observe how the sages instituted rites, which were never inappropriate according to how they were applied. Now, what rites value is simply fittingness. Yet although the rites of the sages differed in being internal or external, many or few, how could they ever exceed the mean and fail to attain what is appropriate? Moreover, the sages of antiquity must have been sages who possessed both virtue and position. [Explained clearly; other papers do not mention this.] How, then, did they perform rites? Reaching the utmost reverence with genuine sincerity is the mind lodged within. When the mind is lodged within, the excellence of pure sincerity is deep, hidden, and hard to exhaust; the perfection of the production of virtue is subtle, wondrous, and unfathomable. Within the square inch of the heart, being refined and single-minded—does this not take the internal as exalted? Possessing beauty and refinement with genuine sincerity is the mind lodged in the external. When the mind is lodged in the external, then in nourishing and developing the myriad things, our benevolence takes manifest form; in the grand ordering of the profusion of things, our virtue is displayed and扬spread forth. As mind and things interact in joyous delight, does this not take the external as joyful? Since where the mind is lodged differs, how could the application of rites not also have differences? Therefore, the utmost reverence has no adornment, and the sacrifice to Heaven uses a single victim: this is rites taking the few as noble. Externally exhausting all material offerings and fully performing every ceremonial form: this is rites taking the many as beautiful. As for what is few, is it merely few? The harmony of a single mind suffices to encompass the harmony between Heaven and Earth; the principle of a single mind suffices to embrace the principles of the myriad things—thus one cannot but take the few as noble. As for what is many, is it merely many? If the three sacrificial victims are not complete, it is insufficient to exhaust the sincerity of sacrifice; …

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
八簋不實不足以表吾心之敬故不能不以多為美焉然禮之行如此聖人
制禮豈可以異於此哉吾見古之先王任君師之責秉制禮之柄商度乎多
寡之宜詳審乎時中之道制其禮之少者如天子無介繁纓一就孰不以為
過乎儉也殊不知少者禮之隱隱非不足之謂而不可以增益也苟可以增益
則奢而過於禮安得謂之稱乎制其禮之多者如天子七廟二十有六豆孰不
以為過乎奢也殊不知多者禮之費費非有餘之謂而不可以減損也苟可
以減損則儉而不及於禮矣又安得謂之稱乎吁羔豚而祭百官皆足太牢
而祭不必有餘此之謂稱也聖人制禮豈有不稱哉大抵心者禮之存禮者心
之發天下之禮簡者非徒簡也必有為之簡者焉詳者非徒詳也必有為
===
之詳者焉記禮者於此既曰古之聖人又曰先王皆欲其禮之稱是拳拳然致謹
於後人者深矣學者豈可以不法先王之遺意哉然則管仲之山節藻梲
晏嬰之豚肩不掩豆〔結尤妙〕是皆謂之不知禮
punctuated: 八簋不實，不足以表吾心之敬，故不能不以多為美焉。然禮之行如此，聖人制禮豈可以異於此哉？吾見古之先王，任君師之責，秉制禮之柄，商度乎多寡之宜，詳審乎時中之道。制其禮之少者，如天子無介、繁纓一就，孰不以為過乎儉也？殊不知少者禮之隱，隱非不足之謂，而不可以增益也；苟可以增益，則奢而過於禮，安得謂之稱乎？制其禮之多者，如天子七廟、二十有六豆，孰不以為過乎奢也？殊不知多者禮之費，費非有餘之謂，而不可以減損也；苟可以減損，則儉而不及於禮矣，又安得謂之稱乎？吁！羔豚而祭，百官皆足；太牢而祭，不必有餘，此之謂稱也。聖人制禮，豈有不稱哉？大抵心者禮之存，禮者心之發。天下之禮，簡者非徒簡也，必有為之簡者焉；詳者非徒詳也，必有為之詳者焉。記禮者於此，既曰「古之聖人」，又曰「先王」，皆欲其禮之稱，是拳拳然致謹於後人者深矣，學者豈可以不法先王之遺意哉？然則管仲之山節藻梲，晏嬰之豚肩不掩豆〔結尤妙〕，是皆謂之不知禮。
translation_en: …if the eight ritual vessels (gui) are not filled, it is insufficient to express the reverence of one's mind; therefore one cannot but take abundance as fine. Yet since the practice of ritual is like this, how could the sages' institution of ritual differ from it? I see that the former kings of antiquity bore the responsibility of ruler and teacher and held the authority to institute ritual, weighing the appropriateness of abundance and paucity and carefully examining the Way of timely equilibrium. When they instituted rituals characterized by paucity—such as the Son of Heaven having no attendant in ritual, or his horse's breast-trapping having only a single loop of dyed silk—who would not consider this overly frugal? Yet they fail to realize that paucity is the subtleness of ritual; subtleness does not mean insufficiency, and it cannot be augmented. If it could be augmented, it would be extravagant and exceed proper ritual—how could it be called fitting? When they instituted rituals characterized by abundance—such as the Son of Heaven having seven ancestral temples and twenty-six offering dishes (dou)—who would not consider this overly extravagant? Yet they fail to realize that abundance is the expansiveness of ritual; expansiveness does not mean surplus, and it cannot be diminished. If it could be diminished, it would be frugal and fall short of proper ritual—how again could it be called fitting? Ah! "When sacrificing with a lamb and suckling pig, all the officials are satisfied; when sacrificing with the Grand Offering of three livestock (tailao), there is not necessarily a surplus"—this is what is meant by being fitting. When the sages instituted ritual, how could anything fail to be fitting? In general, the mind is where ritual is preserved, and ritual is the manifestation of the mind. Among the rituals of the world, those that are simple are not merely simple—there is necessarily a reason that makes them simple; those that are elaborate are not merely elaborate—there is necessarily a reason that makes them elaborate. In this passage, the recorder of the rites first says "the sages of antiquity" and then says "the former kings," in both cases desiring that their rituals be fitting; in this, his earnest care in admonishing later generations is profound indeed! How could scholars fail to model themselves on the bequeathed intentions of the former kings? If that is so, then Guan Zhong's capitals carved with mountains and joists painted with water-plants, and Yan Ying's suckling-pig shoulder not even covering the offering dish [Annotation: The conclusion is especially marvelous.]—both of these are called not knowing ritual.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
第二場
論
繼天立極
一名林時望
同考試官進士方批議論發越層見疊出如行雲流水畧無滯礙異於衆作
考試官教諭邵批立論正大行文精案發明聖人継天立極之意無餘蘊矣
考試官前侍講余批〔文勢沛然其歸美之辭所以立極承天尤為切實結語有力〕
論曰一氣渾然斯道具乎太極兩儀闢矣斯道在乎聖人是則天者道
之所自出聖人者道之所由立天生聖人豈偶然哉盖將以繼天而立民
極也歟今夫穹穹窿窿冲漠無朕蒼然而形乎上者天也蚩蚩蠢蠢聚
===
廬托處林然而散乎下者民也天之於人固未甞不賦之以仁義禮智
之性人之於天亦未甞不得是理以為性也然其氣質之禀或不能齊
是以不能皆有以知其性之所有而全之也一有聰明睿知能盡其性
者出於其間則天必命之以為億兆之君師使之立極以導乎民也
為聖人者知天能賦人以性不能使民皆全其性所以繼天立極之道
當任其責焉故立天下之標準建天下之儀刑語父子則極其親而
天下之為父子者於此而取則焉語君臣則極其義而天下之為君
臣者於此而視傚焉語夫婦則極其别語長幼則極其序而天下之
為夫婦長幼者亦莫不於此而取法焉凡其一動一靜之微一事一
punctuated:
第二場。

論：繼天立極。

一名，林時望。
同考試官、進士方批：議論發越，層見疊出，如行雲流水，畧無滯礙，異於衆作。
考試官、教諭邵批：立論正大，行文精案，發明聖人継天立極之意，無餘蘊矣。
考試官、前侍講余批：〔文勢沛然，其歸美之辭，所以立極承天，尤為切實，結語有力。〕

論曰：一氣渾然，斯道具乎太極；兩儀闢矣，斯道在乎聖人。是則天者，道之所自出；聖人者，道之所由立。天生聖人，豈偶然哉？盖將以繼天而立民極也歟！

今夫穹穹窿窿，冲漠無朕，蒼然而形乎上者，天也；蚩蚩蠢蠢，聚廬托處，林然而散乎下者，民也。天之於人，固未甞不賦之以仁義禮智之性；人之於天，亦未甞不得是理以為性也。然其氣質之禀或不能齊，是以不能皆有以知其性之所有而全之也。一有聰明睿知、能盡其性者出於其間，則天必命之以為億兆之君師，使之立極以導乎民也。為聖人者，知天能賦人以性，不能使民皆全其性，所以繼天立極之道，當任其責焉。故立天下之標準，建天下之儀刑。語父子則極其親，而天下之為父子者於此而取則焉；語君臣則極其義，而天下之為君臣者於此而視傚焉；語夫婦則極其别，語長幼則極其序，而天下之為夫婦長幼者亦莫不於此而取法焉。凡其一動一靜之微，一事一
translation_en:
Second Session.

Discourse: "Succeeding Heaven and Establishing the Ultimate Standard" (Ji Tian li ji).

First-ranked candidate: Lin Shiwang 林時望.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: The argument is spirited and elevated, with points emerging layer upon layer; like drifting clouds and flowing water, it is completely free of obstruction and stands apart from the other compositions.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao 邵: The thesis is upright and grand, and the composition is refined and well-considered [? 案 for 密/妥]; it elucidates the meaning of how the sage succeeds Heaven and establishes the ultimate standard without leaving anything unexpressed.
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Yu 余: [The momentum of the prose is torrential. Its words of praise regarding how the ultimate standard is established in succession to Heaven are especially concrete and substantial, and the concluding remarks are forceful.]

The discourse reads: When the single vital force (qi) was an undifferentiated whole, this Way was complete within the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji); once the Two Modes (Heaven and Earth) opened apart, this Way resided in the sages. Thus, Heaven is that from which the Way originates, and the sage is that through whom the Way is established. When Heaven gives birth to a sage, how could it be by chance? Surely it is in order to succeed Heaven and establish the ultimate standard for the people!

Now, that which arches high and vast, empty and boundless without a trace, taking form in azure above, is Heaven; those who are simple and teeming, gathering in huts to dwell, scattered like a forest below, are the people. In its relation to human beings, Heaven has never failed to endow them with a nature of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom; and in their relation to Heaven, human beings have likewise never failed to obtain this principle as their nature. Yet because the endowments of their physical constitution (qizhi) cannot be uniform, they cannot all know what their nature possesses and keep it whole. Once there appears among them someone of acute hearing, clear sight, and profound wisdom who is able to fully realize his nature, Heaven inevitably commands him to act as ruler and teacher of the millions of people, causing him to establish the ultimate standard in order to guide the people. He who is a sage knows that while Heaven can endow human beings with their nature, it cannot cause the people all to keep their nature whole; therefore, he must take upon himself the responsibility for the Way of succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard. Thus he sets up the criterion for the world and erects the model for the world. Speaking of father and son, he carries affection to the utmost, and all fathers and sons in the world take their rule from this; speaking of ruler and minister, he carries righteousness to the utmost, and all rulers and ministers in the world look to and emulate this; speaking of husband and wife, he carries distinction to the utmost, and speaking of elder and younger, he carries order to the utmost, and none of the husbands and wives or elders and youths in the world fail to take their model from this. In all the subtleties of a single movement or a single moment of quiescence, and in the course of every single affair and every single…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
物之際莫不極其義理之當然盡其精微之極致足以為天下法而
後継天立極之責始盡矣然天不徒曰極而必謂之繼者于以見天不
能為而繼之者在乎聖人極不徒曰極而必謂之立者于以見民不自
立而立之者在乎聖人聖人也者其繼天立極之宗主也歟夷考諸古
伏羲神農黃帝繼天立極其來尚矣其見於經允執厥中堯之所
以授舜舜之所以授禹也此堯舜禹以繼天為心而盡其立極之責也
建中於民者商湯也皇建其有極者周武也此湯武以継天為心而
盡其立極之道也然是極也不以前聖而能立不以後聖而不盡洪惟
太祖高皇帝全聰明睿智之資備聖神文武之德龍飛淮甸統一萬方申
===
明五常之誥奉乎續篇之首五教育民之條諄諄乎
聖誥之中其繼天立極之責無不盡矣
太宗文皇帝纘承
鴻基盡繼述之大孝尊臨
大寶統馭華夷慮民之不為善也則為善陰隲之書昭如也恐民之不
盡孝也則孝順事實之書秩如也其繼天立極之道亦無不至矣
論至於是則堯舜禹湯之所執所建者此極也
太祖
太宗之所頒所輯者亦立此極也世有先後而継天立極曠百世而同一心時
punctuated: 物之際，莫不極其義理之當然，盡其精微之極致，足以為天下法，而後継天立極之責始盡矣。然天不徒曰極，而必謂之繼者，于以見天不能為而繼之者在乎聖人；極不徒曰極，而必謂之立者，于以見民不自立而立之者在乎聖人。聖人也者，其繼天立極之宗主也歟！夷考諸古，伏羲、神農、黃帝繼天立極，其來尚矣。其見於經：「允執厥中」，堯之所以授舜、舜之所以授禹也，此堯、舜、禹以繼天為心而盡其立極之責也；「建中於民」者，商湯也；「皇建其有極」者，周武也，此湯、武以継天為心而盡其立極之道也。然是極也，不以前聖而能立，不以後聖而不盡。洪惟太祖高皇帝，全聰明睿智之資，備聖神文武之德，龍飛淮甸，統一萬方，《申明五常之誥》奉乎續篇之首，五教育民之條諄諄乎《聖誥》之中，其繼天立極之責無不盡矣。太宗文皇帝纘承鴻基，盡繼述之大孝，尊臨大寶，統馭華夷，慮民之不為善也，則《為善陰隲》之書昭如也；恐民之不盡孝也，則《孝順事實》之書秩如也，其繼天立極之道亦無不至矣。論至於是，則堯、舜、禹、湯之所執、所建者，此極也；太祖、太宗之所頒、所輯者，亦立此極也。世有先後，而継天立極，曠百世而同一心；時有…
translation_en:
…and thing, there is none in which he does not reach the ultimate of what moral principle requires and exhaust the utmost limit of subtlety and refinement, sufficient to serve as a model for all under Heaven; only then is the responsibility of succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard finally fulfilled. Yet as for Heaven, one does not merely speak of the ultimate standard, but must call it "succeeding"—by this we see that what Heaven cannot do for itself, it is the sage who succeeds in doing it. And as for the ultimate standard, one does not merely speak of the ultimate standard, but must call it "establishing"—by this we see that the common people cannot establish it for themselves, and it is the sage who establishes it. The sage—is he not the sovereign master of succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard!

When we calmly examine antiquity, Fuxi, Shennong, and the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) succeeded Heaven and established the ultimate standard; its origins go back a very long way. As for what appears in the Classics: "Sincerely hold fast the Mean" is what Yao transmitted to Shun, and what Shun transmitted to Yu. In this, Yao, Shun, and Yu took succeeding Heaven as their mind and fulfilled their responsibility of establishing the ultimate standard. He who "established the Mean among the people" was Tang of Shang; he who declared "the Sovereign establishes his ultimate standard" was Wu of Zhou. In this, Tang and Wu took succeeding Heaven as their mind and exhausted the Way of establishing the ultimate standard. Yet this ultimate standard is not something that could be established only by the former sages, nor something that fails to be fully realized by the later sages.

We humbly reflect upon Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), who possessed in full a nature of intelligence and perspicacious wisdom, and was endowed completely with sagely, divine, civil, and martial virtue. Like a dragon taking flight from the Huai region, he unified the myriad regions. The Proclamation Clarifying the Five Constant Virtues (Shenming wuchang zhi gao) was revered at the head of the Sequel compilation, and the articles on the five teachings for instructing the people were earnestly repeated throughout the Sacred Proclamations (Shenggao); his responsibility in succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard was fulfilled in every respect. Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor) inherited the great foundation and fulfilled the great filial piety of continuing and transmitting. Ascending in majesty to the Great Treasure, he governed both Chinese and non-Chinese. Concerned lest the people not do good, the book Rewards of Doing Good in Secret (Weishan yinzhi) was made radiant; fearing lest the people not exhaust filial piety, the book True Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) was set in orderly array. His Way of succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard likewise reached the utmost in every respect.

When our discussion reaches this point, what Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang held fast to and established was this very ultimate standard; and what the Grand Progenitor (Taizu) and Grand Ancestor (Taizong) promulgated and compiled was likewise the establishment of this very ultimate standard. Generations come earlier and later, yet in succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard, across a hundred generations there is the same single mind; eras…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
有古今而繼天立極越萬古而同一道曽謂前聖後聖而有異哉噫
堯舜逺矣湯武邈矣承
列聖之統盡繼天立極之道幸有今日
聖人在上愚何幸身親見之
同前三名鄭亮
同考試官訓導柴批〔起語好中間以中字發越使繼立之意明白可見乞辨初場〕
考試官教諭邵批命意措辭異於衆作
考試官前侍講余批筆力老健文辭簡潔
夫天之生聖人也豈偶然哉兩儀聚精貞元會合然後一聖人出焉生
===
而神靈聰明睿智而任乎參賛之重茫茫乎其大窈窈乎其神以此知
天之生聖人者不偶也天之生聖人者不偶則所以繼天之道立人之極
為天地立心為生民立命為萬世開太平者安得不資於聖人者
哉紫陽朱夫子所謂上古聖神繼天立極者愚請得而論之夫
太古鴻荒之世風氣未開人文未著民方巢居穴處茹毛飲血
又烏知其孰為天道孰為人極也由是天之生聖人有伏羲氏畫
八卦以發天地之藏神農氏作耒耜以教天下之耕黄帝作律吕
以宣天地之和制衣裳以法乾坤之象神而化之使民宜之裁成天
地之道輔相天地之宜逮乎風氣既宣人文已著堯命官造曆而敬
punctuated:
有古今，而繼天立極，越萬古而同一道。曽謂前聖後聖而有異哉？噫！堯、舜逺矣，湯、武邈矣。承列聖之統，盡繼天立極之道，幸有今日聖人在上，愚何幸身親見之。

同前，三名鄭亮。
同考試官訓導柴批：〔起語好，中間以「中」字發越，使繼、立之意明白，可見乞辨初場。〕
考試官教諭邵批：命意措辭，異於衆作。
考試官前侍講余批：筆力老健，文辭簡潔。

夫天之生聖人也，豈偶然哉？兩儀聚精，貞元會合，然後一聖人出焉。生而神靈，聰明睿智，而任乎參賛之重。茫茫乎其大，窈窈乎其神，以此知天之生聖人者不偶也。天之生聖人者不偶，則所以繼天之道、立人之極，為天地立心、為生民立命、為萬世開太平者，安得不資於聖人者哉？紫陽朱夫子所謂「上古聖神，繼天立極」者，愚請得而論之。夫太古鴻荒之世，風氣未開，人文未著，民方巢居穴處，茹毛飲血，又烏知其孰為天道、孰為人極也？由是天之生聖人，有伏羲氏畫八卦以發天地之藏；神農氏作耒耜以教天下之耕；黄帝作律吕以宣天地之和，制衣裳以法乾坤之象，神而化之，使民宜之，裁成天地之道，輔相天地之宜。逮乎風氣既宣，人文已著，堯命官造曆而敬
translation_en:
…times may be ancient or modern, yet in succeeding to Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard, across ten thousand ages it is the same single Way. Could it ever be said that the former sages and later sages differed? Alas! Yao and Shun are distant; Tang and Wu are far away. Yet in inheriting the succession of the line of sages and fulfilling the Way of succeeding to Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard, how fortunate that today there is a Sage on high, and how fortunate am I, ignorant though I am, to witness it in person!

On the same topic as the preceding; third-ranked candidate, Zheng Liang 鄭亮.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Chai 柴: [The opening words are good. In the middle section, he develops the theme through the word "equilibrium" (zhong 中), making the meaning of "succeeding" and "establishing" clear. From this one can discern the quality of his first-session papers [?].]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao 邵: Its conception and phrasing stand apart from the ordinary compositions.
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-Waiting Yu 余: The brushwork is mature and vigorous; the diction is concise and clean.

Now when Heaven gives birth to a sage, how could it be by chance? The Two Modes gather their essence, the cosmic cycles of completion and renewal converge, and only then does a sage emerge. Born divine and numinous, intelligent, perspicacious, and wise, he shoulders the grave responsibility of participating in the transformative nourishing of Heaven and Earth. Vast is his greatness, profound is his inscrutable spirit! By this we know that Heaven's giving birth to a sage is no accident. Since Heaven's giving birth to a sage is no accident, then when it comes to succeeding to the Way of Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard for humanity—establishing a heart for Heaven and Earth, establishing a destiny for the living people, and opening up great peace for ten thousand generations—how could this not depend upon the sage? As for what Master Zhu 朱 of Ziyang 紫陽 (Zhu Xi 朱熹) called "the divine sages of high antiquity succeeding to Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard," I humbly beg leave to discuss it. In the primordial age of remote antiquity, civilizing influences had not yet opened and human culture was not yet manifest. The people were still dwelling in nests and living in caves, eating hair and drinking blood—how could they know what was the Way of Heaven or what was the Supreme Standard of humanity? Therefore Heaven gave birth to sages: there was Fuxi 伏羲, who drew the Eight Trigrams to reveal the hidden treasures of Heaven and Earth; Shennong 神農, who fashioned plows and plowshares to teach the world agriculture; and the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi 黄帝), who created the pitch-pipes to diffuse the harmony of Heaven and Earth, and tailored upper and lower garments in imitation of the images of Qian 乾 and Kun 坤, spiritually transforming things so as to make them fitting for the people, regulating and completing the Way of Heaven and Earth, and assisting the suitability of Heaven and Earth. Coming down to the time when civilizing influences had been diffused and human culture had become manifest, Yao 堯 commanded his officials to devise the calendar and reverently…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
授人時舜在璇璣玉衡以齊七政則制器尚象上有以推測乎天
道慎徽五典下有以明叙乎人倫皆所以繼天立極者也堯傳之舜
舜傳之禹則曰允執厥中是聖人繼天立極之道不外乎中也湯曰
建中建極武王曰皇建其有極是繼天之道亦不外乎中也中也極
也皆自上古聖神相繼而傳道統者也觀其叙曰天叙秩曰天秩
立父子之親定君臣之義於夫婦也教之以有别於長幼朋友也教
之以序以信所謂立人極者此也蓋全體自然曰天聖人承其自然
故於天而謂之繼人物標準曰極聖人制其當然故於極而謂之
立天道也人極也皆具於聖人之心而敷教於天下後世者也故子朱
===
子序中庸之書而著其繼天立極之言以見聖人之相傳有自來
矣吁達而上古聖神二帝三王有以行繼天立極之道於當時窮而
在下有孔子顏曾思孟有以傳繼天立極之道於萬世堯舜遠
矣孔子邈矣洪惟
太祖高皇帝禀聖神文武之資備仁義禮智之德
太宗文皇帝道包六合德冠百王
仁宗昭皇帝行二帝三王之道體二帝三王之心是皆繼天立極以傳前聖
之統者也
皇上德侔天地明並日月繼志述事以承
punctuated: 授人時，舜在璇璣玉衡以齊七政。則制器尚象，上有以推測乎天道；慎徽五典，下有以明叙乎人倫，皆所以繼天立極者也。堯傳之舜，舜傳之禹，則曰「允執厥中」，是聖人繼天立極之道不外乎中也。湯曰「建中建極」，武王曰「皇建其有極」，是繼天之道亦不外乎中也。中也，極也，皆自上古聖神相繼而傳道統者也。觀其叙曰「天叙」，秩曰「天秩」，立父子之親，定君臣之義；於夫婦也，教之以有别；於長幼、朋友也，教之以序、以信，所謂立人極者此也。蓋全體自然曰天，聖人承其自然，故於天而謂之繼；人物標準曰極，聖人制其當然，故於極而謂之立。天道也，人極也，皆具於聖人之心，而敷教於天下後世者也。故子朱子序《中庸》之書，而著其「繼天立極」之言，以見聖人之相傳有自來矣。吁！達而上古聖神、二帝、三王，有以行繼天立極之道於當時；窮而在下，有孔子、顏、曾、思、孟，有以傳繼天立極之道於萬世。堯、舜遠矣，孔子邈矣！洪惟太祖高皇帝禀聖神文武之資，備仁義禮智之德；太宗文皇帝道包六合，德冠百王；仁宗昭皇帝行二帝三王之道，體二帝三王之心，是皆繼天立極以傳前聖之統者也。皇上德侔天地，明並日月，繼志述事，以承
translation_en:
… deliver the seasons to the people, and Shun examined the jade-adorned armillary sphere and sighting tube to align the Seven Regulators. Thus, by fashioning instruments and valuing symbolic representations, above they had the means to calculate and fathom the Way of Heaven; by carefullybeautifying the Five Cardinal Duties, below they had the means to clarify and order human relationships—all of this was whereby they succeeded Heaven and established the Supreme Standard. When Yao transmitted it to Shun, and Shun transmitted it to Yu, it was said, "Sincerely hold fast the Mean"; thus the Way by which the sages succeeded Heaven and established the Supreme Standard lies in nothing outside the Mean. Tang said, "Establish the Mean and establish the Standard," and King Wu said, "The august sovereign establishes his Supreme Standard"; thus the Way of succeeding Heaven also lies in nothing outside the Mean. Both the Mean and the Standard have been passed down in succession from the divine sages of high antiquity in transmitting the orthodoxy of the Way (daotong). Observe how the social arrangements are called "Heaven's arrangements" and the ritual order is called "Heaven's order": establishing the affection between father and son, fixing the righteousness between ruler and minister, teaching distinction between husband and wife, and teaching precedence between old and young and trustworthiness between friends—this is what is meant by establishing the Supreme Standard for humanity. Indeed, that whose entire substance is natural spontaneity is called Heaven; the sage inherits its natural spontaneity, and therefore with respect to Heaven it is called "succeeding." The standard for human beings and things is called the Supreme Standard; the sage institutes what ought to be, and therefore with respect to the Supreme Standard it is called "establishing." Both the Way of Heaven and the Supreme Standard for humanity are complete within the mind of the sage and are spread forth as teachings to all under Heaven and to future generations. Therefore Master Zhu [Zhu Xi], in writing his preface to the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), set forth his words on "succeeding Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard" in order to show that the transmission from sage to sage had its origin.

Alas! When in high station, the divine sages of high antiquity, the Two Emperors, and the Three Kings had the means to put into practice the Way of succeeding Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard in their own times; when in obscurity and in a lowly position, Confucius, Yan [Hui], Zeng [Can], Zisi, and Mencius had the means to transmit the Way of succeeding Heaven and establishing the Supreme Standard to ten thousand generations. Yao and Shun are distant indeed; Confucius is far away indeed! Yet we reverently reflect that Grand Progenitor the Exalted Emperor (Taizu Gao Huangdi) was endowed with sagely, divine, civil, and martial qualities and was complete in the virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom; Grand Ancestor the Cultured Emperor (Taizong Wen Huangdi) encompassed the six directions with his Way and crowned the hundred kings with his virtue; and Benevolent Ancestor the Illustrious Emperor (Renzong Zhao Huangdi) practiced the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings and embodied the minds of the Two Emperors and Three Kings—all of them succeeded Heaven and established the Supreme Standard so as to transmit the line of the former sages. His Majesty the Reigning Emperor equals Heaven and Earth in virtue, matches the sun and moon in brilliance, carries forward their intentions and continues their enterprises, so as to inherit …

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
三聖之統故曰先聖後聖其揆一也敢以是為論
擬唐虞世南上聖德論表十九名龔錡
考試官教諭邵批表得唐體詞不雷同
考試官前侍講余批典雅可觀
切以
天開景運膺曆數之在躬世際雍熈握乾符而受命一人有慶四海
咸歸六合同春兆民是賴恭惟
○○○○天錫勇智大興湯武之師日新聖明上継唐虞之治功高莫極
德盛難名得惟精惟一之傳紹乃武乃文之聖求賢常若不及
===
從諫有如轉丸惟五帝足以比其休匪三王莫能方其盛山高
海闊曷伸賛頌之辞日照月臨奚罄名言之妙臣一介賤士三
才末流叨蒙舘職之榮素乏論思之益丹衷激切敢効言於芻
蕘
睿覽昭明庶鍳誠於葵藿尚冀緝熈聖學川方至而日方升鞏固
皇圖天與長而地與久謹撰聖德論随表上進
第三塲
策
第一問一名林時望
punctuated:
三聖之統，故曰：「先聖後聖，其揆一也。」敢以是為論。

擬唐虞世南上《聖德論》表。十九名龔錡。
考試官教諭邵批：表得唐體，詞不雷同。
考試官前侍講余批：典雅可觀。

切以天開景運，膺曆數之在躬；世際雍熈，握乾符而受命。一人有慶，四海咸歸；六合同春，兆民是賴。恭惟○○○○，天錫勇智，大興湯、武之師；日新聖明，上継唐、虞之治。功高莫極，德盛難名。得惟精惟一之傳，紹乃武乃文之聖。求賢常若不及，從諫有如轉丸。惟五帝足以比其休，匪三王莫能方其盛。山高海闊，曷伸賛頌之辞；日照月臨，奚罄名言之妙。臣一介賤士，三才末流，叨蒙舘職之榮，素乏論思之益。丹衷激切，敢効言於芻蕘；睿覽昭明，庶鍳誠於葵藿。尚冀緝熈聖學，川方至而日方升；鞏固皇圖，天與長而地與久。謹撰《聖德論》随表上進。

第三塲
策
第一問。一名林時望。
translation_en:
… the succession of the Three Sages. Therefore it is said: "Earlier sages and later sages, their principles are one and the same." I venture to offer this as my discourse.

Memorial Imitating Yu Shinan 虞世南 of the Tang Presenting the "Discourse on Sagely Virtue" (Shengde lun). 19th-ranked Gong Qi 龔錡.
Examiner, Instructor Shao 邵, comments: The memorial captures the Tang style, and its phrasing is not hackneyed.
Examiner, Former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余, comments: Classically elegant and worthy of appreciation.

Your servant竊 [humbly] reflects that as Heaven opens an auspicious destiny, Your Majesty bears the calendrical mandate in your own person; as the world meets with harmonious peace, You grasp the talisman of Heaven and receive the Mandate. When the One Man rejoices, all within the four seas submit in allegiance; the six directions share in a common spring, and the myriad people depend upon You. Reverently considering [Your Majesty, ○○○○], Heaven has bestowed courage and wisdom upon You, and You grandly raised armies like those of Tang 湯 and Wu 武; daily renewing Your sagely enlightenment, You continue above the governance of Yao 唐 and Shun 虞. Your achievements are so lofty as to have no limit; Your virtue is so flourishing as to defy naming. You have attained the transmission of "being refined and being single-minded," and succeeded to the sageliness of "being martial and being civil." You seek out the worthy as if never quite reaching them, and follow remonstrance as effortlessly as rolling a pellet. Only the Five Emperors suffice to be compared to Your felicity; none but the Three Kings can match Your splendor. High as the mountains and vast as the seas, how could one fully extend words of praise and eulogy? Shining like the sun and overseeing like the moon, how could one exhaust the subtlety of descriptive language? Your servant is a lowly scholar of mean estate, at the very bottom of the Three Powers; having undeservedly received the honor of an historiography-academy post, I have ever lacked the benefit of offering deliberative counsel. With my sincere heart deeply stirred, I dare to offer the words of a grass-cutter and firewood-gatherer; before Your sagely and luminous perusal, may my sunflower-like devotion be discerned. I still hope that You will continue to render radiant Your sagely learning, like a stream just arriving and the sun just rising; and consolidate the imperial domain, enduring as long as Heaven and lasting as long as Earth. I have reverently composed the "Discourse on Sagely Virtue" and present it accompanying this memorial.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question. 1st-ranked Lin Shiwang 林時望.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
同考試官進士方批〔文勢滔滔不冗不泛重以四君子自期誠抱負卓然之士矣〕
考試官敎諭邵批〔此策不拘拘於問目以胷中素蘊吐辭成文學識優長抱負不小他日所就其可量乎深加敬羨〕
考試官前侍講余批〔辭意高邁志氣超卓出群拔萃者也〕
高崗之鳳必於隆盛之世而始鳴大野之麟必於文明之時而始見
負有為之人才必於聖明之君而後出焉此氣類之相感理勢之必然
夫豈偶然之故哉棘闈秋開多士雲集執事典文衡策承學首
以
大誥陰隲書為問豈以當代之制作正學者所當講也請因明問以復可乎夫
有一代之君必有一代之臣有一代之臣必匡一代之治恭惟
===
太祖高皇帝稟聰明睿智之資備聖神文武之德龍飛江左統馭華夷拳
拳以福民為心切切以圖治為務萬機之暇條成
大誥於序有曰立綱陳紀為民造福又曰君臣同心志同一氣大哉
皇言乎其望群臣同心輔弼共成一代之治乎故自涖祚以來餘六十年其間
或以碩才而居廟堂或以正直而司風紀職方面者濟濟乎有為之
賢任守令者彬彬乎有能之士內外之臣不同而立綱陳紀者同一心大
小之職不一而為民造福者同一志故能措天下於泰山躋黎元於仁壽
材生總聚者咸席景星慶雲之下聚廬托處者同囿春臺玉燭之中
其治效之隆殆與唐虞黎民於變之風三代直道而行之俗同一轍矣
punctuated:
同考試官進士方批：〔文勢滔滔，不冗不泛，重以四君子自期，誠抱負卓然之士矣。〕
考試官敎諭邵批：〔此策不拘拘於問目，以胷中素蘊，吐辭成文。學識優長，抱負不小，他日所就，其可量乎？深加敬羨。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔辭意高邁，志氣超卓，出群拔萃者也。〕
高崗之鳳，必於隆盛之世而始鳴；大野之麟，必於文明之時而始見；負有為之人才，必於聖明之君而後出焉。此氣類之相感，理勢之必然，夫豈偶然之故哉？棘闈秋開，多士雲集，執事典文衡，策承學，首以《大誥》、《陰隲》書為問，豈以當代之制作，正學者所當講也？請因明問以復，可乎？夫有一代之君，必有一代之臣；有一代之臣，必匡一代之治。恭惟太祖高皇帝稟聰明睿智之資，備聖神文武之德，龍飛江左，統馭華夷。拳拳以福民為心，切切以圖治為務。萬機之暇，條成《大誥》，於序有曰：「立綱陳紀，為民造福。」又曰：「君臣同心，志同一氣。」大哉皇言乎！其望群臣同心輔弼，共成一代之治乎！故自涖祚以來，餘六十年，其間或以碩才而居廟堂，或以正直而司風紀，職方面者濟濟乎有為之賢，任守令者彬彬乎有能之士。內外之臣不同，而立綱陳紀者同一心；大小之職不一，而為民造福者同一志。故能措天下於泰山，躋黎元於仁壽，材生總聚者咸席景星慶雲之下，聚廬托處者同囿春臺玉燭之中。其治效之隆，殆與唐虞黎民於變之風、三代直道而行之俗，同一轍矣。
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang: [The momentum of the writing surges forth, neither verbose nor diffuse. Moreover, he holds himself to the standard of the Four Worthies; truly he is a scholar of outstanding aspirations.]
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao: [This policy essay does not rigidly bind itself to the sub-topics of the question, but pours forth words into prose from the long-held stores of his breast. His learning and insight are superior, and his aspirations are not small. How could his future achievements be measured? I deeply admire and esteem him.]
Comment by Examiner, former Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Yu: [His words and ideas are lofty and surpassing, his ambition and spirit transcendent—one who stands out far above the crowd.]

The phoenix on the high ridge sings only in an age of flourishing prosperity; the unicorn in the great wilderness appears only in a time of civil enlightenment; and men of talent who possess the capacity for great deeds emerge only under a sage and enlightened ruler. This is the mutual resonance of kindred qi and the inevitable course of principle and circumstance—how could it be a matter of mere chance? In autumn the thorny examination compound opens and the multitude of scholars gather like clouds. Your Excellency presides over the literary balance and puts policy questions to us junior scholars, asking first about the books Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) and Secret Blessings (Yinzhi). Is it not because the institutions and works of our own dynasty are precisely what scholars ought to study and discuss? May I request permission to reply by following your enlightened question?

Now, where there is the ruler of an era, there must be the ministers of that era; where there are the ministers of an era, they must assist in bringing about the governance of that era. Reverently we reflect that Emperor Gao, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu), was endowed with a nature of keen intelligence and profound wisdom, and possessed to the full the virtues of sagehood, divinity, civil attainment, and martial vigor. Like a dragon he soared from the lower Yangtze (Jiangzuo) to unify and rule both Chinese and barbarians. Earnestly he took blessing the people as his heart, and urgently he took planning for good governance as his task. In his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, he compiled the articles of the Grand Pronouncements. In its preface it is said: "To establish the major cords and set forth the minor meshes of the law, creating blessings for the people." And again it says: "Ruler and ministers of one mind, their wills united in a single qi." Great indeed are the Imperial words! How deeply he hoped that all his ministers would assist him with one heart, together accomplishing the governance of an era!

Therefore, since the founding of the throne more than sixty years ago, during that time some have occupied the imperial court by virtue of great talent, while others have presided over discipline and law through uprightness; those charged with regional administration have been an abundant multitude of capable worthies, and those appointed as prefects and magistrates have been a refined array of able scholars. Officials of the inner court and outer provinces differ, yet in establishing the major cords and setting forth the minor meshes they are of one mind; offices great and small are not the same, yet in creating blessings for the people they are of one will. Thus they have been able to place the realm upon the security of Mount Tai and raise the common people to benevolence and longevity. Those of talent who gather together all sit beneath auspicious stars and felicitous clouds; those who cluster their huts and find shelter all dwell together within the vernal terrace and the jade-like harmony of the seasons. The flourishing efficacy of this governance follows almost the very same track as the wind of the black-haired people being transformed under Tang Yao and Yu Shun, and the customs of walking the straight path during the Three Dynasties.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
太宗文皇帝纘承丕緒一遵
成憲道已至矣而尤以為未至治已隆矣而尤以為未隆心
太祖之心法
太祖之法庶務之餘采輯古今為善陰隲者百六十五人纂次成書梓行天
下其間若仲淹之經濟安撫江淮則民懷賑恤元昊犯順則請自
行邊趙抃之讞疑節度武安而辨赦後之冤出知成都而宥劔
民之死富弼守青州而活京東之流民蘇軾知徐州而禦彭城之
水患之數君子者無非政績之顯於當時者也然
太祖大誥之頒豈徒然歟蓋欲群臣佩服
===
聖誥之㫖而以福民為心也
太宗陰隲之布豈無意歟蓋欲天下遍觀前代之賢以為今日之法也愚
也欽承三誥一書已久樂菁莪之教已深其於明體適用之
學雖未可知與斯賓興之典行將嚮用使他日居廟堂之
高必以仲淹之心為心司風紀之要必以趙抃之法為法方面
之職必欲踵跡於富弼守令之任必欲比肩於蘇軾豈使數
君子專美於前代乎恭承明問姑述其槩以復願進教之
幸甚
punctuated:
太宗文皇帝纘承丕緒，一遵成憲，道已至矣，而尤以為未至；治已隆矣，而尤以為未隆。心太祖之心，法太祖之法，庶務之餘，采輯古今《為善陰隲》者百六十五人，纂次成書，梓行天下。其間若仲淹之經濟，安撫江淮則民懷賑恤，元昊犯順則請自行邊；趙抃之讞疑，節度武安而辨赦後之冤，出知成都而宥劔民之死；富弼守青州而活京東之流民；蘇軾知徐州而禦彭城之水患。之數君子者，無非政績之顯於當時者也。然太祖《大誥》之頒，豈徒然歟？蓋欲群臣佩服聖誥之㫖，而以福民為心也。太宗《陰隲》之布，豈無意歟？蓋欲天下遍觀前代之賢，以為今日之法也。

愚也欽承三《誥》、一書已久，樂菁莪之教已深。其於明體適用之學雖未可知，與斯賓興之典，行將嚮用。使他日居廟堂之高，必以仲淹之心為心；司風紀之要，必以趙抃之法為法；方面之職，必欲踵跡於富弼；守令之任，必欲比肩於蘇軾。豈使數君子專美於前代乎？恭承明問，姑述其槩以復，願進教之，幸甚。
translation_en:
Emperor Wen, the Grand Ancestor (Taizong 太宗), succeeded to the great enterprise and wholly followed the established constitutions. Although the Way had already reached perfection, he still considered it imperfect; although governance had already reached the height of prosperity, he still considered it insufficiently prosperous. Taking the mind of the Grand Progenitor (Taizu 太祖) as his mind and modeling himself on the laws of the Grand Progenitor, in his leisure from the myriad affairs of state he gathered accounts from antiquity to the present of one hundred and sixty-five individuals who did good and accrued hidden virtue (Weishan yinzhi 為善陰隲), compiling them in order into a book and printing it for circulation throughout the realm. Among those included: there was the statecraft of Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹—when serving as Pacification Commissioner of the Jiang-Huai region, the people cherished his famine relief, and when Yuanhao 元昊 rebelled against allegiance, he requested to go in person to patrol the frontier; there was Zhao Bian 趙抃's adjudication of doubtful cases—serving on the staff of the Military Commissioner of Wu'an, he cleared up an injustice committed after an amnesty, and going out as Prefect of Chengdu, he pardoned the death sentence of the people of Jianzhou; there was Fu Bi 富弼, who as Prefect of Qingzhou saved the refugees of Jingdong; and there was Su Shi 蘇軾, who as Prefect of Xuzhou warded off the flood disaster at Pengcheng. Every one of these several gentlemen was renowned in his own time for administrative achievements. Yet was the Grand Progenitor's promulgation of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao 大誥) done in vain? Surely he desired that all ministers take to heart the purport of the sacred pronouncements and make blessing the people their mind. And was the Grand Ancestor's dissemination of the Hidden Virtue (Yinzhi 陰隲) devoid of intent? Surely he desired that the whole realm survey the worthies of former dynasties and take them as models for today.

In my simplicity, I have long reverently received the three Grand Pronouncements and this one book, and have deeply delighted in the nurturing education of the schools. Although I cannot yet claim to know the learning that illuminates fundamental substance and applies it to practical use, having participated in this ceremony of recommending worthies (the Provincial Examination), I am about to be advanced for employment. Should I some day occupy a high position in the imperial court, I will surely take the mind of Fan Zhongyan as my mind; should I be in charge of an important post maintaining moral discipline and the laws, I will surely take the methods of Zhao Bian as my model; in a regional or provincial post, I will surely wish to follow in the footsteps of Fu Bi; and in the office of prefect or magistrate, I will surely wish to stand shoulder to shoulder with Su Shi. How could I let those several gentlemen monopolize such excellence in former dynasties? Reverently receiving your enlightened question, I tentatively set forth this general outline in reply, and earnestly pray that you will grant me further instruction—it would be my greatest fortune.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
第二問
一名林時望
同考試官進士方批〔文辭典實敷荅詳明終以心貫六經之義尤見本識〕
考試官敎諭邵批〔觀此一策學識深遠筆力老蒼論六經之用雖殊而其理則一貫而通之皆本於聖人之心非〕
〔有卓然之見者不能發明如此宜魁多士〕
考試官前侍講余批〔文有鋪叙荅亦明超於他作〕
甚矣聖人之道著於書而具於心也著於書其用各有不同具於心
其理未嘗不一窮經者可專一經之義而不求其理之所以同乎秋
闈大開多士雲集執事發策而以六經相通之義為問其嘉
惠承學之意深矣愚雖不敏敢不悉心以對夫六經未作聖人之
===
道蘊蓄於一心六經旣作聖人之道垂憲於萬世經非道無以成
道非經無以著是六經者所以明聖道也故易作而吉凶消長之
道進退存亡之機所以明所以明陰陽也書作而二帝三王之道
典謨訓誥誓命之文以具所以道政事也詩有賦比興之不同風雅
頌之或異善者可以感發人之善心惡者可以懲創人之逸志
則詩者所以理性情也禮以恭敬辭讓為本而有節文度數
之詳可以固人肌膚之會筋骸之束非所以制事乎樂有五音六
律之不拂其倫清濁高下之不紊其序可以蕩滌其邪穢消
融其查滓非所以和心乎春秋著十二公之首末二百四十二年之
punctuated:
第二問

一名林時望
同考試官進士方批〔文辭典實，敷荅詳明，終以心貫六經之義，尤見本識。〕
考試官敎諭邵批〔觀此一策，學識深遠，筆力老蒼。論六經之用雖殊，而其理則一貫而通之，皆本於聖人之心。非〕〔有卓然之見者，不能發明如此，宜魁多士。〕
考試官前侍講余批〔文有鋪叙，荅亦明，超於他作。〕

甚矣，聖人之道著於書而具於心也！著於書，其用各有不同；具於心，其理未嘗不一。窮經者可專一經之義，而不求其理之所以同乎？秋闈大開，多士雲集，執事發策，而以六經相通之義為問，其嘉惠承學之意深矣。愚雖不敏，敢不悉心以對？夫六經未作，聖人之道蘊蓄於一心；六經旣作，聖人之道垂憲於萬世。經非道無以成，道非經無以著，是六經者，所以明聖道也。故《易》作而吉凶消長之道、進退存亡之機所以明，所以明陰陽也。《書》作而二帝三王之道、典謨訓誥誓命之文以具，所以道政事也。《詩》有賦、比、興之不同，風、雅、頌之或異，善者可以感發人之善心，惡者可以懲創人之逸志，則《詩》者所以理性情也。《禮》以恭敬辭讓為本，而有節文度數之詳，可以固人肌膚之會、筋骸之束，非所以制事乎？《樂》有五音六律之不拂其倫，清濁高下之不紊其序，可以蕩滌其邪穢，消融其查滓，非所以和心乎？《春秋》著十二公之首末、二百四十二年之
translation_en:
Second Question

First Place: Lin Shiwang 林時望
Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [The diction is classical and substantive, and the exposition and replies are detailed and clear. Concluding with the principle that the mind penetrates the Six Classics especially shows fundamental insight.]
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shao 邵: [Examining this policy essay, its learning and insight are profound and far-reaching, and its brushwork is mature and vigorous. It argues that although the functions of the Six Classics differ, their principle is threaded together in a single unity, all rooted in the mind of the sages. Without] [outstanding discernment, one could not elucidate it like this; he deserves to stand first among the many scholars.]
Comment by Examiner, former Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Yu 余: [The essay is well-structured in its exposition, and the answers are also clear, surpassing other compositions.]

Great indeed is the way in which the Way of the sages is made manifest in books and yet is complete within the mind! Made manifest in books, its functions each differ; complete within the mind, its principle has never been anything but one. How can those who exhaustively study the Classics focus solely on the meaning of a single Classic without seeking the reason why their principle is the same? Now that the autumn examination compound is grandly opened and the many scholars have gathered like clouds, Your Excellency has issued this policy question asking about the interconnected meaning of the Six Classics; profound indeed is your intention to bestow favor upon subsequent learners. Though I am愚 (unintelligent), how dare I not devote my whole mind to replying? Before the Six Classics were created, the Way of the sages was stored up within a single mind; once the Six Classics were created, the Way of the sages handed down models for ten thousand generations. Without the Way, the Classics have nothing by which to be formed; without the Classics, the Way has nothing by which to be made manifest. Thus, the Six Classics are that by which the sagely Way is illuminated. Therefore, when the Book of Changes (Yi) was created, the way of good fortune and calamity, of waxing and waning, and the mechanisms of advancing and retreating, of survival and ruin, were thereby illuminated—it is that by which yin and yang are illuminated. When the Book of Documents (Shu) was created, the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings and the texts of canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths, and charges were thereby provided—it is that by which governance is spoken of. The Book of Odes (Shi) has the differences among narrative (fu), metaphor (bi), and evocative image (xing), as well as the distinctions among the Airs (feng), Odes (ya), and Hymns (song); what is good in it can inspire people's good minds, and what is bad can admonish and restrain people's unruly inclinations—thus the Book of Odes is that by which human nature and emotions are regulated. The Book of Rites (Li) takes reverence, respect, deference, and yielding as its root, and possesses the detailed gradations of ritual forms and measures, which can strengthen the joining of people's flesh and skin and the binding of their sinews and bones—is it not that by which affairs are regulated? The Book of Music (Yue) has the five tones and six pitch-pipes not violating their natural relations, and clear and turbid, high and low notes not disordering their sequence, which can wash away one's evil impurities and melt away one's dregs—is it not that by which the mind is harmonized? The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) sets forth the beginning and end of the twelve dukes and the [events] of two hundred and forty-two years…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
行事一字之褒喻於華袞一字之貶嚴於鈇鉞則春秋者又所
以正名分也是六經各專其一似不可以相通矣殊不知論其用雖
不同論其理則無不該觀夫書之稽疑即易之卜筮也虞廷賡
歌即詩之雅頌也伯夷所典之禮后夔所掌之樂豈非書之禮
樂乎有德之命有罪之討豈非書之春秋乎其義之相貫者如
此宜乎說者謂一經之內諸經之理無不該信不誣矣然不特書
也春秋之公好惡則發乎詩之情也酌古今則貫乎書之事也
所興之常典則體乎禮之序所本之忠恕則導乎樂之和若夫
世子之賢必嘉之翬氏之惡必貶之則公好惡之實可知誅少正
===
卯而警亂賊尊周室而抑諸侯則興常典之實可見至於酌古
今本忠恕又莫不各有其實焉他如易著小人勿用之戒即春
秋之褒貶也卜筮之用即書之稽疑也詩之篇什本乎虞廷賡
歌之體禮之節文原於伯夷所典之職又豈有不可貫於諸經之
義乎雖然六經之義固可相通而所以通之者亦以心而貫之耳故
易以道陰陽即吾心太極之理也書以道政事即吾心體用之迹
也詩之理情性則吾心好惡之正也禮之制事樂之和心即吾心中和之德
也春秋之正名分豈非吾心褒貶之正乎學者不以經視經而以心視
經則六經相通之義斷可識矣敢以心為終篇獻
punctuated: 行事，一字之褒喻於華袞，一字之貶嚴於鈇鉞，則《春秋》者，又所以正名分也。是六經各專其一，似不可以相通矣。殊不知論其用雖不同，論其理則無不該。觀夫《書》之稽疑，即《易》之卜筮也；虞廷賡歌，即《詩》之《雅》《頌》也；伯夷所典之禮，后夔所掌之樂，豈非《書》之禮樂乎？有德之命，有罪之討，豈非《書》之《春秋》乎？其義之相貫者如此，宜乎說者謂「一經之內，諸經之理無不該」，信不誣矣。然不特《書》也，《春秋》之公好惡，則發乎《詩》之情也；酌古今，則貫乎《書》之事也；所興之常典，則體乎《禮》之序；所本之忠恕，則導乎《樂》之和。若夫世子之賢必嘉之，翬氏之惡必貶之，則公好惡之實可知；誅少正卯而警亂賊，尊周室而抑諸侯，則興常典之實可見；至於酌古今、本忠恕，又莫不各有其實焉。他如《易》著「小人勿用」之戒，即《春秋》之褒貶也；卜筮之用，即《書》之稽疑也。《詩》之篇什，本乎虞廷賡歌之體；《禮》之節文，原於伯夷所典之職，又豈有不可貫於諸經之義乎？雖然，六經之義固可相通，而所以通之者，亦以心而貫之耳。故《易》以道陰陽，即吾心太極之理也；《書》以道政事，即吾心體用之迹也；《詩》之理情性，則吾心好惡之正也；《禮》之制事、《樂》之和心，即吾心中和之德也；《春秋》之正名分，豈非吾心褒貶之正乎？學者不以經視經，而以心視經，則六經相通之義斷可識矣。敢以心為終篇獻。
translation_en:
…deeds and affairs; a single word of praise is more glorious than ceremonial robes of state, and a single word of censure is more severe than the executioner's axe. Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is the means to rectify names and statuses. Since each of the Six Classics specializes in one domain, it might seem that they cannot be interconnected. Yet little do people realize that although their functions differ when discussed separately, when we examine their underlying principles, there is nothing they do not encompass together. Consider how the "Examination of Doubts" in the Book of Documents (Shu) is none other than the divination of the Book of Changes (Yi); the responsive songs of the虞 (Yu) court are none other than the Odes (Ya) and Hymns (Song) of the Book of Poetry (Shi); the rites directed by Boyi and the music overseen by Hou Kui—are these not the rites and music within the Book of Documents? The investiture of the virtuous and the punitive expeditions against the guilty—are these not the Spring and Autumn Annals within the Book of Documents? Since their meanings interpenetrate in this way, it is fitting that commentators say, "Within a single Classic, the principles of all the Classics are fully encompassed." Truly, this is no exaggeration!

Yet this is true not only of the Book of Documents. In the Spring and Autumn Annals, its impartial likes and dislikes issue from the sentiments of the Book of Poetry; its weighing of past and present threads through the affairs of the Book of Documents; the enduring norms it upholds embody the order of the Book of Rites (Li); and the loyalty and reciprocity upon which it is founded guide the harmony of the Book of Music (Yue). For instance, when the worthiness of an heir apparent is invariably commended and the wickedness of Hui [Prince Hui of Lu] is invariably censured, the reality of impartial likes and dislikes can be known; when Shaozheng Mao is executed to warn rebellious villains, and the House of Zhou is honored while the feudal lords are restrained, the reality of upholding enduring norms can be seen. As for weighing past and present and taking loyalty and reciprocity as the foundation, each likewise possesses its own concrete reality. In other cases, when the Book of Changes sets forth the warning that "petty men should not be employed," that is the praise and censure of the Spring and Autumn Annals; its use of divination by tortoise shell and milfoil stalks is the "Examination of Doubts" of the Book of Documents. The verses of the Book of Poetry are rooted in the form of the responsive songs of the Yu court, and the ceremonial regulations of the Book of Rites originate in the office directed by Boyi—how could there be any meaning that does not thread through all the Classics?

Even so, while the meanings of the Six Classics certainly interpenetrate, that by which one connects them is simply threading them together through the mind. Therefore, the Book of Changes speaks of yin and yang, which is the principle of the Supreme Ultimate in our own mind; the Book of Documents speaks of governance, which is the trace of substance and function in our own mind; the Book of Poetry regulates emotions and nature, which is the correctness of likes and dislikes in our own mind; the Book of Rites regulates affairs and the Book of Music harmonizes the mind, which is the virtue of equilibrium and harmony in our own mind; and the Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies names and statuses—is this not the correctness of praise and censure in our own mind? If scholars do not view the Classics merely through the Classics, but rather view the Classics through the mind, then the principle of how the Six Classics interpenetrate can decidedly be understood. I venture to offer "the mind" as the conclusion to this essay.

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
第三問一名林時望
同考試官進士方批〔鋪叙簡嚴議論切當必優於策學者〕
考試官教諭邵批〔此策能分別漢唐諸儒之優劣發明宋諸儒有功於道學筆下滔滔大有斷制必有識之士也宜置首選〕
考試官前侍講余批〔此題於他卷中論諸儒稱其善則不能指其實貶其過則不能指其疵此篇皆有考据文辭暢達高薦無疑〕
天朝設學校育人材以圖至治之隆執事典文衡策承學下詢諸儒
之策甚盛心也敢不悉心以對粤自聖賢道否道學不明裔是而後
儒者之作莫盛於漢唐宋焉以言乎漢董仲舒天人三策之陳賈誼
治安一策之進鄭玄之疏九經劉向之諫疏懇切皆一代之鉅儒也後之
===
稱者惟以董賈而不與於鄭劉者豈以鄭玄之學雖勞矣而未
免有穿鑿之弊劉向著述雖切矣而未醇乎正大之言獨賈誼治
安之策拳拳乎以救時為心董仲舒天人之策切切乎以教化為大
務况其正誼明道之言道之大原出於天之論又有得夫道學之要
乎此所以稱賈董而不及鄭劉也以言乎唐王仲淹十五為人師教河
汾為學者所宗所著之書有曰文中子當時薛收之徒莫不尊
其教亦可謂大儒矣韓昌黎著原道一篇以繼前聖之道統佛
骨一表以正萬世之人心可謂醇儒矣然仲淹不知分量妄為著述以
續六經比之韓子翼正闢邪有功吾道大有逕庭則其優劣可見矣殆
punctuated:
第三問一名：林時望。
同考試官進士方批：〔鋪叙簡嚴，議論切當，必優於策學者。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔此策能分別漢、唐諸儒之優劣，發明宋諸儒有功於道學，筆下滔滔，大有斷制，必有識之士也，宜置首選。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔此題於他卷中論諸儒，稱其善則不能指其實，貶其過則不能指其疵。此篇皆有考据，文辭暢達，高薦無疑。〕

天朝設學校、育人材，以圖至治之隆。執事典文衡，策承學，下詢諸儒之策，甚盛心也，敢不悉心以對？粤自聖賢道否，道學不明，裔是而後，儒者之作莫盛於漢、唐、宋焉。以言乎漢：董仲舒《天人三策》之陳，賈誼《治安》一策之進，鄭玄之疏九經，劉向之諫疏懇切，皆一代之鉅儒也。後之稱者惟以董、賈而不與於鄭、劉者，豈以鄭玄之學雖勞矣，而未免有穿鑿之弊；劉向著述雖切矣，而未醇乎正大之言？獨賈誼《治安》之策，拳拳乎以救時為心；董仲舒《天人》之策，切切乎以教化為大務。况其「正誼明道」之言、「道之大原出於天」之論，又有得夫道學之要乎！此所以稱賈、董而不及鄭、劉也。以言乎唐：王仲淹十五為人師，教河、汾，為學者所宗，所著之書有曰《文中子》，當時薛收之徒莫不尊其教，亦可謂大儒矣；韓昌黎著《原道》一篇以繼前聖之道統，《佛骨》一表以正萬世之人心，可謂醇儒矣。然仲淹不知分量，妄為著述以續六經，比之韓子翼正闢邪、有功吾道，大有逕庭，則其優劣可見矣。殆…
translation_en:
Third Policy Question, one candidate: Lin Shiwang 林時望.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [The exposition is concise and rigorous, and the arguments are pertinent and apt; he must be someone who excels in the study of policy questions.]
Comment by Examiner, Instructor Shao 邵: [This policy essay is able to distinguish the relative merits and defects of the various Confucian scholars of the Han and Tang dynasties, and to elucidate the contributions made by the Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty to the Learning of the Way (Daoxue). His brush flows torrentially and displays great decisiveness of judgment; he must be a gentleman of insight, and ought to be placed at the head of the list.]
Comment by Examiner, former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余: [On this topic, when other papers discuss the various Confucian scholars, in praising their merits they cannot point to concrete realities, and in criticizing their faults they cannot point to their specific flaws. This essay is well-grounded in textual evidence throughout, and its diction is fluent and lucid; it deserves a high recommendation without a doubt.]

The Sacred Dynasty has established schools and nurtured men of talent in order to achieve the flourishing of supreme governance. Your Excellency presides over the literary balance and examines us junior scholars by posing a policy question inquiring into the writings and teachings of the various Confucian scholars. This is a most magnanimous intention; how could I dare not reply with all my heart? Ever since the Way of the sages and worthies fell into eclipse and the Learning of the Way became obscured, from that time onward [?], the works of Confucian scholars have been most flourishing in the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties. To speak of the Han: Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 setting forth his Three Policy Essays on Heaven and Man (Tianren sance), Jia Yi 賈誼 presenting his single Policy Essay on Peace and Order (Zhi'an ce), Zheng Xuan 鄭玄 writing subcommentaries on the Nine Classics, and Liu Xiang 劉向 submitting earnestly sincere remonstrance memorials—all of them were great Confucian scholars of their age. Yet why is it that those of later times who offer praise single out only Dong and Jia, without including Zheng and Liu? Is it not because Zheng Xuan's scholarship, though painstaking, could not avoid the flaw of forced interpretations, and Liu Xiang's writings, though earnest, were not purely words of uprightness and breadth? Only Jia Yi's Policy Essay on Peace and Order was earnestly devoted to saving the times, and Dong Zhongshu's Policy Essays on Heaven and Man were urgently focused on taking moral transformation through education as the great task. How much more so given that Dong's words on "rectifying righteousness and clarifying the Way" and his thesis that "the great source of the Way comes from Heaven" furthermore grasped the essentials of the Learning of the Way! This is why people praise Jia and Dong without extending the same credit to Zheng and Liu. To speak of the Tang: Wang Zhongyan 王仲淹 [Wang Tong 王通] became a teacher of men at the age of fifteen, instructing in the region of the Yellow and Fen rivers, and was revered as a master by scholars; the book he wrote is called Master Wenzhong (Wenzhongzi), and at the time disciples such as Xue Shou 薛收 all revered his teachings—so he too may be called a great Confucian scholar. Han Changli 韓昌黎 [Han Yu 韓愈] wrote the essay "Tracing the Way" (Yuandao) to continue the Transmission of the Way (daotong) of the former sages, and the Memorial on the Buddha's Bone (Fener biao / Fogu biao) to rectify the minds of men for ten thousand generations—so he may be called a pure Confucian scholar. Yet Zhongyan did not know his own measure and presumptuously composed writings in order to continue the Six Classics; compared to Master Han's defense of orthodoxy and refutation of heterodoxy, which rendered meritorious service to our Way, there is a vast discrepancy between them, and thus their relative superiority and inferiority can be clearly seen. When it came to [the great Song dynasty…]…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
大有宋五星聚奎真儒輩出上接鄒魯之緒下開伊洛之源不由師
傳默契道體著太極一圖以闡性命之微易通一書以發性理之祕此
濂溪之濬道學之源也明道之規模廣濶德性醇粹伊川之氣質剛
方文理密察語學者以誠敬為入門以踐履為實地此二程之揚道學
之波也當時若張橫渠之早談孫吳晚逃佛老勇撤皐比一變至道且
語門人曰吾平日所講者皆亂道也觀於此言則張子之合於周程者
可知矣邵康節之手探月窟足躡天根閑中今古靜裏乾坤著
經世之書以闡造化之祕則邵子之有合於周程者可見矣至若司
馬公之上無師傳其有合於周程者豈非有取於資治之鑑潛虛
===
之書乎繼是而後惟朱子義理精微蚕絲牛毛心胷開豁海濶天
高年弥高而德弥邵傳之最得其宗也當時陸子靜鵝湖無極
太極之辨雖往復不屈難免後世之公論矣東萊呂祖謙講道於
金華南軒張敬夫講學於廣漢皆一時朱子之所重者其論道之
功始雖各執其一偏終則同歸于一致若春秋博議之作四書傳註之解
無非當時之所論也雖然董賈鄭劉漢之儒也仲淹昌黎唐之儒也然
論漢唐諸子惟董韓為最醇周程張邵宋君子也朱陸張呂宋大賢
也然論宋諸儒惟周程朱子為尤善愚以管窺蠡測之庸才辨漢唐宋諸
儒之道學固未盡知第以明問所及不容以默遂補綴以復幸恕其言之狂
punctuated: 大有宋五星聚奎，真儒輩出。上接鄒魯之緒，下開伊洛之源，不由師傳，默契道體，著《太極》一圖以闡性命之微，《易通》一書以發性理之祕，此濂溪之濬道學之源也。明道之規模廣濶，德性醇粹；伊川之氣質剛方，文理密察。語學者以誠敬為入門，以踐履為實地，此二程之揚道學之波也。當時若張橫渠之早談孫吳，晚逃佛老，勇撤皐比，一變至道，且語門人曰：「吾平日所講者，皆亂道也。」觀於此言，則張子之合於周、程者可知矣。邵康節之手探月窟，足躡天根，閑中今古，靜裏乾坤，著《經世》之書以闡造化之祕，則邵子之有合於周、程者可見矣。至若司馬公之上無師傳，其有合於周、程者，豈非有取於《資治》之鑑、《潛虛》之書乎？繼是而後，惟朱子義理精微，蚕絲牛毛，心胷開豁，海濶天高，年弥高而德弥邵，傳之最得其宗也。當時陸子靜鵝湖無極、太極之辨，雖往復不屈，難免後世之公論矣。東萊呂祖謙講道於金華，南軒張敬夫講學於廣漢，皆一時朱子之所重者。其論道之功，始雖各執其一偏，終則同歸于一致。若《春秋博議》之作、四書傳註之解，無非當時之所論也。雖然，董、賈、鄭、劉，漢之儒也；仲淹、昌黎，唐之儒也。然論漢、唐諸子，惟董、韓為最醇。周、程、張、邵，宋君子也；朱、陸、張、呂，宋大賢也。然論宋諸儒，惟周、程、朱子為尤善。愚以管窺蠡測之庸才，辨漢、唐、宋諸儒之道學，固未盡知；第以明問所及，不容以默，遂補綴以復，幸恕其言之狂…
translation_en:
…the great Song dynasty, when the five planets gathered in the Kui constellation and true Confucians emerged in succession. Continuing the heritage of Zou and Lu [Mencius and Confucius] above and opening the fountainhead of the Yi and Luo rivers below, without relying on transmission from a teacher he silently comprehended the substance of the Way. He composed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu) to elucidate the subtleties of human nature and destiny, and the book Penetrating the Book of Changes (Yitong [Tongshu]) to reveal the mysteries of nature and principle—this was how Lianxi [Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤] dredged the source of the Learning of the Way (Daoxue). Mingdao [Cheng Hao 程顥] was broad in scope and pure in moral nature; Yichuan [Cheng Yi 程頤] was firm and upright in temperament and closely observant of pattern and principle. Teaching scholars to take sincerity and reverence as the entry gate and practical conduct as the solid ground—this was how the two Chengs raised the waves of the Learning of the Way. At that time, someone like Zhang Hengqu [Zhang Zai 張載] spoke of Sunzi and Wu Qi in his early years and later fled into Buddhism and Daoism, yet bravely removed his tiger-skin lecturing mat and in a single transformation reached the Way. Moreover, he told his disciples: "What I ordinarily lectured on were all disorderly ways." Looking at these words, one can know how Master Zhang accorded with Zhou and the Chengs. Shao Kangjie [Shao Yong 邵雍], whose hands probed the cavern of the moon and whose feet trod the roots of heaven, contemplating past and present in leisure and heaven and earth in stillness, wrote the Book of Supreme World Ordering (Huangji jingshi shu) to elucidate the secrets of creation—thus it can be seen how Master Shao accorded with Zhou and the Chengs. As for Lord Sima [Sima Guang 司馬光], who had no transmission from a teacher above, is not his accord with Zhou and the Chengs drawn from his Mirror of Aid in Governance (Zizhi tongjian) and his Book of the Hidden Void (Qianxu)?

Following after this, only Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹], whose grasp of moral principle was as fine and subtle as silkworm threads and ox hairs, whose mind was as open and expansive as the wide sea and high sky, and whose virtue grew ever more eminent as his years advanced, most truly obtained the main lineage of transmission. At that time, Lu Zijing [Lu Jiuyuan 陸九淵], in his debate at Goose Lake (Ehu) over the Non-Ultimate and the Supreme Ultimate, though going back and forth without yielding, could hardly escape the impartial judgment of later generations. Donglai Lü Zuqian [呂祖謙] lectured on the Way in Jinhua, and Nanxuan Zhang Jingfu [Zhang Shi 張栻] lectured on learning in Guanghan; both were held in high regard by Master Zhu in their time. In their efforts at discussing the Way, although at first each held to a one-sided view, in the end they converged in agreement. Works such as the Extensive Discussions on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu boyi) and the commentaries and explanations on the Four Books were none other than what they discussed at the time.

Even so, Dong [Zhongshu], Jia [Yi], Zheng [Xuan], and Liu [Xiang] were the Confucians of the Han; Zhongyan [Wang Tong] and Changli [Han Yu] were the Confucians of the Tang. Yet in assessing the masters of the Han and Tang, only Dong and Han were the purest. Zhou, the Chengs, Zhang [Zai], and Shao were the noble men of the Song; Zhu, Lu, Zhang [Shi], and Lü were the great worthies of the Song. Yet in assessing the Confucians of the Song, only Zhou, the Chengs, and Master Zhu were especially admirable. With my mediocre talent—likepeering through a tube or measuring the sea with a gourd—in distinguishing the Learning of the Way of the Confucians of the Han, Tang, and Song, I certainly do not know it exhaustively. Merely because your enlightened question has touched upon it, I dare not remain silent, and so I have patched together these words in reply, hoping you will forgive the rashness of my speech…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
斐進而教之
同前
一名鄭建
同考試官進士方批〔初場七篇縝密純粹瑩然無可指之瑕五策詳瞻隨問隨答如長江大河滔滔不竭此答諸儒始則詳〕
〔其學術之異終則約其心術之同非識見超卓者不能言也〕
考試官教諭邵批〔策題多撫前言往行之疑而未明者欲與辨析異同使歸于正此答考究精詳斷制明白可謂策場之超凡者〕
考試官前侍講余批〔三場文字皆詳整豐贍有發明有關鍵非熟於經史者不能此篇答諸儒之問尤為精案斷制嚴〕
〔明文辭滂沛且五策俱稱皆自胸中流出有非牽強掇拾者之比宜寘前列〕
論漢唐諸儒要當辨其學術之醇論趙宋諸儒惟當考其理學之
正學術醇則著書立言之功有可取理學正則垂世立教之道無以
===
加知乎此則可與論漢唐宋諸儒之學矣粤自杏壇教息木鐸音
稀嬴秦奮暴戾之心吾道遭薄蝕之患迨夫劉漢肇興而滌坑灰
之虐焰文武繼作而廣儒雅之旁求於是賈誼以洛陽年少之才而
膺秀才之選觀其治安之策有忠愛之至誠勸興禮樂得教化之
先務董仲舒之天人三策非道不陳繁露等篇於經有益正誼明
道之言得聖賢上義下利之旨正心正朝廷之語有大學誠意正
心之功是二子之事業同可觀矣劉向之著說苑寓古今事物之理
請立辟雍而有興禮樂之誠鄭玄之學問該博訓誥經傳刪裁
煩蕪刋改漏失是二子之著述亦可取矣然其洪範傳論未免
punctuated:
斐，進而教之。

同前。
一名鄭建。
同考試官進士方批：〔初場七篇縝密純粹，瑩然無可指之瑕。五策詳瞻，隨問隨答，如長江大河，滔滔不竭。此答諸儒，始則詳〕〔其學術之異，終則約其心術之同，非識見超卓者不能言也。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔策題多撫前言往行之疑而未明者，欲與辨析異同，使歸于正。此答考究精詳，斷制明白，可謂策場之超凡者。〕
考試官前侍講余批：〔三場文字皆詳整豐贍，有發明，有關鍵，非熟於經史者不能。此篇答諸儒之問，尤為精案，斷制嚴〕〔明，文辭滂沛。且五策俱稱，皆自胸中流出，有非牽強掇拾者之比，宜寘前列。〕

論漢、唐諸儒，要當辨其學術之醇；論趙宋諸儒，惟當考其理學之正。學術醇則著書立言之功有可取，理學正則垂世立教之道無以加。知乎此，則可與論漢、唐、宋諸儒之學矣。粤自杏壇教息，木鐸音稀，嬴秦奮暴戾之心，吾道遭薄蝕之患。迨夫劉漢肇興，而滌坑灰之虐焰；文、武繼作，而廣儒雅之旁求。於是賈誼以洛陽年少之才，而膺秀才之選。觀其治安之策，有忠愛之至誠；勸興禮樂，得教化之先務。董仲舒之天人三策，非道不陳；《繁露》等篇，於經有益。「正誼明道」之言，得聖賢上義下利之旨；「正心正朝廷」之語，有《大學》誠意正心之功。是二子之事業同可觀矣。劉向之著《說苑》，寓古今事物之理；請立辟雍，而有興禮樂之誠。鄭玄之學問該博，訓誥經傳，刪裁煩蕪，刋改漏失。是二子之著述亦可取矣。然其《洪範傳論》未免…
translation_en:
… [rash and] unrefined words, and bring me forward to instruct me.

Same question as the preceding.
One candidate, Zheng Jian 鄭建.
Comment by Associate Examiner and metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [The seven essays of the first session are meticulous and pure, lustrous and without a single flaw that could be pointed out. The five policy essays are detailed and rich, answering each question as it comes, like the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers flowing on inexhaustibly. In answering the question on the various Confucian scholars, this essay begins by detailing] [the differences in their scholarship and ends by summarizing the commonality in their dispositions of mind; none without extraordinary insight could express this.]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao 邵: [The policy question mostly gathers doubtful and unclarified points from past words and deeds, seeking to analyze their similarities and differences so as to bring them back to what is orthodox. This answer is precise and thorough in its investigation and clear in its judgments; it may truly be called an extraordinary piece in the policy session.]
Comment by Examiner and Former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余: [The writings across all three sessions are detailed, well-ordered, and abundant, showing both original elucidation and a grasp of key points, which no one unfamiliar with the Classics and Histories could achieve. This essay answering the question on the various Confucian scholars is especially precise [?], with rigorous and clear judgments] [and a surging, abundant style. Moreover, all five policy essays are well-matched, each flowing naturally from within his own breast and incomparable to forced patchwork; he ought to be placed in the front ranks.]

In evaluating the Confucian scholars of the Han and Tang dynasties, the essential thing is to discern the purity of their scholarship; in evaluating the Confucian scholars of the Zhao Song dynasty, one must only examine the orthodoxy of their learning of Principle (lixue 理學). When their scholarship is pure, their achievements in writing books and establishing teachings are worthy of adoption; when their learning of Principle is orthodox, nothing further can be added to their Way of handing down teachings to future generations. Once one understands this, one can discuss the learning of the Confucian scholars of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties. Ever since the teaching at the Apricot Altar ceased and the sound of the wooden bell-clapper grew rare, the Ying Qin dynasty unleashed its violent and ruthless heart, and our Way suffered the calamity of eclipse. When the Liu Han dynasty first rose, it washed away the cruel flames of the scholar-pits and ashes; when Emperors Wen and Wu successively arose, they broadened the extensive search for men of Confucian refinement. Thereupon Jia Yi 賈誼, with the talent of a youth from Luoyang 洛陽, was selected as a Cultivated Talent (xiucai 秀才). Looking at his policy memorial on securing order (Zhi'an zhi ce 治安之策), it possesses the utmost sincerity of loyalty and affection; in urging the revival of ritual and music, he grasped the foremost priority of moral transformation. As for Dong Zhongshu's 董仲舒 three policy essays on Heaven and Man (Tianren sance 天人三策), he set forth nothing that was not the Way; his Luxuriant Gems of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu fanlu 春秋繁露) and other pieces are beneficial to the Classics. His words on "rectifying righteousness and clarifying the Way" captured the sages' and worthies' purport of prizing righteousness above profit; his statement on "rectifying the mind to rectify the court" embodies the Great Learning's (Daxue 大學) work of making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind. Thus the achievements and undertakings of these two masters are equally worthy of admiration. Liu Xiang 劉向, in authoring the Garden of Persuasions (Shuoyuan 說苑), lodged within it the principles of affairs and things ancient and modern; in petitioning to establish the Imperial College (Biyong 辟雍), he showed the sincerity of reviving ritual and music. Zheng Xuan's 鄭玄 learning was broad and comprehensive; he wrote commentaries and glosses on the Classics and traditions, pruning away prolixity and weeds and correcting omissions and errors. Thus the writings of these two masters are also worthy of adoption. Yet the Discourse on the Commentary to the Great Plan (Hongfan zhuanlun 洪範傳論) could not avoid…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
有膠固之談專門名家未免有黨伐之論後世獨稱董賈而不
及鄭劉者非以其學術固未有醇操守固未有正歟至於隋王
通之著作其論天地而必継以君臣論教化而必終以禮樂與董
常荅問之際未嘗不本於仁義忠信其醇曷可訾哉及其續詩而
不足以導意續書而不足以導事作元經以擬易作中說以擬
論語非其妄自尊大歟唐韓愈五箴所戒動無非法三原所
述言無非道廻異端之狂瀾聳後學之山斗其醇亦可取矣
奈何性本善也而分為三品博愛之謂仁行而宜之謂義未免言
用而不及本也然二子之學雖若相當而其得失亦且相半矣奚可
===
辨其優劣哉迨至有宋之興星聚奎而文風振起水泝洛而道
統流傳時則有若濂溪浚其源二程導其流張朱助其瀾揖
堯舜於夢寐之頃授孔孟於講論之間景星鳳凰天下快
覩太山北斗學者歸依故性理言其二氣五行動靜論其
四時百物誠論其元亨利貞道論其中正仁義則發於通書
之數篇無極而太極太極而两儀两儀而五氣五氣而四時則見於太
極之一圖此濂溪之學本乎易之太極也論性別其所禀本然
之殊論心辨其曰虛曰實之異排異端必正其枯槁恣肆之
弊自致知至知止自誠意至平天下自洒掃應對至精義入神
punctuated: 有膠固之談，專門名家，未免有黨伐之論。後世獨稱董、賈而不及鄭、劉者，非以其學術固未有醇、操守固未有正歟？至於隋王通之著作，其論天地而必継以君臣，論教化而必終以禮樂，與董常荅問之際，未嘗不本於仁義忠信，其醇曷可訾哉？及其續《詩》而不足以導意，續《書》而不足以導事，作《元經》以擬《易》，作《中說》以擬《論語》，非其妄自尊大歟？唐韓愈《五箴》所戒，動無非法；《三原》所述，言無非道。廻異端之狂瀾，聳後學之山斗，其醇亦可取矣。奈何性本善也，而分為三品；「博愛之謂仁，行而宜之謂義」，未免言用而不及本也。然二子之學雖若相當，而其得失亦且相半矣，奚可辨其優劣哉？迨至有宋之興，星聚奎而文風振起，水泝洛而道統流傳。時則有若濂溪浚其源，二程導其流，張、朱助其瀾，揖堯、舜於夢寐之頃，授孔、孟於講論之間。景星鳳凰，天下快覩；太山北斗，學者歸依。故性理言其二氣五行，動靜論其四時百物，誠論其元亨利貞，道論其中正仁義，則發於《通書》之數篇；無極而太極，太極而两儀，两儀而五氣，五氣而四時，則見於《太極》之一圖。此濂溪之學本乎《易》之太極也。論性別其所禀、本然之殊，論心辨其曰虛、曰實之異，排異端必正其枯槁、恣肆之弊，自致知至知止，自誠意至平天下，自洒掃應對至精義入神，
translation_en: …cannot avoid pedantic and rigid assertions, and in his specialized school of scholarship, he cannot avoid partisan attacks. That later generations praised only Dong Zhongshu and Jia Yi without extending the same to Zheng Xuan and Liu Xiang—was it not because the latter's scholarship was not yet pure and their personal integrity not yet upright? As for the writings of Wang Tong 王通 of the Sui dynasty, when he discussed heaven and earth he invariably continued with ruler and minister, and when he discussed moral transformation he invariably concluded with ritual and music; in his questions and answers with Dong Chang 董常, he never failed to ground himself in benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness—how could the purity of his learning be disparaged? Yet when he went on to continue the Book of Odes (Shi) though it was insufficient to convey intent, to continue the Book of Documents (Shu) though it was insufficient to convey events, to compose the Primal Classic (Yuanjing) in imitation of the Book of Changes (Yi), and to compose the Discourses of the Mean (Zhongshuo) in imitation of the Analects (Lunyu)—was this not presumptuous self-aggrandizement on his part? As for Han Yu 韓愈 of the Tang dynasty, in the admonitions of his "Five Admonitions" (Wuzhen), no action was contrary to the model; in the expositions of his "Three Essays on Origins" (Sanyuan), no word was contrary to the Way. He turned back the raging waves of heterodoxy and stood towering like Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper for later scholars; the purity of his learning is likewise worthy of adoption. Yet how is it that, whereas human nature is originally good, he divided it into three grades, and in saying "universal love is called benevolence, and acting appropriately is called righteousness," he could not avoid speaking of function without reaching the root? Thus, although the learning of these two masters seems roughly comparable, their merits and defects are also half and half—how can one distinguish their relative superiority? When it came to the rise of the Song dynasty, the stars gathered in the Kui constellation and literary culture was roused; the waters were traced back to the Luo River and the transmission of the Way was handed down. At that time there were figures such as Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤 (Lianxi 濂溪), who dredged its source; the two Cheng brothers 二程, who channeled its stream; and Zhang Zai 張載 and Zhu Xi 朱熹, who swelled its waves—bowing to Yao and Shun in the space of dreams and waking, and transmitting Confucius and Mencius in the midst of lectures and discussions. Like auspicious stars and phoenixes, the world rejoiced to behold them; like Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper, scholars turned to them in allegiance. Therefore, in discussing nature and principle in terms of the two vital forces and the Five Phases, motion and stillness in terms of the four seasons and the myriad things,誠 (sincerity) in terms of origination, flourishing, advantage, and firmness, and the Way in terms of centrality, correctness, benevolence, and righteousness—these were set forth in several chapters of the Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu); and as for the Non-Ultimate and also the Supreme Ultimate, the Supreme Ultimate generating the Two Modes, the Two Modes generating the Five Vital Forces, and the Five Vital Forces generating the four seasons—these are seen in the single Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu). This is how the learning of Master Lianxi was rooted in the Supreme Ultimate of the Book of Changes. Discussing human nature by distinguishing between what is endowed and what is original, discussing the mind by differentiating between what is called empty and what is called real, refuting heterodoxies by invariably correcting their abuses of withered asceticism and unbridled license, proceeding from the extension of knowledge to knowing where to abide, from making the intentions sincere to bringing peace to the world, and from sprinkling and sweeping and responding to inquiries to refining righteousness to enter the marvelous…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
此二程之學本乎中庸之誠也訂頑砭愚有亞聖性善養氣之
論正蒙理窟發前聖所未言之蘊正容謹節凛若神明窮理盡
性瑩如氷壺西銘之一既合乎太極之一遺書之仁又合乎西銘之仁
此非橫渠之晚變至道歟若邵子以起震終艮明伏羲之八卦以
天地定位明文王之八卦聖飾性而不加增狂染聖而不加損即發
明孟子性命之旨習知而智習愚而愚又發明夫子習性之言以至
於觀性觀心之說治怒治懼之言又無非與周程相脗合者則知
康節之學初非外理而求數也司馬溫公之視國家猶家夷險
不變待人猶已公私無間至誠自得之學見於立朝行已之間非
===
有道者能之乎故其潜虛之書既明乎大易之旨德業之著而
夷狄有仰慕之誠則溫公之學又詎可無合於周程乎南渡以
來于朱子以豪傑之才聖賢之學集群賢之大成四書傳註
為六經之階梯綱目謹嚴得春秋之微旨時則有若南軒張宣
公之四書傳註羽翼聖人之經東萊吕成公之春秋博議發明聖
經之旨二公輔翼斯道之傳其功大矣以至於象山陸子靜其學尤
崇信孟子在白鹿講君子小人義利之分其人為朱子所重在
鵝湖無極太極之辨殆未免於後世之公論焉先儒謂一則尊德
之功多一則道問學之功至是德性也問學也奚可以岐而二歟由
punctuated: 此二程之學，本乎《中庸》之誠也。《訂頑》、《砭愚》，有亞聖性善養氣之論；《正蒙》、《理窟》，發前聖所未言之蘊。正容謹節，凛若神明；窮理盡性，瑩如氷壺。《西銘》之一，既合乎《太極》之一；《遺書》之仁，又合乎《西銘》之仁。此非橫渠之晚變至道歟？若邵子以起震終艮明伏羲之八卦，以天地定位明文王之八卦。「聖飾性而不加增，狂染聖而不加損」，即發明孟子性命之旨；「習知而智，習愚而愚」，又發明夫子習性之言。以至於觀性、觀心之說，治怒、治懼之言，又無非與周、程相脗合者，則知康節之學初非外理而求數也。司馬溫公之視國家猶家，夷險不變；待人猶已，公私無間。至誠自得之學，見於立朝行已之間，非有道者能之乎？故其《潜虛》之書，既明乎《大易》之旨；德業之著，而夷狄有仰慕之誠。則溫公之學，又詎可無合於周、程乎？南渡以來，于朱子以豪傑之才、聖賢之學，集群賢之大成。《四書》傳註，為《六經》之階梯；《綱目》謹嚴，得《春秋》之微旨。時則有若南軒張宣公之《四書》傳註，羽翼聖人之經；東萊吕成公之《春秋博議》，發明聖經之旨。二公輔翼斯道之傳，其功大矣。以至於象山陸子靜，其學尤崇信孟子。在白鹿講君子小人義利之分，其人為朱子所重；在鵝湖無極太極之辨，殆未免於後世之公論焉。先儒謂一則尊德之功多，一則道問學之功至。是德性也，問學也，奚可以岐而二歟？由
translation_en:
…this learning of the two Cheng brothers [Cheng Hao 程顥 and Cheng Yi 程頤] is rooted in the "sincerity" (cheng) of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong). Correcting the Obstinate (Dingwan) and Needling the Foolish (Bianyu) embody the Second Sage's [Mencius's] discussions on the goodness of human nature and the nourishing of vital energy (qi); Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng) and The Cavern of Principle (Liku) reveal profound meanings unspoken by former sages. Dignified in demeanor and careful in conduct, he was awe-inspiring like a spirit; investigating principle to the utmost and fulfilling his nature, he was as pure and clear as an ice-jade pitcher. The "oneness" of the Western Inscription (Ximing) accords with the "oneness" of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu); the "humaneness" (ren) in the Surviving Works (Yishu) likewise accords with the "humaneness" of the Western Inscription. Is this not Hengqu's [Zhang Zai 張載] transformation in his later years to reach the Ultimate Way?
