As for Master Shao [Shao Yong 邵雍], he used the sequence beginning with Zhen and ending with Gen to elucidate Fuxi's eight trigrams, and used "Heaven and Earth fix their positions" to elucidate King Wen's eight trigrams. His saying that "sagehood adorns nature without adding to it, and madness taints sagehood [read: nature] without detracting from it" elucidates Mencius's purport on nature and destiny; his saying that "practicing wisdom makes one wise, and practicing folly makes one foolish" further elucidates the Master's [Confucius's] words on practice and nature. Even his doctrines on observing nature and observing the mind, and his words on governing anger and governing fear, all tally seamlessly with Zhou [Dunyi 周敦頤] and the Chengs—from which we know that Kangjie's [Shao Yong's] learning never sought numerology outside of principle.

Sima Wengong [Sima Guang 司馬光] regarded the state as his own family, remaining unchanged in smooth or perilous times; he treated others as himself, making no division between public and private. His learning of utmost sincerity and personal realization was manifest in his standing at court and his personal conduct—how could anyone who did not possess the Way achieve this? Therefore, his book Latent Vacuity (Qianxu) elucidates the purport of the Great Changes (Dayi), and as his virtue and achievements became manifest, even the foreign tribes held a sincere admiration for him. How then could Wengong's learning fail to accord with Zhou and the Chengs?

Since the Southern Crossing, Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹], with the talent of a hero and the learning of sages and worthies, synthesized the great achievements of all the worthies. His commentaries and annotations on the Four Books serve as the stepping-stones to the Six Classics; his Outline and Details (Gangmu) is rigorous and strict, capturing the subtle purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). At that time there were also figures like Zhang Xuangong of Nanxuan [Zhang Shi 張栻], whose commentaries on the Four Books served as wings to the classics of the sages, and Lü Chenggong of Donglai [Lü Zuqian 呂祖謙], whose Extensive Discussions on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu boyi) elucidated the purport of the sage's classic. Great indeed were the merits of these two dukes in assisting the transmission of this Way!

As for Lu Zijing of Xiangshan [Lu Jiuyuan 陸九淵], his learning especially revered and trusted Mencius. At the White Deer Grotto he lectured on the distinction between righteousness and profit in the gentleman and the petty man, and he himself was held in high esteem by Master Zhu; yet at Goose Lake, his debate over the Ultimateless (wuji) and the Supreme Ultimate (taiji) could hardly escape the public judgment of later generations. Former Confucian scholars said that the one devoted more effort to honoring the moral nature, while the other carried the effort of pursuing inquiry and study to the utmost. Yet how can moral nature and inquiry and study be split into two divergent paths? From…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
是觀之聖賢有異學而同其本彼此雖異議而同其原是窮
今博古以垂後者此道也救時行道以立功者亦此道也正心誠
誠意以自養者此道也治國齊家以兼善者非此道乎況數
子之學其傳均出於孔孟其說均出於六經其持論均尊王而
黜伯其論道均排異端而明正統不可以出處之迹異其議也
不可以理數之名殊其觀也愚安敢辨其疑似之差哉
第四問
一名鄭建
同考試官進士方批〔此篇塲中作者頗衆多不詳悉唯此敷答條暢大有斷制歷代立法之詳燦然可見傑作也〕
考試官教諭邵批〔答屯田策而能舉井田為證可知其見識不凡而行文步驟迥出流輩愛羨〕
===
考試官前侍講余批考論精詳褒貶切當深得所問之旨有學有〔識之士也〕
三代以上兵農合而屯田之名未立三代以下兵農分而屯田之法始
興何也三代之時井田之法行兵農合一所以無屯田之制漢唐之世
井田之法廢兵農始分所以有屯田之名無其制者國用常見
其有餘立其名者國用僅致於充足知此則足以議屯田之制矣
甞觀三代之時分井受田而野無不耕之民有常業而国無游
惰之禁井田之中卒伍具焉耒耜之暇干戈屬焉而國無養兵
之費有警則荷戈以擊無事則執耒以耕而民無常役之勞
此所以無屯田之制也迨夫春秋之時暴君代作慢其經界宣公
punctuated:
是觀之，聖賢有異學而同其本，彼此雖異議而同其原。是窮今博古以垂後者，此道也；救時行道以立功者，亦此道也；正心誠誠意以自養者，此道也；治國齊家以兼善者，非此道乎？況數子之學，其傳均出於孔、孟，其說均出於《六經》，其持論均尊王而黜伯，其論道均排異端而明正統。不可以出處之迹異其議也，不可以理數之名殊其觀也。愚安敢辨其疑似之差哉！

第四問
一名鄭建
同考試官進士方批：〔此篇塲中作者頗衆，多不詳悉。唯此敷答條暢，大有斷制，歷代立法之詳，燦然可見，傑作也。〕
考試官教諭邵批：〔答屯田策而能舉井田為證，可知其見識不凡，而行文步驟迥出流輩，愛羨。〕
考試官前侍講余批：考論精詳，褒貶切當，深得所問之旨，有學有〔識之士也。〕

三代以上，兵農合而屯田之名未立；三代以下，兵農分而屯田之法始興。何也？三代之時，井田之法行，兵農合一，所以無屯田之制；漢、唐之世，井田之法廢，兵農始分，所以有屯田之名。無其制者，國用常見其有餘；立其名者，國用僅致於充足。知此，則足以議屯田之制矣。甞觀三代之時，分井受田，而野無不耕之民；有常業，而国無游惰之禁。井田之中，卒伍具焉；耒耜之暇，干戈屬焉，而國無養兵之費。有警則荷戈以擊，無事則執耒以耕，而民無常役之勞。此所以無屯田之制也。迨夫春秋之時，暴君代作，慢其經界。宣公
translation_en:
…Viewed from this perspective, the sages and worthies had different teachings yet shared the same root; although they held different opinions from one another, they shared the same origin. Thus, thoroughly investigating the present and broadly studying antiquity to pass down a legacy to posterity is this Way; rescuing the times and practicing the Way to establish meritorious achievements is also this Way; rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere to cultivate oneself is this Way; and governing the state and regulating the family to bring good to the world as well—is that not also this Way? Moreover, the learning of these several masters was in every case transmitted from Confucius and Mencius, their doctrines all derived from the Six Classics, their arguments all revered the Kingly Way and rejected the Hegemonic, and their discussions of the Way all repudiated heterodoxy and clarified the orthodox transmission. One cannot differentiate their views based on the outward traces of their serving in or withdrawing from office, nor can one view them differently based on the designations of principle and number. How would this ignorant student dare to distinguish the subtle discrepancies of resemblance and difference among them?

Fourth Question
First-ranked: Zheng Jian 鄭建
Comment by Associate Examiner and Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [Quite a number of candidates in the examination hall wrote on this topic, but most were not detailed or thorough. Only this essay sets forth its reply with clear fluency and possesses great decisiveness; the details of how laws were established through successive dynasties can be brilliantly seen. It is a masterpiece.]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Shao 邵: [In answering the policy question on military agricultural colonies (tuntian 屯田), he is able to cite the well-field system (jingtian 井田) as evidence, from which one can know that his insight is extraordinary, while the pacing and structure of his prose far surpass those of his peers. Admirable and enviable.]
Comment by Examiner and Former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余: His historical investigation and discussion are precise and detailed, and his praise and censure hit the mark, deeply grasping the purport of the question asked. He is a scholar of both learning and [insight.]

From the Three Dynasties and earlier, soldiers and farmers were united, and the name "military agricultural colonies" (tuntian) had not yet been established; after the Three Dynasties, soldiers and farmers were separated, and the method of military agricultural colonies first arose. Why is this? In the time of the Three Dynasties, the method of the well-field system was practiced, uniting soldiers and farmers into one, which is why there was no institution of military agricultural colonies. In the eras of Han and Tang, the method of the well-field system fell into disuse, and soldiers and farmers were first separated, which is why the name "military agricultural colonies" came into being. When the institution did not exist, state finances constantly showed a surplus; when the name was established, state finances merely managed to reach sufficiency. Once one understands this, one is equipped to discuss the institution of military agricultural colonies.

I have observed that in the time of the Three Dynasties, land was divided into well-fields and allotted, so that in the countryside there were no uncultivating people; they had constant livelihoods, so the state had no prohibitions against vagrancy and idleness. Within the well-fields, military squads and ranks were fully provided for; in the leisure time from plow and share, shield and spear were attended to, and the state had no expense for maintaining an army. When there was an alarm, they shouldered spears to attack; when there were no incidents, they grasped plows to till, and the people did not suffer the toil of constant service. This is why there was no institution of military agricultural colonies. Coming down to the Spring and Autumn period, tyrannical rulers arose one after another and neglected the field boundaries. Duke Xuan 宣公…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
稅畝於其始成公作丘甲於其中哀公加田賦於其後而井田之法
始廢於是管仲變州兵為內政罷衞士業農桑兵不諳耒耜之
勤民不識干戈之具而兵農之制始分至於戰國之時李悝說
魏文侯作盡地力之數逐畝徵科而民始困矣迨至漢文帝從鼂
錯之請遣卒耕輪臺而屯田之法始立宣帝從桑弘羊之議而屯
田之制盛行當時先零諸羌寇叛於是命趙充國以擊之充國上
屯田之策請擊虜以殄滅為期願罷騎兵留步兵屯田大獲其利
坐困西羌遂致單于慕義稽首稱藩此充國屯田於金城者也唐
玄帝開元之初當府兵之制旣壞之時口分世業已廢之日遂置屯
===
隸司農之官其給牛之數硬地則一頃二十畝而配一牛軟地一頃五
十畝而配一牛是其為富國足民之計亦可觀也先儒謂其可以
周時下農夫為率一夫所耕可食五人則其制度之詳亦可謂得
時之宜也大抵自昔屯田之法立有屯於中國以甦民力者有田於
邊郡以省漕費者有田於塞外以禦戎虜者有田於要地以傾敵
國者然田於內地者為力易田於邊遠者為功難漢之屯田以民
斯可以免軍旅坐食之費唐之屯田以兵亦可以足國家儲備之
資其餘或兵或民盖不一也方今
聖人承重熙累洽之運屯田之法一遵
punctuated: 稅畝於其始，成公作丘甲於其中，哀公加田賦於其後，而井田之法始廢。於是管仲變州兵為內政，罷衞士業農桑，兵不諳耒耜之勤，民不識干戈之具，而兵農之制始分。至於戰國之時，李悝說魏文侯作盡地力之數，逐畝徵科，而民始困矣。迨至漢文帝從鼂錯之請，遣卒耕輪臺，而屯田之法始立。宣帝從桑弘羊之議，而屯田之制盛行。當時先零諸羌寇叛，於是命趙充國以擊之。充國上屯田之策，請擊虜以殄滅為期，願罷騎兵，留步兵屯田。大獲其利，坐困西羌，遂致單于慕義，稽首稱藩，此充國屯田於金城者也。唐玄帝開元之初，當府兵之制旣壞之時，口分世業已廢之日，遂置屯隸司農之官。其給牛之數，硬地則一頃二十畝而配一牛，軟地一頃五十畝而配一牛，是其為富國足民之計亦可觀也。先儒謂其可以周時下農夫為率，一夫所耕可食五人，則其制度之詳亦可謂得時之宜也。大抵自昔屯田之法立，有屯於中國以甦民力者，有田於邊郡以省漕費者，有田於塞外以禦戎虜者，有田於要地以傾敵國者。然田於內地者為力易，田於邊遠者為功難。漢之屯田以民，斯可以免軍旅坐食之費；唐之屯田以兵，亦可以足國家儲備之資，其餘或兵或民，盖不一也。方今聖人承重熙累洽之運，屯田之法一遵…
translation_en: … first taxed the fields by the mu at the beginning, Duke Cheng instituted the military levy by the qiu in the middle, and Duke Ai increased the land tax afterward, whereupon the well-field system was first abolished. Consequently, Guan Zhong 管仲 transformed the district soldiery through his internal administration and stopped guardsmen from engaging in farming and sericulture; soldiers no longer knew the toil of the plowshare, the common people no longer recognized the implements of war, and thus the institutions of soldiery and agriculture first separated. By the Warring States period, Li Kui 李悝 persuaded Marquis Wen of Wei 魏文侯 to formulate the method of exhausting the strength of the soil, levying taxes mu by mu, and the people first fell into distress. Coming down to the Han, Emperor Wen 漢文帝 followed the request of Chao Cuo 鼂錯 and sent soldiers to cultivate Luntai 輪臺 [?], and thus the system of state farms (tuntian) was first established. Emperor Xuan 宣帝 followed the counsel of Sang Hongyang 桑弘羊 [?], and the state-farm institution flourished. At that time the Xian 零 and other Qiang 羌 tribes raided and rebelled, whereupon Zhao Chongguo 趙充國 was ordered to attack them. Chongguo submitted a policy proposal on state farms, requesting that the attack on the caitiffs be set with their utter annihilation as the term, and asking to disband the cavalry while retaining the infantry to work state farms. Great benefit was reaped from this, effortlessly wearing down the Western Qiang, and eventually causing the Chanyu 單于 to admire righteousness, bow his head to the ground, and declare himself a vassal; such was Chongguo's establishment of state farms at Jincheng 金城. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan 開元 era of Emperor Xuan [Xuanzong] of the Tang 唐玄帝, at a time when the garrison militia (fubing) system had already broken down and the personal-share and hereditary-land allotments had already fallen into disuse, state farms were accordingly established and placed under the officials of the Court of the National Granaries (Sinong). As for the number of oxen allotted, on hard soil one ox was assigned to every one qing and twenty mu, while on soft soil one ox was assigned to every one qing and fifty mu; as a plan for enriching the state and sufficing the people, this too was impressive. Former Confucians remarked that this could be compared to the standard of a lower-grade farmer in Zhou times, where what one man cultivated could feed five people; thus the thoroughness of its institutional design may also be said to have suited the needs of the age. On the whole, since antiquity when the methods of state farms were established, there have been those stationed in the central states to revive the strength of the people, those farmed in frontier commanderies to save on grain-transport costs, those farmed beyond the passes to ward off western and northern barbarians, and those farmed at strategic points to bring down enemy states. Yet farming in the interior requires easy effort, whereas farming in distant borderlands achieves results with difficulty. The state farms of the Han used commoners, which could avoid the expense of armies sitting idle and eating; the state farms of the Tang used soldiers, which could likewise suffice for the state's reserve supplies; as for the rest, whether using soldiers or commoners, they were not uniform. At present, the Sage Ruler inherits a fortune of accumulated peace and harmony, and the laws of the state farms wholly follow…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
聖祖之規或屯於中夏以寬民力或屯於邊地以省轉輸其足國裕民之
道視漢唐則有加焉噫盛哉故以是為對
第五問〔一名鄭建〕
同考試官進士方批〔文詞通暢考究明白講制作之本原辨音律之高下節節詳悉迥出人意表非平昔學問該博優於策場者不能會闈角勝予不多讓〕
考試官教諭邵批〔此策於律呂取義損益相生歴代制律之由本末兼該纖悉不遺操觚之際必心融意會如有源之水滔滔不竭非博學君子未易至此尤宜高薦〕
考試官前侍講余批〔場中之作於律呂之學鮮有精者或能僅答其一二多失之膚淺此篇其制度音律極為詳善有得於朱夫子蔡西山之旨深矣〕
===
論作樂者固莫先於審律呂審律呂者尤莫先於定黃鍾律
呂為音樂之本而黃鍾又為律呂之本也盖陽聲之動陽氣
之始断竹為管吹之而聲和候之而氣應均其長得九寸審其
圍得九分度量衡由是而受法十二律由兹而損益八十四調之
中最為純粹者也粵自黃帝命伶倫取竹於嶰谷断而吹
之以應鳳之鳴六陽為律六陰為呂所謂黃鍾宣養六氣九
德也太簇金奏陰賛出滯也姑洗清潔百物考神納賓也蕤
賓安靖神人獻酬交酢也夷則詠歌九則平民無貳也無射
宣布哲人令德示民軌儀也大呂助宣物也夾鍾出四隙之細也
punctuated:
聖祖之規，或屯於中夏以寬民力，或屯於邊地以省轉輸。其足國裕民之道，視漢、唐則有加焉。噫，盛哉！故以是為對。

第五問〔一名鄭建〕
同考試官進士方批〔文詞通暢，考究明白。講制作之本原，辨音律之高下，節節詳悉，迥出人意表。非平昔學問該博、優於策場者不能。會闈角勝，予不多讓。〕
考試官教諭邵批〔此策於律呂取義、損益相生、歴代制律之由，本末兼該，纖悉不遺。操觚之際，必心融意會，如有源之水滔滔不竭，非博學君子未易至此，尤宜高薦。〕
考試官前侍講余批〔場中之作，於律呂之學鮮有精者；或能僅答其一二，多失之膚淺。此篇其制度、音律極為詳善，有得於朱夫子、蔡西山之旨深矣。〕

論作樂者，固莫先於審律呂；審律呂者，尤莫先於定黃鍾。律呂為音樂之本，而黃鍾又為律呂之本也。盖陽聲之動，陽氣之始，断竹為管，吹之而聲和，候之而氣應。均其長得九寸，審其圍得九分，度量衡由是而受法，十二律由兹而損益，八十四調之中最為純粹者也。粵自黃帝命伶倫取竹於嶰谷，断而吹之，以應鳳之鳴，六陽為律，六陰為呂。所謂黃鍾，宣養六氣、九德也；太簇，金奏陰賛出滯也；姑洗，清潔百物，考神納賓也；蕤賓，安靖神人，獻酬交酢也；夷則，詠歌九則，平民無貳也；無射，宣布哲人令德，示民軌儀也。大呂，助宣物也；夾鍾，出四隙之細也；
translation_en:
… the regulations of the Sacred Ancestor (Hongwu Emperor), whether establishing state farms in the central heartland to relieve the strength of the people, or establishing them in frontier regions to reduce transport and supply costs. This way of enriching the state and bringing abundance to the people surpasses even that of the Han and Tang dynasties. Ah, how magnificent! Therefore, I offer this as my reply.

Fifth Policy Question [First-ranked: Zheng Jian 鄭建]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方: [The diction is fluent and the investigation is clear. In discussing the fundamental origins of musical creation and distinguishing the high and low pitches of the musical temperaments, every point is detailed and thorough, far surpassing expectations. None could achieve this who is not ordinarily of broad learning and excelled in the policy examination arena. When competing for victory in the Metropolitan Examination, I expect he will yield to few.]
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Shao 邵: [Regarding the meaning derived from the standard pitches (lülü), their mutual generation through subtraction and addition, and the origins of pitch-pipe fabrication across successive dynasties, this policy essay encompasses both root and branch, omitting not the slightest detail. When taking up the writing tablet, his mind and intent must have been thoroughly fused, pouring forth endlessly like water from a deep spring. No one who is not a gentleman of broad learning could easily reach this level; he especially deserves a high recommendation.]
Comment by Examiner and former Expositor-in-waiting Yu 余: [Among the compositions in the examination compound, few show mastery of the study of musical pitches; those who can answer just one or two points mostly fail by being superficial. This essay is extremely detailed and admirable in its treatment of the institutional systems and musical temperaments, having deeply grasped the teachings of Master Zhu (Zhu Xi 朱熹) and Cai Xishan (Cai Yuanding 蔡元定).]

In discussing the creation of music, nothing takes precedence over examining the Yang and Yin standard pitches (lülü); and in examining the standard pitches, nothing takes precedence over fixing the Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) pitch. The standard pitches are the foundation of music, and the Yellow Bell is in turn the foundation of the standard pitches. For it is the movement of the Yang sound and the beginning of the Yang vital energy (qi). One cuts bamboo to make a pipe; when blown, its sound is harmonious, and when used to observe the seasonal ether, the vital energy responds. Adjusting its length yields nine cun, and examining its circumference yields nine fen. Measures of length, capacity, and weight receive their standards from this, and the twelve pitches are generated by subtraction and addition from here; among the eighty-four modes, it is the purest of all. Ever since the Yellow Emperor ordered Ling Lun 伶倫 to take bamboo from Xie Valley (Xiegu 嶰谷), cutting and blowing it to correspond to the calls of the phoenix, the six Yang pitches have served as lü and the six Yin pitches as lü. What is called Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) is that which disseminates and nourishes the six qi and the nine virtues; Great Cluster (Taicu) is the metallic performance that assists the Yin in bringing forth what was stagnant; Maiden Washed (Guxi) cleanses and purifies the hundred things, accomplishing the rites for the spirits and welcoming guests; Luxuriant Guest (Ruibin) brings peace and tranquility to spirits and men through the mutual offering and returning of toasts; Equalizing Rule (Yize) chants the nine rules, pacifying the people so that they have no duplicity; Without Tire (Wuyi) proclaims the admirable virtue of wise men, showing the people standard models and deportment. Great吕 (Dalü) assists in manifesting things; Clasped Bell (Jiazhong) brings forth the minute things from the four crevices of the seasons; …

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
仲吕宣中氣也林鍾和展百事任忠恪也南吕賛陽秀也應
鍾均利器用俾應復也通典云黃者土之色也鍾者聚也陽氣
潜動於黃泉聚養萬物故曰黃鍾太者大也簇者臻也正
月萬物簇地而出故曰太簇姑之言枯也洗者洗濯之義也三
月時物改柯易葉故曰姑洗蕤者葳蕤垂下之義賓者敬
也五月陽下降陰始起共相賓敬故曰蕤賓夷平也則法也七月
時物平均結實皆有法則故曰夷則至於佐陽聚物曰夾鍾應
陽積聚為應鍾陽無終極曰無射陰任陽功曰南吕物茂成
林曰林鍾其子母之相生夫婦之相配莫匪自然而然一毫之智
===
力不與也以其相生之法而論之陽律生陰吕曰下生三分長而損
一陰吕生陽律曰上生三分〔長〕而益一黃鍾下生林鍾、、上生太簇
太簇下生南吕、、上生姑洗、、下生應鍾、、上生蕤賓、、
重上生大吕、、下生夷則、、上生夾鍾、、下生無射、、上
生仲吕皆隔八律而左旋盖以黃鍾為宫太簇為商姑洗為
角林鍾為徴南吕為羽五音有清濁長短必和之以十二律
乃能成文而不亂此所謂旋相為宫也至漢京房論相生之
法以上生下皆三生以下生上皆三生四黃鍾下生林鍾、、上生
太簇陽下生陰、上生陽終於中吕十二律畢矣中吕上生執始
punctuated:
仲吕，宣中氣也；林鍾，和展百事，任忠恪也；南吕，賛陽秀也；應鍾，均利器用，俾應復也。《通典》云：黃者，土之色也；鍾者，聚也。陽氣潜動於黃泉，聚養萬物，故曰黃鍾。太者，大也；簇者，臻也。正月萬物簇地而出，故曰太簇。姑之言枯也，洗者洗濯之義也。三月時物改柯易葉，故曰姑洗。蕤者，葳蕤垂下之義；賓者，敬也。五月陽下降，陰始起，共相賓敬，故曰蕤賓。夷，平也；則，法也。七月時物平均結實，皆有法則，故曰夷則。至於佐陽聚物曰夾鍾，應陽積聚為應鍾，陽無終極曰無射，陰任陽功曰南吕，物茂成林曰林鍾。其子母之相生、夫婦之相配，莫匪自然而然，一毫之智力不與也。
以其相生之法而論之：陽律生陰吕曰下生，三分長而損一；陰吕生陽律曰上生，三分〔長〕而益一。黃鍾下生林鍾，、、上生太簇，太簇下生南吕，、、上生姑洗，、、下生應鍾，、、上生蕤賓，、、重上生大吕，、、下生夷則，、、上生夾鍾，、、下生無射，、、上生仲吕，皆隔八律而左旋。盖以黃鍾為宫，太簇為商，姑洗為角，林鍾為徴，南吕為羽，五音有清濁長短，必和之以十二律，乃能成文而不亂，此所謂旋相為宫也。至漢京房論相生之法，以上生下皆三生，以下生上皆三生四。黃鍾下生林鍾，、、上生太簇，陽下生陰，、上生陽，終於中吕，十二律畢矣。中吕上生執始，
translation_en:
… Zhonglü propagates the central qi; Linzhong harmoniously extends the hundred affairs and fosters loyalty and reverence; Nanlü assists the flourishing of yang; and Yingzhong equalizes and benefits implements and utilities, causing them to respond and return. The Comprehensive Statutes (Tongdian) states: "Yellow (huang) is the color of earth; bell (zhong) means to gather. Yang qi stirs latently in the Yellow Springs, gathering and nourishing the myriad things; therefore it is called Huangzhong. Tai means great; cu means to arrive in multitude. In the first month, the myriad things crowd forth from the earth; therefore it is called Taicu. Gu means withered (ku); xian means to wash clean. In the third month, seasonal things change their branches and renew their leaves; therefore it is called Guxian. Rui means luxuriant and drooping down; bin means respect. In the fifth month, yang descends and yin begins to rise, treating each other as respected guests; therefore it is called Ruibin. Yi means level; ze means rule. In the seventh month, seasonal things evenly bear fruit, all following rules and laws; therefore it is called Yize." As for assisting yang in gathering things, it is called Jiazhong; responding to yang by accumulating and gathering is Yingzhong; yang having no end or limit is called Wuyi; yin carrying on the work of yang is called Nanlü; and things flourishing to form a forest is called Linzhong. This mutual generation of mother and child, and mutual pairing of husband and wife, are nothing other than spontaneously so by nature; not a hair's breadth of human intelligence or effort participates in it.

Discussing this in terms of the method of their mutual generation: when a yang pitch-pipe generates a yin pitch-pipe, it is called "downward generation" (xiasheng), dividing the length into three parts and subtracting one; when a yin pitch-pipe generates a yang pitch-pipe, it is called "upward generation" (shangsheng), dividing the [length] into three parts and adding one. Huangzhong generates Linzhong downward; Linzhong generates Taicu upward; Taicu generates Nanlü downward; Nanlü generates Guxian upward; Guxian generates Yingzhong downward; Yingzhong generates Ruibin upward; Ruibin again generates Dalü upward; Dalü generates Yize downward; Yize generates Jiazhong upward; Jiazhong generates Wuyi downward; and Wuyi generates Zhonglü upward—all at intervals of eight pitch-pipes, rotating to the left. For with Huangzhong as gong, Taicu as shang, Guxian as jue, Linzhong as zhi, and Nanlü as yu, the five tones have their clear and turbid, long and short qualities, which must be harmonized by means of the twelve pitch-pipes before they can form patterned music without disorder; this is what is called "rotating to serve successively as the gong tonic" (xuan xiang wei gong). Coming to the Han dynasty, Jing Fang Jing Fang 京房 discussed the method of mutual generation: generating downward from above is in all cases three generating [two] [?], and generating upward from below is in all cases three generating four. Huangzhong generates Linzhong downward, and Linzhong generates Taicu upward; yang generates yin downward, and yin generates yang upward, ending at Zhonglü, whereupon the twelve pitch-pipes are complete. Zhonglü generates Zhishi upward…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
執始下生去滅上下相生終於南事而六十律畢矣十二律之變
於六十猶八卦之變於六十四卦也五音之中宮為君商為臣角
為民徵為事羽為物臣有常職民有常業物有常形君總
萬務不可執於一事事通萬物不可滯於一隅此二聲所以有變也
蔡氏謂宮與商商與角徵與羽皆近隔一律角與徵羽與宮獨遠
隔二律隔一律則聲近而和隔二律則聲遠而不和故近宮收一
聲少高於宮謂之變宮近徵收一聲比徵稍下謂之變徵所以濟
五聲之不及也十二律之相生於六十律備矣後世以變宮變徵參
為八十四調非古人之意也律呂之中其用全律則為正聲用半
===
律則為子聲蓋樂聲最忌相凌如黃鍾為宮其律最長以
次諸律用正聲固順若以他律為宮則長短必有相凌故折半用
子聲然後高下得以相依清濁得以相間而樂無不和矣宋初
命王朴竇儼所定周樂繼以和峴所定則下王朴一律李照所
定則下王朴三律然五音之中宮為君也王朴則虛其中而不用
而和李則用之是虛宮不若用宮之正也議者謂朴之所知者音
照之所知者器音也器也果可岐而二歟是數子之論未免局於
器數之末迨夫西山蔡季通律呂新書之作則本原器數咸
備矣朱子謂其深沉而縝密明白而通暢不為牽合附會之
punctuated: 執始下生去滅，上下相生，終於南事，而六十律畢矣。十二律之變於六十，猶八卦之變於六十四卦也。五音之中，宮為君，商為臣，角為民，徵為事，羽為物。臣有常職，民有常業，物有常形；君總萬務，不可執於一事，事通萬物，不可滯於一隅，此二聲所以有變也。蔡氏謂宮與商、商與角、徵與羽，皆近隔一律；角與徵、羽與宮，獨遠隔二律。隔一律則聲近而和，隔二律則聲遠而不和。故近宮收一聲，少高於宮，謂之變宮；近徵收一聲，比徵稍下，謂之變徵，所以濟五聲之不及也。十二律之相生，於六十律備矣。後世以變宮、變徵參為八十四調，非古人之意也。律呂之中，其用全律則為正聲，用半律則為子聲。蓋樂聲最忌相凌，如黃鍾為宮，其律最長，以次諸律用正聲固順；若以他律為宮，則長短必有相凌，故折半用子聲，然後高下得以相依，清濁得以相間，而樂無不和矣。宋初，命王朴、竇儼所定周樂，繼以和峴所定，則下王朴一律；李照所定，則下王朴三律。然五音之中，宮為君也，王朴則虛其中而不用，而和、李則用之，是虛宮不若用宮之正也。議者謂朴之所知者音，照之所知者器。音也，器也，果可岐而二歟？是數子之論，未免局於器數之末。迨夫西山蔡季通《律呂新書》之作，則本原器數咸備矣。朱子謂其深沉而縝密，明白而通暢，不為牽合附會之
translation_en:
… Zhishi generates Qumie downward; through alternating upward and downward generation, the cycle ends at Nanshi, and thus the sixty pitch-pipes are completed. The transformation of the twelve pitch-pipes into sixty is just like the transformation of the eight trigrams into the sixty-four hexagrams.

Among the five tones, Gong represents the ruler, Shang the minister, Jue the people, Zhi affairs, and Yu things. Ministers have constant duties, the people have constant occupations, and things have constant forms; the ruler, however, oversees myriad affairs and cannot cling to a single matter, while affairs pervade myriad things and cannot be confined to a single corner. This is why these two tones have altered forms. Master Cai [Cai Yuanding 蔡元定] said that between Gong and Shang, Shang and Jue, and Zhi and Yu, the intervals are all close, separated by one pitch-pipe; only between Jue and Zhi, and between Yu and Gong, are the intervals distant, separated by two pitch-pipes. When separated by one pitch-pipe, the sounds are close and harmonious; when separated by two pitch-pipes, the sounds are distant and unharmonious. Therefore, a sound is taken near Gong, slightly higher than Gong, which is called Altered Gong (biangong); a sound is taken near Zhi, slightly lower than Zhi, which is called Altered Zhi (bianzhi). These serve to remedy where the five tones fall short. The mutual generation of the twelve pitch-pipes is fully realized in the sixty pitch-pipes. When later ages incorporated Altered Gong and Altered Zhi to form eighty-four modes, this was not the intention of the ancients.

Among the yang and yin pitch-pipes (lülü), using the full length of a pipe produces the standard sound (zhengsheng), whereas using half the length of a pipe produces the衍生/subsidiary sound (zisheng). This is because musical sounds most shun encroaching upon one another. For instance, when Huangzhong serves as Gong, its pipe is the longest, so using the standard sounds for the subsequent pipes in order is naturally smooth. However, if another pitch-pipe serves as Gong, their lengths will inevitably encroach upon one another. Therefore, one halves the length to use the subsidiary sound; only then can high and low rely upon each other, clear and turbid alternate with each other, and the music be completely harmonious.

At the beginning of the Song dynasty, orders were given to adopt the Zhou music determined by Wang Pu 王朴 and Dou Yan 竇儼. Subsequently, what He Xian 和峴 determined was one pitch-pipe lower than Wang Pu's, and what Li Zhao 李照 determined was three pitch-pipes lower than Wang Pu's. Yet among the five tones, Gong represents the ruler; Wang Pu left it vacant in the middle and did not use it, whereas He and Li used it—leaving Gong vacant is not as proper as using Gong. Commentators said that what Pu understood was sound, while what Zhao understood was instruments. Sound and instruments—can they truly be bifurcated into two? The theories of these several masters could not avoid being confined to the trivialities of instruments and numbers. When it came to the composition of the New Treatise on the Pitch-Pipes (Lülü xinshu) by Cai Jitong 蔡季通 [Cai Yuanding] of Xishan, both fundamental principles and instruments and numbers were completely provided for. Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] said that it was profound and meticulous, clear and fluent, without making forced or strained…

title: 宣德元年福建鄉試錄
text:
說其言雖出於世之所未講而實無一不本於古人已試之成法也
觀其黃鍾圍徑之數則漢斛之積分可考寸以九分為法則
淮南太史小司馬之說可推五聲二變之數變律半聲之例則
杜氏之通典可見至於先求聲氣之原而因律以生尺尤所
卓然者而亦雜見於两漢志蔡邕之說焉由是觀之樂律之用
廣矣大矣以之候氣則如太史公所謂聞聲而知勝負班志所
謂合氣而生風以之制曆則劉歆所謂黃鍾為天統林鍾為地
統太簇為人統以之制器則九十黍為黃鍾之長千二百黍
為黃鍾之廣樂聲之高下由此而和度之長短由此而定量之
===
多少由此而審衡之輕重由此而平此所謂天地間何莫而非
律而律又何往而不本於黃鍾哉管見區區惟執事其教之
punctuated: 說，其言雖出於世之所未講，而實無一不本於古人已試之成法也。觀其黃鍾圍徑之數，則漢斛之積分可考；寸以九分為法，則淮南、太史、小司馬之說可推；五聲、二變之數，變律、半聲之例，則杜氏之《通典》可見；至於先求聲氣之原，而因律以生尺，尤所卓然者，而亦雜見於两漢志、蔡邕之說焉。由是觀之，樂律之用，廣矣大矣！以之候氣，則如太史公所謂「聞聲而知勝負」，班志所謂「合氣而生風」；以之制曆，則劉歆所謂「黃鍾為天統，林鍾為地統，太簇為人統」；以之制器，則九十黍為黃鍾之長，千二百黍為黃鍾之廣。樂聲之高下由此而和，度之長短由此而定，量之多少由此而審，衡之輕重由此而平。此所謂天地間何莫而非律，而律又何往而不本於黃鍾哉！管見區區，惟執事其教之。
translation_en: … theories. Although his words go beyond what the world had previously discussed, in truth there is not a single point that is not rooted in the established methods already tested by the ancients. If we examine his figures for the circumference and diameter of the Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) pitch-pipe, the cumulative fractions of the Han-dynasty standard dry measure (hu) can be verified; for his rule of dividing the inch into nine parts, the accounts of the Prince of Huainan (Liu An 劉安), the Grand Scribe (Sima Qian 司馬遷), and the Junior Sima (Sima Zhen 司馬貞) can be deduced; for the numbers of the five tones and two altered tones, and the rules of altered pitch-pipes and half-tones, they can be seen in Du You's 杜佑 Comprehensive Statutes (Tongdian 通典); and as for first seeking the origin of sound and qi and deriving the foot-measure from the pitch-pipe—which is especially outstanding—this too appears scattered across the treatises of the two Han histories and the writings of Cai Yong 蔡邕. Viewed from this perspective, the applications of musical pitch-standards are vast and great indeed! When used to observe the seasonal qi, it is as the Grand Scribe said, "hearing the sound, one knows victory or defeat," and as Ban Gu's 班固 treatise said, "harmonizing the qi to generate the winds"; when used to construct the calendar, it is as Liu Xin 劉歆 said, "the Yellow Bell (Huangzhong) is the Heaven-triad, the Forest Bell (Linzhong) is the Earth-triad, and the Great Cluster (Taicu) is the Man-triad"; when used to fashion standard vessels, ninety millet grains make the length of the Yellow Bell, and twelve hundred millet grains make the capacity of the Yellow Bell. Through this, the high and low of musical sounds are harmonized, the long and short of linear measures are fixed, the much and little of capacities are ascertained, and the heavy and light of weights are balanced. This is what is meant by saying: between Heaven and Earth, what is not governed by pitch-standards, and where do the pitch-standards ever go without being rooted in the Yellow Bell! Such is my humble, narrow view; I pray only that Your Excellency will instruct me.
